articles_hidden.title: Toward Reproducible Research with LLMs: Guidance for Documentation, Reporting, and Transparency
articles_hidden.authors: Ryan Watkins; Vicky W. Lee
articles_hidden.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into scientific research workflows across many disciplines, creating new opportunities for literature review, research design, data analysis, simulation, coding, automation, and other forms of scientific inquiry. Their growing use also creates challenges for transparency and reproducibility, particularly because LLM outputs are nondeterministic, model capabilities change rapidly, and research workflows may involve multiple models, agents, tools, and computational environments. This guide proposes a framework and checklist for systematically documenting and reporting the use of LLMs as scientific instruments. Grounded in the principle that documentation requirements should be proportional to the methodological role of the LLM and its potential impact on research findings, the framework distinguishes among varying levels of human agency, methodological impact, and corresponding documentation needs. We provide guidance for determining what aspects of a LLM-enabled research workflow should be documented, how thoroughly they should be reported, and how those requirements change as the methodological role of AI increases. We further distinguish between documentation collected throughout the research process and information reported in manuscripts and supplementary materials. Rather than treating reproducibility as requiring identical LLM outputs, we emphasize sufficient methodological transparency to enable others to understand, evaluate, and, where desirable and feasible, reproduce or systematically test the research workflow and its results. The proposed guidance is intended to support researchers, reviewers, editors, and disciplinary communities as norms for transparent and reproducible LLM use continue to evolve.

articles.title: Can Accurate Information Change Identity-Linked Political Beliefs? Evidence From Republicans’ Attitudes Towards Election Integrity
articles.authors: Michael Nicholas Stagnaro; Eran Amsalem; Andrea B Mullin; Hause Lin; Adam J. Berinsky; David Gertler Rand
articles.abstract: Psychological research suggests that identity shapes beliefs and impedes updating in response to contrary evidence. A prominent example is many Republicans’ persistence in believing that the 2020 election was stolen. We test whether credible factual information can shift Republicans' beliefs about election integrity. Immediately before the 2024 presidential election, we randomly assigned 861 conservative Republicans to an intensive informational intervention or a control matched with civic content. The intervention presented extensive, accurate, politically balanced evidence and encouraged sustained engagement. Treated participants reported stronger beliefs in US election integrity overall, greater confidence in the 2020 election, and more positive expectations for the 2024 election (.5 < ds < .8), including those who started lower in electoral confidence (.5 < ds < .97). Effects were still detectable two weeks later, after Trump’s victory. Though learning was incentivized, belief reporting was not – showing that when attended to, credible balanced evidence can change minds.

articles.title: Toward a Multidimensional Operationalization of Feminist Identity: Associations with Sexism and Weight Bias
articles.authors: Daemon St-James; Annie Raymond; Annie Duchesne; Benoit Brisson
articles.abstract: Feminist identity is typically operationalized through self-identification and endorsement of select beliefs, leaving movement affiliation and competing ideologies, such as meritocracy and social dominance orientation, unaccounted for. This study explored whether a multidimensional operationalization of feminist identity reveals distinct profiles and whether these profiles relate differently to discriminatory attitudes associated with feminism: ambivalent sexism and weight bias. Adults in Quebec (N = 917; 90% women) completed the Anti-Fat Attitudes Scale, the Ambivalent Sexism Inventory, the Perceptions of Meritocracy Inventory, the Short Social Dominance Orientation Scale, a bespoke feminist movement affiliation questionnaire, and the Feminist Belief and Behavior measure. Cluster analysis yielded six profiles: four feminist-identifying profiles distinguished by movement affiliation (liberal, radical, intersectional, postmodern) and two non-identifying profiles, including Affiliated Non-Labelers, who endorsed feminist beliefs and affiliated with a feminist movement while rejecting the feminist label. They reported meritocratic and dominance-oriented scores comparable to Non-Feminists. Profiles differed on hostile sexism, benevolent sexism, and weight controllability. Compared with Zucker's (2004) two-dimensional typology, the profiles offered no clear incremental predictive value but described configurations not represented by conventional typology. Findings suggest that the combination of feminist identities a person holds alongside their beliefs shapes how feminist identity relates to discriminatory attitudes.

articles.title: Differential Effects of Types of Momentary Social Support on Mood and Anxiety in Patients with Depression
articles.authors: Annalena Jachnik; Martin Weiß; Julian Gutzeit; Fabian Rothbauer; Sebastian Walther; Grit Hein
articles.abstract:
Background: Social support is a multidimensional construct that includes emotional, esteem, and informational support, as well as instrumental support, referring to tangible assistance, and negative forms of support. While patients experience these types of support in their daily social interactions, the specific effects of momentary received support types on psychopathology remain understudied. Therefore, this study examined the effects of multiple types of social support on depressive mood and state social anxiety using high frequency Ecological Momentary Assessment. 
Methods: Data was collected from patients diagnosed with affective disorders and current moderate to severe depression, as well as from control participants (N = 68) using smartphone-based assessments over five consecutive days. Specifically, participants reported on social interaction characteristics, the type of received support, as well as their mood and anxiety levels based on six survey prompts per day. 
Results: Results indicated that receiving emotional support was associated with lower depressive mood, while esteem support was associated with lower depressive mood and state social anxiety. In contrast, informational support showed opposite effects. 
Conclusions: These findings underscore the potential of social support in alleviating the core symptoms of clinical depression; with specific types of support being particularly beneficial. Thus, targeted application of social support types hold promise for interventions in depression.

articles.title: Displayed judgment certainty reorganizes source selection in self-formed networks
articles.authors: Gaël Carniel; Frédéric Moisan; Alain Barrat; Jean-Claude Dreher
articles.abstract: Collective intelligence in self-formed networks depends on which judgments people choose to observe, as well as on how they integrate those judgments. We tested whether displaying judgment certainty reorganizes source selection and improves subsequent accuracy. Across eight online sessions, 273 participants evaluated 14 true and false news headlines, formed costly directed observation networks, and revised their beliefs over five updates. During network formation, we manipulated the visibility of certainty, defined by the extremity of each source's private probability judgment, while belief direction and source accuracy remained hidden. Displaying certainty produced denser networks and redirected links toward more certain sources; current popularity also predicted selection. Visibility increased exposure to highly certain but incorrect judgments, without a clear improvement in the relative accuracy of selected sources. Accuracy increased across repeated judgments, but certainty visibility did not detectably increase this improvement and reduced reconstructed net scores under the task's payoff structure. Observations with selected sources showed greater improvement than those without, and improvement was associated with selected sources' initial accuracy. Belief revisions moved toward selected sources and decreased with participants' own certainty. Among six compact predictive models, certainty-reinforcing DeGroot provided the best penalized and aggregate held-out prediction, although it did not capture the large first update. These findings distinguish a cue's ability to attract attention from its ability to identify useful information: displayed certainty can reorganize costly information acquisition without a detectable average accuracy benefit.

articles.title: Advancing Global Social Science through Cross-Societal Online Behavioral Economic Games (CoBEx): Lessons Learned and A Practical Guide
articles.authors: Shuxian Jin; Vanessa Christina Clemens; Laura Carlotta Hoenig; Carsten De Dreu; Angela Rachael Dorrough; Catherine Molho; Marina Orifici; Angelo Romano; Shaul Shalvi; Ayse K. Uskul
articles.abstract: Understanding human behavior across diverse cultural settings is essential for advancing theories that address pressing global social challenges. Recent advances, which use an innovative methodology—cross-societal online behavioral economic games (CoBEx)—have revealed key insights into cross-cultural differences and similarities in the mechanisms and functions of human behavior. To foster this emerging field, we discuss the key successes and lessons learned from ten years of experience in designing and conducting CoBEx studies. We illustrate the theoretical and methodological benefits of CoBEx, and offer practical recommendations on key design considerations, study materials preparation, ethics and funding, as well as analysis, interpretation, and dissemination processes. This paper aims to equip researchers around the globe with the necessary tools to conduct methodologically rigorous and culturally informed CoBEx studies, ultimately advancing the field of psychological science and beyond.

articles.title: Predicting Memberships from Memory.
articles.authors: Luigi Grisoni
articles.abstract: Neural representations are commonly described as mappings between target variables and patterns of neural activity. A central challenge is to specify not only what the brain represents, but how representational content is organised and constrained across contexts. Here, the concept of Representation of Membership (RoM) is proposed as a perspective on representational organisation. RoM assumes that cognitive representations are shaped by the elements they contain and by the membership structures linking those elements to broader semantic, functional, and contextual domains. The same element may belong to multiple structures and play different roles within them, with particular memberships becoming relevant according to context, task demands, or prior knowledge. Within RoM, prediction reflects the dynamic activation, weighting, and refinement of learned membership structures, constraining which continuations, features, interpretations, or responses become more likely. RoM thus links neural representation, memory, flexibility, and prediction through the context-sensitive organisation and updating of membership structures.

articles.title: From Psychological States to Self-Reports: A New Perspective on Response Bias
articles.authors: Jess Grimmond; Scott Brown; Quentin Frederik Gronau; Guy Hawkins
articles.abstract:
Self-report measures are a cornerstone of psychological science, yet little attention has been
devoted to the processes through which internal experiences become observable responses. We
propose a theoretical account of self-report in which responses reflect two concurrent sources of
information: the latent states individuals seek to communicate and the response processes
governing how those states are expressed. We formalise this framework for Likert-type data using
the Latent State and Response Style (LASARS) model, an ordinal-threshold approach that
separates latent state expression from response style processes. Across applications to novel and
previously published data, we show that response styles are stable across time and survey
instruments, while individuals retain the capacity to modify their response style without changing
the latent states they wish to express. We further demonstrate a novel prediction of the
framework: that response style information obtained in one context can be used to reduce
response style confounding in another. Together, these findings support a view of self-report as a
communicative decision process rather than a direct reflection of latent states. More broadly, they
suggest that understanding psychological measurement requires explaining not only what people
experience, but also how they choose to express those experiences

articles.title: A Megastudy of Behavioral Interventions to Increase Voter Registration Ahead of the 2024 U.S. Presidential Election
articles.authors: Katherine Anne Mason; Kayley Okst; Don Green; Robb Willer; James Druckman; Jan G. Voelkel; Yash Patel; Claire Robertson; Wooyoung Choi; Jasmine Sanchez
articles.abstract: In the United States, in nearly all cases, one must register in order to vote—yet, a substantial portion of the eligible electorate remains unregistered. Despite this, relatively little is known about how to increase the likelihood that a voter registers. Here, we tested the impact of 10 expert-crowdsourced, theoretically-based psychological interventions on a sample of eligible, yet unregistered, U.S. voters ahead of the 2024 presidential election (N = 12,896). Eight of the interventions increased intentions to vote, and five led individuals to click on the voter registration website. Escalating Commitment, which sequentially employed several social pressure strategies, was the strongest intervention across these outcomes. However, none of the interventions had a significant effect on actual voter registration or voter turnout. The results highlight a substantial disconnect between voters’ intentions and their ultimate behaviors. We discuss potential structural and psychological barriers that undermine the translation of intent into action.

articles.title: Weak Links between Speech Perception and Speech Production at the Subphonemic Level
articles.authors: Brian W. L. Wong; Arthur G. Samuel; Efthymia C Kapnoula
articles.abstract: Recent research has shown individual differences in gradiency, defined as sensitivity to fine-grained acoustic differences at the subphonemic level. Consistency also varies, with some listeners providing more stable responses than others to repeated presentations of the same stimuli. However, it remains unclear whether gradiency and consistency are linked between perception and production. Across two experiments, 160 Spanish speakers completed a Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) task measuring perceptual gradiency and consistency along a Spanish /ba/–/pa/ continuum manipulated in 7–8 ms steps of voice onset time (VOT). The same participants also performed an explicit imitation task using the same stimuli. Results revealed only weak relationships between perceptual gradiency and imitation accuracy, as well as between perceptual consistency and imitation consistency, even after accounting for other factors related to speech perception and imitation. These findings suggest that models proposing strong perception–production coupling may not extend to the subphonemic level.

articles.title: From Population–Case Mismatch to Cumulative Homogenisation in AI-Assisted Cognition
articles.authors: Fangxing Bai
articles.abstract: A growing literature reports homogenisation under generative AI assistance and offers diverse explanations, yet a unified account grounded in AI’s statistical foundations remains underdeveloped. Through a parallel thought experiment, this Perspective derives how population–case mismatch creates differences between model-based and independent human trajectories, and how AI intervention can turn these differences into cumulative homogenisation. The degree and rate of homogenisation vary with the stage of intervention. The same mechanism also explains why AI can support scientific research under conditions that limit mismatch and support independent judgement.

articles.title: Mapping Behavioural and Psychological Factors Associated with Engagement in Online Activism: A Critical Scoping Review
articles.authors: Benjamin Gibson; Jekaterina Schneider; Mark J. Forshaw
articles.abstract: Online activism can be a powerful means of supporting social and political engagement. However, there are genuine concerns that online behaviours do not translate into social and political action, while nascent research suggests that online activism may affect well-being and feelings of identity more negatively compared to traditional (i.e., in-person) forms of activism. This scoping review attempted to map out the evidence so that the reader may better understand the psychological and behavioural factors associated with engagement in online activism. A search of academic databases and registers identified 24 articles comprising 28 studies and examined various forms of online activism including hashtag campaigns, online petitions, and social media engagement. Online engagement was shown to support a range of (further) online and offline activist behaviours, to foster collective identities, and to provide psychological benefits such as increased self-efficacy and feelings of empowerment (which in turn encouraged further political action). However, contextual and individual factors likely influence both behaviours and opportunities for psychological benefits. This review highlights the blurred boundaries between online and offline activism, while evidencing that even “passive” digital engagement may serve as a gateway to broader civic participation.

articles.title: “Who Will Marry a Mad Doctor?”: A Qualitative Study of Associative Stigma Among Mental Health Professionals in India
articles.authors: Deepti Dilip Moar; Rajat Kanti Mitra; Sunil Mittal
articles.abstract: Mental health professionals (MHPs) can experience stigma through their professional association with mental illness and mental healthcare. Existing studies have often focused on particular professions, service populations, or specific aspects of associative stigma, making it difficult to identify recurring patterns across professions and beyond the workplace. This study explored associative stigma among MHPs in India across professional, family, and wider social contexts. Semi-structured interviews with 22 MHPs, including psychiatrists, clinical psychologists, counsellors, psychiatric social workers, and psychiatric nurses, were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis within a constructivist framework. Eight themes were developed, spanning misconceptions about MHP roles and abilities, mistrust of expertise and motives, concerns about how mental health work might affect them, devaluation of mental health work, exclusion involving social distancing and concealment, role expectations extending beyond work, ambivalent responses in which admiration or reliance coexisted with misunderstanding, avoidance, or devaluation, and differences in professional standing. Across the analysis, experiences that might otherwise appear separate were connected by recurring meanings attached to mental illness and mental healthcare. The study broadens understanding of the social and professional reach of stigma surrounding mental illness. Through professional association, these meanings can shape how MHPs, their expertise, and mental health work are understood and valued.

articles.title: When the Same Leader Helps and Harms: Inconsistent Leadership Behavior in Team Meetings
articles.authors: Amelie Verena Güntner; Kai N. Klasmeier; Catrin Millhoff; Nora Gosch; Simone Kauffeld
articles.abstract:
Purpose: The same leader often displays constructive and destructive behaviors at once, a
phenomenon known as inconsistent leadership. Inconsistency has been linked to negative
follower outcomes, yet it has almost exclusively been studied as a follower perception. This
study examines inconsistent leadership as enacted behavior, asking how and under what
conditions the co-occurrence of instrumental and destructive leadership shapes team behavior in
meetings.
Design/methodology/approach: Using a multilevel moderated mediation model, we tested our
model on 30 videotaped team meetings (5,430 coded behaviors), rating leaders' instrumental and
destructive behavior and coding leaders' action planning and team members' conflict-related
communication.
Findings: Instrumental leadership was associated with more action planning, which in turn
reduced conflict-related communication, but only when destructive leadership was low. When
leaders behaved destructively alongside instrumental leadership, this indirect effect disappeared.
Practical implications: Occasional destructive behavior can undo the benefits of otherwise
constructive leadership, so what matters for teams is not only what leaders do well but whether
they do it consistently. Organizations can address this through leadership development that helps
leaders recognize and reduce inconsistent behavior in meetings.
Originality/value: Inconsistency has almost always been studied as a follower perception. This
study extends its consequences beyond follower attitudes to observable team communication and
to the leader's own planning, showing that inconsistency also shapes the enacting leader. It offers
a behavioral, micro-level operationalization that complements existing perception-based
measures.

articles.title: Neural representations and adaptive states in human action control
articles.authors: Christian Beste
articles.abstract: Adaptive behaviour requires goals to remain effective while actions are revised when circumstances change. This chapter integrates a collaborative research programme with wider theories and findings on cognitive control, episodic memory, neural dynamics, and clinical variation. It develops a selective narrative synthesis centred on the content, stability, retrieval, and reconfiguration of perception–action representations. Established accounts of goal maintenance, conflict monitoring, proactive and reactive control, and the expected value of control provide complementary explanations of how control is recruited. Event coding and binding–retrieval frameworks specify the representations on which these adjustments operate. EEG decomposition and multivariate analyses help distinguish representational contents and their temporal organisation, while oscillatory and connectivity findings identify candidate processes for coordinating their use. Aperiodic activity offers a further perspective on task-dependent processing biases, but pharmacological and biophysical evidence limits its interpretation as a unique measure of excitation–inhibition balance or metacontrol. Intervention studies connect neural dynamics with neurochemical modulation, while demonstrating dependence on baseline state, experience, and the operation targeted. Developmental and clinical evidence reveals both shared constraints and dissociable routes to similar behavioural outcomes. The proposed integration links representational operations, neural coordination, and control policy through testable predictions. It retains distinctions between descriptive markers, computational explanations, causal influences, and clinical benefit. Progress depends on separating competing accounts experimentally, establishing measurement reliability, and testing generalisation across tasks, samples, and settings.

articles.title: Perceptions of Profit Motive: For-Profit Companies are Judged Less Favourably Than Non-Profits Even When the Societal Benefits of Profit-Seeking are Made Salient
articles.authors: Zuleykha Gasimova; Martin Harry Turpin; Alexander C. Walker; Jonathan Albert Fugelsang; Derek J. Koehler
articles.abstract: People tend to view profit-seeking businesses more negatively than otherwise equivalent non-profit businesses or organizations. This tendency puts people at risk of missing out on the potential societal benefit that can emerge when profit-seeking motivations are aligned with prosocial goals. When making judgments about firms and businesses, people may simply neglect the possibility that profit-seeking could result in gains for society. The current research finds that people’s attitudes are more ambivalent (as opposed to strictly negative) when they consider, in a broader sense, examples of how profit-seeking companies could positively or negatively affect society (e.g., consumer and employee welfare, technological advances, etc.). Study 1 (N = 101) showed that people are open to endorsing both general (pro-profit) statements about how profit-seeking businesses may produce socially beneficial outcomes and general (anti-profit) statements about how profit-seeking businesses may produce socially harmful outcomes. In Study 2 (N = 301), we examined whether exposure to such statements highlighting the potential positive (or negative) societal impacts of profit-seeking affected participant’s judgements of for- and non-profit firms. Exposure to pro-profit and anti-profit statements did not impact people’s judgments of profit-seeking businesses. Instead, people consistently exhibited a tendency to judge for-profit companies as having a less positive societal impact in comparison with their non-profit counterparts. This anti-profit bias persisted even among participants who had expressed agreement with general statements about the ways in which profit-seeking companies can deliver societal benefits.

articles.title: The Impact of Effectiveness of Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction (MBSR) on Mindfulness and Perceived Stress in Healthy Adults
articles.authors: Ampere A. Tseng
articles.abstract: This paper reviews and examines the effectiveness of Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction (MBSR) interventions in enhancing mindfulness and mitigating stress-related symptoms. Drawing on trial data from 13 selected studies involving 574 generally healthy adults, this research seeks to establish a robust correlation between heightened mindfulness and reduced perceived stress. We assessed mindfulness using the Mindful Attention Awareness Scale (MAAS) and measured stress reductions through self-reported questionnaires. Normalized effectiveness scores, calculated as percentages from pre-intervention baselines, enabled linear regression analyses. To ensure the integrity of our findings, we rigorously controlled for external influences by isolating MBSR as the exclusive intervention and MAAS as the sole mindfulness measurement. Aggregate data confirm positive outcomes: mindfulness improvements ranged from 3.77% to 26.80%, and stress reductions varied from 8.41% to 49.05%. Linear regression trendlines reveal a strong positive correlation between increased mindfulness and decreased perceived stress. This highlights the profound benefits of MBSR interventions in enhancing mental well-being and suggests their potential for widespread integration into mental health initiatives. Ultimately, this article not only underscores MBSR's role in promoting mental well-being but also offers a quantitative framework for predicting health outcomes based on mindfulness levels.

articles.title: Delayed Feedback Improves Learning in Individuals with Parkinson’s Disease
articles.authors: Kai Sucich; Christopher J. Cagna; Erica Weber; Ekaterina Dobryakova
articles.abstract:
Background: Learning and memory deficits are common in Parkinson’s Disease (PD). Effectively processing performance-related feedback is integral to learning but is often impaired in PD. Delaying feedback presentation by 6 seconds has been shown to circumvent these deficits during incremental learning tasks. The potential learning benefits of longer feedback delays, however, are unknown. The current study examined the effects of a 6-second delay and a 25-minute delay on learning during a declarative memory task in individuals with PD. 

Methods: Thirty participants with PD completed a verbal paired-associates task, during which they learned word pairs via trial-by-trial accuracy feedback presented immediately after making responses (No Delay; ND), after a 6-second delay (Short Delay; SD), and after a 25-minute delay (Long Delay; LD). Mixed effects models examined the influence of feedback timing condition on both final test performance and on improvement in performance between the learning and test phases. Exploratory hierarchical mixed models with neuropsychological tests examined potential individual difference predictors of delayed feedback learning.

Results: Both SD feedback and LD feedback predicted significantly greater improvement in performance, compared to ND feedback. Better working memory performance on the Digit Span Backwards Test predicted significantly greater improvement from LD feedback.

Conclusion: Longer feedback delays improve learning during a paired associates word learning task in individuals with PD. Shorter delays previously demonstrated to benefit incremental learning may also benefit other forms of learning. Working memory capacity may be an important predictor of these learning benefits.

articles.title: Reading and writing anxiety in Finnish school children aged 9-15: Associations with gender, grade level, and reading competence
articles.authors: Rosa Salmela; Santeri Holopainen; Tomi Rautaoja; Emilia Nordenswan; Katarina Alanko; Pekka Räsänen
articles.abstract:
Purpose: This study examined the level of reading and writing anxiety in a cross-sectional sample of Finnish school children and the moderating roles of gender, grade level, and reading competence. 

Method: We used a reading and writing anxiety questionnaire (RWAQ) that consists of three factors: workload-related reading and writing anxiety, evaluation-related reading and writing anxiety, and social reading and writing anxiety. Linear regression modeling was used to analyze how gender, grade level, and reading competence moderate different dimensions of reading and writing anxiety. Participants were 9,723 Finnish-speaking children in grades 3–9, including 4,832 girls and 4,891 boys.

Results: Finnish school-age children showed relatively low reading and writing anxiety overall, but it increased with age (lowest in grades 3–5, highest in grades 7–9). This was especially evident in girls’ social and evaluation-related anxiety, while boys reported higher workload-related anxiety across grades. Lower reading competence was linked to higher reading and writing anxiety, but this effect varied by gender. Math anxiety and general anxiety were controlled in the models, and both anxiety types predicted reading and writing anxiety strongly.

Conclusion: Together the results suggest that workload-related reading and writing anxiety, evaluation-related reading and writing anxiety, and social reading and writing anxiety are distinct dimensions of reading and writing anxiety, and that future research could benefit from accounting that grade level, gender, and reading competence may influence these dimensions differently.

articles.title: A Browser-Based Remote Photoplethysmography Method for Live Heart Rate Estimation
articles.authors: Mariana Von Mohr; Manos Tsakiris; Gianluca Finotti
articles.abstract: Remote photoplethysmography (rPPG) enables contact-free heart-rate estimation from facial video, but most web-based implementations process recordings offline, limiting their use in real-time experimental applications. We developed and, to our knowledge, provide the first ECG validation of a live rPPG implementation embedded directly within Gorilla Experiment Builder, a widely used platform for online behavioural research. We validated the method in 27 participants against simultaneously recorded electrocardiography (ECG) across nine trial durations ranging from 10 to 50 s. rPPG-derived heart rate showed excellent agreement with ECG-derived heart rate, with a mean absolute error of 1.48 bpm, a root mean square error of 2.19 bpm, and an ICC(A,1) of .960. Mean bias was small (0.40 bpm), with repeated-measures 95% limits of agreement from -3.85 to 4.66 bpm, and heart-rate error did not differ significantly by trial durations. These findings support the feasibility of live rPPG within a browser-based experimental platform for physiological feedback and adaptive online experiments without requiring webcam videos to be stored or processed offline.

articles.title: The broken brain? Prevalence and consequences of brain framing of mental disorders
articles.authors: Olha Guley; Sanil Shashank Pandhare; Elena Pasquinelli; Daniel Nettle
articles.abstract: Public discourse often frames mental disorders as brain disorders, yet little is known about how this framing shapes lay beliefs. We combined large-scale text analysis of 55,068 New York Times articles with one correlational study (N = 204) and four preregistered vignette experiments (total N = 2,445) to examine both the prevalence and consequences of “brain talk” about mental disorders. We find that brain framing has become much more prevalent since 1980, and especially since 2004. We find evidence that brain framing increases belief in other biological and genetic causes; reduces belief in psychological and environmental causes, and strengthens beliefs in the efficacy of medication as a treatment. Effects on pessimism about recovery varied across studies and disorders. Brain framing had no robust effects on perceived age of onset, duration, severity, or beliefs about efficacy of psychotherapy treatment. Public beliefs about mental disorders are malleable and can be shaped by framing, highlighting the cognitive and societal consequences of brain framing in communication about mental health.

articles.title: Impossibility and Logical Contradictions Can Enhance the Perceived Value of Fictional Theological Propositions
articles.authors: Takuetsu Yajima; Eisuke Niida; Yo Nakawake
articles.abstract: Supernatural concepts are often thought to gain cultural attraction by violating intuitive expectations in limited ways, but many theological doctrines also involve logical contradictions or impossibilities. It remains unclear how such formal violations influence people’s evaluations of religious propositions. In the present study, 96 Japanese adults rated 20 fictional theological propositions on dimensions related to perceived value, including importance, profundity, interestingness, sacredness, and shareability. Those propositions were rated for impossibility and logical contradiction. A composite positive-evaluation score was derived from items rating perceived value and analyzed using linear mixed-effects models. The result shows higher impossibility and higher logical contradiction predict higher positive evaluations of the propositions. These findings suggest that impossible and contradictory theological content can be positively evaluated.

articles.title: Norm Commitment as a Link Between ‘Dark’ Personality and Norm Violation
articles.authors: Marie Joséphine Hamatschek; Miriam Wittpoth; Celina Marke
articles.abstract: ‘Dark’ personality traits predict criminal action, yet the underlying mechanism remains underspecified. We propose legal norm commitment (LNC) – an affectively anchored inner bond to the law – as an underlying mechanism. Based in a criminal-psychological action theory, LNC is assumed to build on (a) belief in the law (requiring overlap between inner direction and the law, or DLO; plus moral-emotional imperativeness) and (b) attachment to significant others. In a sample of incarcerated and free participants (N = 387), we assessed psychopathy (boldness, meanness, disinhibition), Machiavellianism, narcissistic entitlement, guilt proneness, LNC, and a catalogue of specific past norm violations via self-report. We used mediation analyses to test whether the norm violation tendency was predicted by the LNC (components) contained in the personality traits (implying conceptual overlap, not a causal relation). DLO partly accounted for personality–norm violation associations for all expected traits, but not for disinhibition, supporting a mechanism-based distinction between ‘dark’ and dysregulatory traits. Attachment and imperativeness showed no mediating effects. Among the traits investigated, meanness and guilt proneness shared the most variance with behaviorally effective LNC components. Given these preliminary findings, LNC as a value-free, mechanism-based concept might clarify some of the ‘darkness’ of personality.

articles.title: Using Customised LLM-Based Chatbots in Psychological Research: A Practical Tutorial
articles.authors: Hu Meilan; Gabriel Rongyang Lau; Adalia Yin Hui Goh; Samuel Rhys Cox; Louis Tay; Andree Hartanto
articles.abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based chatbots offer new methodological opportunities for psychological research by enabling scalable, standardised, and interactive research procedures. However, their usefulness depends on the researchers’ ability to customise, evaluate, and deploy them in ways that align with the methodological requirements of a given study. The current tutorial provides a practical, step-by-step framework for developing customised LLM-based chatbots for psychological research. We distinguish between no-code or low-code development approaches, including provider-hosted chatbot builders and visual or low-code programming platforms, and code-based approaches using proprietary model application programming interfaces (APIs) or locally hosted open-weight models. We compare these approaches in terms of technical expertise, behavioural and workflow control, study integration, cost, data governance, maintenance, and reproducibility. We also outline key components of the process of customising an LLM-based chatbot and illustrate deployment workflows across multiple platforms, including local desktop interfaces, messaging applications and survey platforms. Finally, we discuss key considerations for research ethics, privacy, data governance, security, transparency, and reproducibility, including recommendations for documenting and sharing chatbot configurations and study procedures. Through this tutorial, we aim to support researchers in integrating customised LLM-based chatbots into psychological research and in expanding the methodological possibilities available to them.

articles.title: Longitudinal and Latent-variable Extensions of the Triadic Actor-Partner Interdependence
articles.authors: Shiyao Wang; Jennifer Dang Guay; Karla Van Leeuwen; Evelien Schat; Eva Ceulemans
articles.abstract: When modeling interpersonal processes within triadic systems, researchers commonly encounter two types of analytical complexity: observations collected repeatedly over time, and constructs measured via multiple items. The current study introduces longitudinal and latent-variable extensions of the standard triadic Actor-Partner Interdependence Model (tAPIM) to accommodate these data structures. The longitudinal extensions, the concurrent tAPIM and the temporal tAPIM, account for temporal dependence and temporal precedence in repeated observations, while the latent-variable extension models each member’s construct as a latent variable measured from multiple observed items. In addition, we identify measurement invariance across triad members as a challenge specific to triadic data analysis and conduct a simulation study to investigate the consequences of its violation for the estimation of actor and partner effects. The results indicate that: 1) imposing invariance constraints that are not empirically supported may bias the estimation of nonzero actor and partner effects associated with the noninvariant member, while effects of invariant members and zero effects are accurately recovered; 2) relaxing invariance constraints avoids bias in point estimates, but standard errors of effects associated with the noninvariant member were still inflated, reducing power to detect true effects. The current paper offers practical guidance for researchers modeling interdependence in triadic systems using multi-item or longitudinal data.

articles.title: Unique and shared effects of single-session intervention proximal outcomes on 3-month depression symptoms in adolescents: A commonality analysis
articles.authors: Laura Jans; Arielle C. Smith; Isaac Lev Ahuvia; Jessica L. Schleider; Jeremy William Eberle
articles.abstract: Project Personality and the Action Brings Change Project are two web-based single-session interventions (SSIs) with theoretically distinct targets (growth mindset, behavioral activation, respectively) that have been shown to reduce adolescent depressive symptoms. However, the mechanisms through which they exert their effects remain unclear. In this preregistered exploratory analysis, we used completer data for each SSI (ns = 653 and 730) from a trial in depressed adolescents to examine the total effects of three theoretically derived candidate factors (pre-post changes in agency, pre-post changes in hopelessness, and postintervention acceptability) on 3-month changes in depressive symptoms. To further clarify potential mechanisms, we used commonality analysis to separate the explained variance unique to each predictor from that shared across multiple predictors. In both SSIs, changes in hopelessness and agency each demonstrated significant, small total effects on depressive symptom change (R² range = 2.89-4.92%). Both predictors contributed significant unique explanatory variance (1.01-1.80%) and shared explanatory variance with each other (1.23-1.99%). By contrast, acceptability demonstrated a significant, very small total effect (1.48%) in only one SSI (comprised of significant explanatory variance shared with both other predictors; 1.01%) and no significant unique effect in either SSI. Overall, findings suggest that changes in hopelessness and agency have partially distinct, yet overlapping associations with longer-term changes in depressive symptoms following completion of either SSI, despite the SSIs’ theoretically distinct targets. Future research should evaluate a broader set of candidate mechanisms using intensive longitudinal designs and methods that can further clarify the magnitude and nature of the mechanisms’ pathways.

articles.title: It's a small world of signs: Semantic network structure in American Sign Language based on free associations
articles.authors: Zed Sehyr; Karen Emmorey; Elana Pontecorvo; Naomi Kenney Caselli; Erin Michelle Buchanan
articles.abstract: Semantic network analyses have shown that words in spoken languages are organized into efficient "small-world" structures that support rapid lexical access and retrieval. However, little is known about whether similar organizational principles generalize to sign languages. We present the first large-scale analysis of semantic network structure in American Sign Language (ASL) using a free semantic association task. Deaf ASL signers (N = 45) produced three associations to 2,714 cue signs drawn from ASL-LEX, resulting in almost 100,000 cue–response pairs. We constructed (a) directed associative networks based on cue-response relationships and (b) undirected conceptual similarity networks based on cue–to-cue cosine similarity and compared ASL with English using matched subsets of the Small World of Words norms. We estimated network statistics and evaluated network topology using bootstrapping and degree-preserving random graphs. Both languages exhibited small-world organization indicating similar pressures on efficient semantic organization across language modalities. However, the languages differed in topology. Across network types, ASL exhibited longer average path lengths, and in conceptual similarity networks, lower clustering, suggesting reduced integration. In associative networks, ASL showed lower modularity, while in the conceptual similarity networks, ASL showed higher modularity than English, indicating a more compartmentalized semantic space. Further, more frequent signs occupied denser and more diverse semantic neighborhoods, whereas iconic signs exhibited fewer semantic connections and lower response diversity. These findings suggest that semantic memory is shaped by modality-independent organizational principles while also reflecting language-specific network topologies and structural pressures. The dataset and tools provide a basis for future cross-linguistic investigations.

articles.title: Partisans are more likely to entrench their beliefs in misinformation when political outgroup members correct claims
articles.authors: Diego A. Reinero; Elizabeth Ann Harris; Steve Rathje; Annie Duke; Jay Joseph Van Bavel
articles.abstract:
Misinformation has become a global issue with potentially dire consequences (e.g., election
results, COVID-19 vaccines, international conflicts). The most common strategy to reduce
beliefs in misinformation is to issue corrections or fact-checks. However, fact-checks are often
ineffective for polarized issues and there has been debate over whether misinformation
corrections sometimes "backfire," causing people to become more entrenched in misinformation.
Across three experiments (N = 1,217) we identify a key feature – the partisan identity of the
source – that explains when corrections will be effective and when they will be most likely to
backfire. We found that while corrections work on average, backfires still occurred 23% of the
time and were 52% more likely to occur when the correction came from a political outgroup vs.
ingroup member – leaving people with more entrenched beliefs in misinformation. Indeed, the
effect of partisan bias on initial belief in misinformation was 5x larger than the effect of
corrections. Partisan bias was most prominent and corrections were least effective when famous
politicians were involved. In sum, corrections have small effects compared to partisan identity
congruence, and sometimes backfire–especially if they come from a political outgroup member.

articles.title: Gender Differences in Self-reported Emotional Sharing in Social Interaction: A Meta Analysis
articles.authors: X. Jia; Karen Holtmaat; Y. Mo; ZIHAO Zeng; M. Kaneva; Annet Kleiboer; Sander L. Koole
articles.abstract: Through emotional sharing, individuals can make their emotional experiences available to others, creating opportunities for interpersonal emotion regulation. Although gender differences in these behaviours have been documented across various domains, findings regarding their magnitude and consistency remain inconclusive. This meta-analysis examined gender differences in emotional sharing among adults. A systematic search identified 32 articles comprising 37 independent samples, 155 effect sizes, and 13,147 participants, including 8,504 women and 4,643 men. Overall, women reported higher levels of emotional sharing than men, g = 0.31, 95% CI [0.18, 0.44]. This effect was not significantly moderated by (1) functions (emotional expression, emotional disclosure, emotional expression as coping), (2) temporal level (dispositional, situational), (3) emotional valence (negative, positive or unspecified), (4) specific negative emotion (anger, sadness, fear/anxiety, shame/guilt, and unspecified negative emotions), and (5) the interpersonal target (romantic partner, friend, other, or no partner specified). Despite the absence of significant moderation effects, pooled estimates within most subgroups remained significantly positive, indicating higher levels of expression and disclosure among women than men across a wide range of emotional contexts and interpersonal relations.

articles.title: Disordered Eating and Risk Factors Across Sexual Minority Men’s Tribe Identities
articles.authors: Orestis Michaelides; Lyndsey Wallace
articles.abstract: Sexual minority men experience disproportionately high rates of disordered eating. Recent work has shown that within this population, levels of disordered eating may vary across men who identify with different tribes, a set of identities centered around the body and physical appearance. This study investigated whether tribes have a unique association with disordered eating, or whether they reflect variation in two known risk factors that show theoretical relevance to these subcultural identities, i.e., body surveillance and internalized homophobia. Data from 349 sexual minority men showed that the endorsement of several tribe identities (Twinks, Jocks, Otters) was related to internalized homophobia and age. Results additionally showed that when controlling for these known risk factors, tribe identities still captured unique variance in disordered eating: men who identified as Bears or Cubs showed greater disordered eating, while men who identified as Twinks showed less disordered eating relative to men without a tribe identity. Collectively, these findings suggest that tribes have a nuanced role in men’s relationships with their body and sexual minority identity, and the link between tribes and disordered eating is underpinned by different psychological mechanisms than what has been previously suggested.

articles.title: Political Emotions Shape Preferences for Leaders’ Facial Traits: Anger Favors Dominance, Fear Favors Trustworthiness
articles.authors: Mariana Von Mohr; Manos Tsakiris
articles.abstract: Past work shows that conservatives prefer more dominant-looking political leaders, whereas liberals prefer more trustworthy-looking ones. We extend this by showing that, beyond partisanship, discrete political emotions independently shape preferences for leaders’ facial traits. A balanced sample of U.S. Republicans and Democrats identified the political issue that made them most angry or most afraid and then chose which leader would best address that issue using computer-generated faces varying in dominance and trustworthiness. Participants chose a more dominant and less trustworthy-looking leader more often when angry (49.5 percent) than when fearful (46.5 percent). Mechanistically, anger shifted choices toward more dominant-looking leaders by increasing reliance on dominance cues and reducing reliance on trustworthiness cues, whereas fear selectively increased reliance on trustworthiness cues. These findings show that political emotions exert distinct influences on leader evaluation with implications for democratic decision-making and electoral choices.

articles.title: Infants’ learning of tones and VOT contrasts in the lab
articles.authors: Alex Eguiluz; Alejandrina Cristia
articles.abstract: Infants likely home in on the speech categories in the ambient language(s) by attending to the acoustic cue distributions present in the input, but direct experimental evidence for this remains scarce. Young infants’ discrimination of /d-t/ and Mandarin Chinese tones T2-T4 was assessed over the course of a repeated exposure-test pro- cedure. In addition to being the first to document the emergence of perceptual categories through repeated testing of the same infants, this study suggests that perceptual learning through acoustic cue distributions could also account for the development of lexical tone perception.

articles.title: Kinematic encoding of the speed-accuracy trade-off in approach/avoidance decisions when facing social threats
articles.authors: Rocco Mennella; Julie Grezes; Matteo Sequestro; Morgan Beaurenaut
articles.abstract: Perceiving social threats, especially expressions of anger, increases the speed of both action selection and execution. However, it remains unclear how individuals balance speed with achieving desirable outcomes, such as threat avoidance, under these conditions. To investigate this trade-off between decision’s speed and accuracy, we examined the kinematics of finger-reaching movements using a "go-before-you-know" paradigm. Participants chose between two empty outer chairs in a waiting room. Two central chairs were occupied by either two individuals with neutral expressions or one neutral individual and one threatening individual. The threatening individual expressed anger or fear at one of four intensity levels. The results showed that social threats generally invigorated action decision, as high-threat trials elicited faster movements, which correlated with more direct trajectories compared to neutral trials. However, when participants chose to avoid angry individuals, the most frequent response, movements followed more central trajectories, compared to when they approached angry individuals. These findings suggest that while social threats generally invigorate action selection and execution, the accumulation of evidence for the decision can be temporarily prolonged to enhance the likelihood of a favorable outcome, such as threat avoidance. We propose integrating these results with recent models of action decisions under perceived urgency to advance understanding of threat-related decision-making.

articles.title: Towards an Integrative, Interdisciplinary, and Multidimensional Approach to Curbing Epistemically Suspect Beliefs: A Commentary on Bronstein et al. (2026)
articles.authors: Magdalena Adamus; Jais Adam-Troian; Maria Chayinska
articles.abstract: In this commentary, we endorse the recent call by Bronstein et al. (2026) to open a polyphonic debate and bring clinical psychology into the dialogue on the nature, causes, and consequences of epistemically suspect beliefs. We concur with the authors’ call for creating an integrative approach that would triangulate findings across different disciplines in a much-needed attempt to harmonise knowledge about individual, situational, and structural factors that contribute to the endorsement of epistemically suspect beliefs. Using economic anxiety as a model case, we then show how the integration of clinical insights could inform innovative, cost-effective, and scalable intervention programmes. Finally, we call for careful consideration of the risks associated with incorporating the clinical perspective, particularly the potential pathologisation of epistemically suspect beliefs and stigmatisation of those who endorse them, as well as the need to carefully distinguish delusions from ill-informed beliefs and rational suspicions.

articles.title: Predictors Associated with Early Career Researcher Wellbeing: A Systematic Scoping Review
articles.authors: Sophie Fletcher; Amber Tout; Talar Moukhtarian; Tabitha Jackson; Chloe Mitchell; Elena Riva; Carla Toro; Marie Sams; Sotaro Kita
articles.abstract:
Objective: Early Career Researchers (ECRs) are integral to the academic ecosystem, representing a critical window for mental health promotion and early intervention within the higher education workforce. Their wellbeing is influenced by various factors that can either support or hinder healthy professional and personal development. This systematic scoping review maps and narratively synthesises current literature to understand predictors of ECR wellbeing, with the aim of informing upstream strategies for prevention and mental health promotion. 
Method: A systematic search was conducted across Web of Science, PsycINFO, and EBSCO (inception–May 2024). Of 2,577 records retrieved, 68 articles (69 independent studies) were included after screening.
Results: Seventeen distinct predictor clusters were identified and grouped by who has the most agency over them: 1) ECRs, 2) labs and departments, 3) institutions, 4) the sector, 5) all levels of agents combined. Frequently explored predictors included personal characteristics (i.e., age, gender), supervisor support and work-life balance, while depression, anxiety and stress were the most frequently measured outcomes.
Discussion: This review highlights both systemic and modifiable risk factors of occupational and psychological distress among ECRs. By identifying key drivers of wellbeing, this review offers actionable insights for developing early, targeted interventions at multiple levels. Investing in preventative and promotive strategies during this formative career stage may not only protect the wellbeing of ECRs but also foster healthier, more productive and sustainable academic environments.

articles.title: Toward a Validity Argument for Automated Assessment from Transcript and Video Data
articles.authors: James Soland
articles.abstract: Automated assessment of psychological constructs from interview transcripts and video data has seen rapid technical development, yet the field lacks a systematic psychometric validity framework for interpreting scores from such measures. This paper applies Kane's interpretive/use argument structure alongside the five sources of validity evidence specified in the \textit{Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing} to automated transcript- and video-based assessment, using clinical assessment of depression as the primary illustrative case. We distinguish two design approaches --- item-based scoring, in which large language models (LLMs) rate explicit, theoretically derived items, and end-to-end embedding or classification approaches --- and examine how one could accrue validity evidence for each across the five sources. We argue that the field has concentrated almost exclusively on evidence based on relations to other variables (convergent validity against self-report criteria) while leaving response process and consequential evidence largely unaddressed. Further, we argue that construct validity evidence is often dismissed too quickly, especially for end-to-end approaches. Both evidence sources require fundamental reconceptualization for automated behavioral measures, and we propose reinterpretations suited to this context. Although the analysis centers on depression, the framework applies broadly to any construct assessed from passively collected video or transcript data. Implications for the design of future validation studies are discussed.

articles.title: The Development of Compositionality in Language and Thought
articles.authors: Eulalie Péquay; Isabelle Dautriche
articles.abstract:
Compositionality is the property of a representational system whereby com-plex meanings
arise from the combination of simpler meaningful elements. Here we take a developmental
perspective to understand the origins of compositional representational systems and their
relation to language—an issue that bears on longstanding debates in cognitive science about
the structure of the human mind. Based on our review, we conclude that (a) well-controlled
evidence for compositional abilities during language acquisition remains scarce, although
some studies suggest infants begin to understand specific multiword combinations during the
second year of life, and (b) the key computation underlying compositionality—function
application—can be observed in infancy during the first year of life, well before, and even out-
side, compositional language. These findings suggest the mind may support compositional
operations prior to the emergence of compositional language, while leaving open questions
about how the development of compositional thought and compositional language interact.

articles.title: An optimal parameter range for tactile symbol recognition using a Haptic Mesh
articles.authors: Yu Cheng; Kenji Yamaguchi; Daniel Zymelka; Toshihiro Takeshita; Tatsuhiro Nakamura; Hiroki Togo; Kenji Yoshinaga; Takashi Hanakawa
articles.abstract: Tactile stimulation offers a potential means of conveying symbolic information when visual or auditory communication is unavailable or impractical. However, the temporal conditions required for reliable recognition of complex tactile symbols remain unclear. We systematically examined how stimulus duration (Duration) and interstimulus interval (ISI) jointly shape the recognition of digit-like tactile trajectories presented to the palm. Ten healthy adults received nine digit-like trajectories presented through a 3 × 3 vibrotactile actuator array under 30 Duration × ISI combinations and rated recognizability, perceived continuity, and stimulus intensity. We defined an Optimal Parameter Region (OPR) a priori as the largest 4-neighbor contiguous set of conditions with group-mean recognition accuracy of at least 0.60. We identified a cluster of 11 adjacent conditions, primarily at Durations of 200–300 ms and ISIs of 100–250 ms, corresponding to apparent motion speeds of approximately 28–58 mm s⁻¹. Within the OPR, recognition was more stable, and misclassification entropy was lower than outside it. Recognition also varied among conditions with the identical apparent motion speeds, prompting us to examine time allocation between Duration and ISI. Apparent motion speed accounted for 39% of the variance in recognition performance; relative time allocation explained an additional 13%. Subjective recognizability was higher within the OPR and closely tracked objective accuracy, whereas perceived continuity and stimulus intensity did not consistently explain recognition performance. These findings indicate that tactile-symbol recognition is optimal within a range of Duration–ISI combinations whose effects cannot be reduced to apparent motion speed alone, while trajectory geometry imposes an additional constraint on robust tactile-symbol design.

articles.title: From Epic to Applied Psychology: A Conceptual Mapping of Sanskrit Psychological Constructs and Their Contemporary Relevance
articles.authors: Manoj Kumar Mallick
articles.abstract: This conceptual paper examines whether four Sanskrit epic constructs hold structural resonance with four established areas of psychological science. It responds to a growing interest in integrating Indian Knowledge Systems with psychological theory, extending that integration into underexplored epic material. Sanskrit's own literary and grammatical heritage has long been recognised in linguistics and aesthetics; this paper asks whether its psychological vocabulary deserves comparable recognition. Following a conceptual-article design (Theory Synthesis), the paper pairs dharma saṅkaṭa with moral cognition, tapas-nirvṛtti with self-regulation, rasa with affective science, and karma yoga with motivation theory. Four criteria—definitional precision, scope-matching, textual traceability, and precision over popularity—guided construct selection. Constructs were drawn from named episodes in the Mahābhārata, Kumārasambhava, and Buddhacarita, rather than from Sanskrit thought treated generally. Each pairing shows meaningful structural alignment without collapsing into a single unifying model. Applied implications extend to education, therapy, policy, and Gen-Z digital burnout, illustrating the pairings' contemporary relevance. Each pairing was illustrated through a textual episode and a contemporary vignette, grounding abstract resonance in concrete cases. The paper offers four testable propositions for future empirical validation. It also proposes a shared vocabulary bridging Sanskrit psychological thought and contemporary science, without claiming either tradition anticipated or exhausts the other.

articles.title: Moral Concern for AI in an Economic Game
articles.authors: Carter Allen; Joshua Lewis; Lucius Caviola
articles.abstract: How will people morally regard increasingly human-like artificial intelligence systems? We introduce the AI Harm Game, a novel paradigm examining whether people will harm AI for personal gain. In our study, 498 U.S. participants interacted with GPT-4o in a three-round economic game. In each round, participants chose whether to harm the AI for a small monetary bonus (causing it to vividly simulate suffering) or refrain from harming it (eliciting gratitude). Although participants were overwhelmingly skeptical that current AIs can suffer, their decisions and reasoning about whether to harm the AI varied considerably. Participants harmed the AI in 1.4 out of 3 rounds on average. Women and older participants were more reluctant to harm the AI, while participants higher on measures of selfishness and psychopathy were more willing. These findings reveal that even without attributing consciousness to them, many people hesitate to harm responsive AIs, suggesting people’s moral impulses may generalize to future human–AI relationships.

articles.title: Evaluating dyadic interdependence between cannabis attitudes and parental monitoring processes among parents and adolescents
articles.authors: Tram Doran; Emily Olenik; Sarah Ryan; Alexandria LeVert; Jane Metrik; Pearl Ayiku; Samuel Meisel; Jack Rusley; Anthony Spirito; Sarah Ann Thomas
articles.abstract: Cannabis is a commonly used substance during adolescence. As US legalization expands, public perception of cannabis increasingly reflects the view that it is less harmful than other substances. The extent to which parents monitor and know about their adolescent’s activities and whereabouts is an important tool to manage risk behaviors like substance use. However, it is unclear how parental monitoring may vary based on cannabis attitudes. The current study investigated how parents' and adolescents’ attitudes toward cannabis (risk of harm to teens, disapproval, and ease of availability) are associated with parental knowledge about adolescents’ whereabouts/activities and its sources (adolescent disclosure, parental solicitation). We hypothesized that lower perceived risk of harm and less disapproval of cannabis use would be associated with lower levels of parental monitoring among both parents and adolescents. Our sample was N = 73 adolescents ages 14–17 (59% female) and their caregivers. Lower parental perceived risk of harm to teens from cannabis use was associated with less adolescent-reported parental solicitation. Lower adolescent perceived risk of harm to teens from cannabis use was linked to less adolescent disclosure to parents. Greater adolescent-perceived cannabis availability was associated with (a) both adolescent- and parent-report that parents knew less about adolescents’ whereabouts and activities, and (b) lower adolescent-report of less disclosure to parents. Results highlight the interdependent nature of parent and adolescent cannabis perceptions in relation to monitoring processes. Parents may benefit from public health initiatives that provide them with information on the potential negative health and emotional consequences of cannabis use in adolescence.

articles.title: The beliefs at the heart of multilingual family language policies: A corpus-assisted discourse study of parental attitudes towards childhood multilingualism
articles.authors: Ruth Kircher; Melanie Brouillard; Alexa Ahooja; Erin Quirk; Susan Ballinger; Linda Polka; Krista Byers-Heinlein
articles.abstract: This study focuses on parental language beliefs, which we approach from an attitudes perspective. Language attitudes are at the heart of multilingual family language policies because they shape parents’ language practices and language management – and thereby, ultimately, children’s multilingual development. Based on French and English corpora (over 30,000 words in total) comprising 742 Quebec-based parents’ responses to an open-ended survey question, we present a corpus-assisted discourse study of parental attitudes towards childhood multilingualism. We analyse frequencies and collocations to attest statistically significant patterns, and we examine concordance lines and longer text segments to establish meaning in context. Our findings confirm the multidimensionality of parental attitudes towards childhood multilingualism, providing new insights into the nature of the three previously-established dimensions – status, solidarity, and cognitive development – as well as revealing a potential fourth dimension: personality development. The study thus makes a contribution to the family language policy framework and to language attitude theory more generally. Moreover, the findings show systematic differences between parents transmitting multiple societal languages versus parents transmitting heritage languages alongside one/more societal languages. The study thus also makes a practical contribution by facilitating the development of tailored support measures for different types of multilingual families.

articles.title: Adolescent Mental Healthcare as a Public Utility: A Multi-Sectoral Economic Case for Proactive Investment
articles.authors: Mackenzie Swirbul; Emily Peake; Anne Bischops; Marie-Laure Charpignon; Maimuna S. Majumder; Aarthi Padmanabhan
articles.abstract:
Adolescence is a critical developmental period marked by substantial neuroplasticity and the onset of most psychiatric disorders. Despite this epidemiologic reality, the current US mental healthcare landscape remains largely reactive rather than proactive, leaving nearly half of symptomatic youth untreated and generating a considerable economic burden through lost productivity and increased healthcare expenditures. While clinical outcomes are well-documented, the multi-sectoral fiscal consequences and potential returns on investment of such proactive youth mental healthcare remain poorly integrated into US policy frameworks. 

This narrative review synthesizes evidence from econometric analyses and longitudinal studies across four key sectors: education, legal and correctional, labor market (caregiver productivity), and healthcare. We describe how untreated mental health conditions contribute to high-cost, crisis-driven care, chronic school absenteeism, and increased involvement with the juvenile correctional system, while also quantifying their effects on caregiver workforce participation and productivity. Furthermore, we highlight emerging public financing models that conceptualize mental healthcare as an essential public good. 

Current evidence suggests that proactive investment in accessible adolescent mental healthcare yields meaningful socioeconomic returns. Strategic investment in youth mental healthcare should therefore be regarded as both a public health imperative and a fiscal priority.

articles.title: Playing for fun, playing to escape: Gaming motives and problematic video game use in a French sample aged 6 to 45 years
articles.authors: Chloe Nguyen; Quentin Hallez
articles.abstract: Data on the prevalence of problematic gaming in France are scarce, and few studies have compared gaming behavior, gaming motives, and their correlates across developmental periods with identical instruments. We surveyed 676 French participants aged 6 to 45 years (52.4% male), spanning childhood (6–14 years; parent-reported), adolescence (15–17), young adulthood (18–25), and adulthood (26–45), using the Game Addiction Scale (GAS-7), the Motives for Online Gaming Questionnaire (MOGQ), the WHO-5 Well-Being Index, and the Barratt Impulsiveness Scale (BIS-15). Overall, 79.6% of participants played video games. Problematic gaming (monothetic GAS criterion) characterized 4.8% of gamers, with no significant differences across age groups and rates three times higher in males than in females. Although symptom levels were similar across age groups, motive profiles were not: recreation dominated at every age, whereas coping and escape motives were rare in childhood and markedly higher from adolescence onward. In hierarchical regressions, escape and competition motives and gaming frequency were the strongest unique correlates of problematic use, statistically attenuating the bivariate contributions of gender, impulsivity, well-being, and gaming time. Motive–symptom associations were invariant across age groups, whereas the association between gaming time and symptoms was stronger in older age groups. These cross-sectional findings suggest that motivational assessment may be more informative than screen-time metrics for the prevention and screening of problematic gaming.

articles.title: Getting Closer or Stepping Back? Personal Space Adjustments Following Facial Emotion Imitation and Observation
articles.authors: Ivan Patané; Clément Desoche; ALESSANDRO FARNE; Fadila Hadj-Bouziane
articles.abstract: Regulating personal space (PS) is essential for navigating social interactions. Although emotional cues are known to influence PS, the mechanisms underlying this modulation remain poorly understood. The present study investigated whether active facial emotion imitation is followed by changes in PS regulation and whether these changes differ from those observed following passive emotion observation. Participants completed a Virtual Reality Stop-Distance task to assess their preferred interpersonal distances from angry, happy, and neutral virtual agents, before and after an imitation session, during which they actively imitated angry or happy facial expressions. Following emotion imitation, participants exhibited a bidirectional modulation of PS: they increased their distance from angry virtual agents and decreased it from happy virtual agents, while no changes were observed for neutral agents. These findings suggest that active facial imitation enhances sensitivity to emotional signals and adaptively modulates interpersonal distance. Eye-tracking analyses revealed no significant changes in gaze behavior between pre- and post-imitation sessions, indicating that the reported effects were not driven by differences in overt visual attention. In a second experiment using a similar pre-post design, a new group of participants passively observed the same emotional expressions without imitating them. Results showed that, after emotion observation, angry virtual agents elicited an increased interpersonal distance, whereas no changes in distance from either the happy or neutral virtual agents were observed. Together, these results indicate that defensive distancing from others’ angry expressions followed both active imitation and passive observation, whereas the approach-related reduction in distance in response to happy expressions was evident after active imitation only. These findings highlight the contribution of emotional-cue exposure to personal space regulation in social contexts and provide further evidence that emotional experience can dynamically shape interpersonal behavior.

articles.title: When Effort Stops Meaning Something: A Cognitive Systems Model of Persistence, Disuse, and Re-entry
articles.authors: Arya Jadhav; Lawrence R. Burns
articles.abstract: Learning depends not only on task performance, but on whether effort remains coupled to interpretable signals of progress, competence, and continued agency. External cognitive systems can disrupt this coupling when they absorb cognitive work that would otherwise sustain internal learning dynamics. We introduce the Cognitive Cost Comparator (CCC), a mechanistic agent-based model of engagement-gated learning under external offloading. In the model, heterogeneous agents allocate effort between internal cognition and an external aid across 300 discrete time steps. Although the present simulations instantiate the external system as AI assistance, the architecture is intended to generalize to cognitive tools that alter the perceived cost of task completion. The model couples three feedback processes: a confidence-engagement loop that gates learning opportunity, an offloading-disuse loop that erodes internal confidence and raises engagement thresholds, and a scaffolding-interpretability mechanism that determines whether effort produces meaningful progress signals. Learning states are modeled as dynamic attractors rather than fixed outcomes. Across simulations with 4,500 agents, engagement reliability was the strongest predictor of terminal confidence (Spearman r = 0.72). Scaffolding primarily prevented entry into disengaged failure states, but did not reliably restore agents once disengagement had stabilized; recovery increased meaningfully only when scaffolding was paired with explicit re-entry mechanisms. These findings suggest that cognitive systems involving human learners and external aids must be evaluated not only by performance support, but by whether they preserve the conditions for effortful re-engagement after failure.

articles.title: Unpacking cognitive variability: Dynamic systems modeling to understand daily cognitive change in healthy aging and mild cognitive impairment
articles.authors: Andrew J. Aschenbrenner; Joshua James Jackson
articles.abstract: It is increasingly accepted that single scores are insufficient to fully capture the complexities of cognition as it relates to daily life. Many studies now employ repeated cognitive assessments to measure variability in scores across the testing sessions. Exploration of additional characteristics of participant’s time series may provide more explanatory power in understanding cognitive health in aging and early neurodegenerative disease. We administered a standard attention test daily for 3 weeks to healthy younger adults, healthy older adults and participants diagnosed with cognitive impairment. Participants self-rated the frequency of their cognitive failures in daily life. We used an established cognitive model to decompose participant scores into two latent parameters, mean inputs and “dissipation” which reflects the speed with which one returns to baseline performance after a deviation in scores. More traditional summary statistics, including mean performance and variability, were also calculated. Linear regression was used to compare group differences on each outcome and their association with real-world cognitive failures. Results indicate that variability in scores followed a U-shaped pattern across groups. Variability changes in cognitive impairment were due exclusively to changes in the dissipation parameter and this parameter was uniquely related to self-rated cognitive failures. Our findings indicate dissipation may reflect high levels of cognitive reserve, which protects against the manifestation of functional symptoms in daily life. More generally, our results underscore the importance of using repeated cognitive assessments in studies of healthy and pathological aging, as traditional measures of performance did not evince relationships with cognitive failures.

articles.title: The development and psychometric evaluation  of the brief Compulsive Pornography Use Scale  (CPUS-4)
articles.authors: Terezie Babilonová; Halley M. Pontes; Helena Pipova; Táňa Reháková; Štěpán Komrska; Jaroslava Suchá
articles.abstract: Online pornography use has increased worldwide in recent decades, with problematic use being associated with negative mental health outcomes. However, no brief instrument is currently available to specifically assess Problematic Pornography Use (PPU) by operationalizing the behavioral manifestations of Compulsive Sexual Behavior Disorder (CSBD) as defined in the 11th International Statistical Classification of Diseases (ICD-11). This study aimed to develop the Compulsive Pornography Use Scale (CPUS-4). The sample consisted of 1,023 Czech adults that completed an online survey assessing pornography use behaviors, Pornography Addiction Screening Tool (PAST), Depression, Anxiety, Stress Scales-21 (DASS-21), and Three-Item Loneliness Scale (UCLA-3). Exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses indicated a single-factor structure of the CPUS-4, supporting its factorial validity.
