The scale demonstrated high internal consistency and significant associations with theoretically related constructs, supporting both convergent and concurrent validity. Overall, the CPUS-4 appears to be a valid and reliable brief instrument for assessing pornography-related behavioral manifestations within the ICD-11 framework for CSBD.

articles.title: Self-Generated Goals in the Age of Foundation Models: Artificial Autotelic Agents and Their Implications for Cognitive Science
articles.authors: Gaia Molinaro; Anne Collins; Pierre-Yves Oudeyer; Cédric Colas
articles.abstract: Goals have traditionally been treated as inputs to intelligent systems, biological and artificial, rather than as products of intelligence itself. A growing body of work in cognitive science and artificial intelligence (AI) challenges this framing through autotelic agents — self-improving systems motivated to represent, generate, select, and pursue their own goals. Recent advances in foundation models (large-scale generative AI models trained on broad datasets) expand this research program by extending the languages and tools through which artificial agents can express, evaluate, and pursue goals. By operating over formats such as natural language and code, foundation models allow agents to generate more abstract and compositional goals, approximate human judgments of interestingness and learnability, and support richer loops of problem generation and problem solving. These advances create new opportunities for cognitive science to model human goal dynamics, for AI to build more adaptive autotelic systems, and for human–AI systems to support shared goal exploration without narrowing human agency.

articles.title: “For me, it is like a tide: it is always there...”: a qualitative exploration of dynamic suicidal thoughts in autistic adolescents
articles.authors: Mirabel Pelton; Lilian Clark; Xinxin Zhu; Ed Flexney; Martha Enticott; Rachael Adams; Olivia King; Maria Gardani; Rachel L Moseley-Braund; Tanya L Procyshyn
articles.abstract:
Background
Autistic young people are twice as likely to die by suicide than their non-autistic peers, but mechanisms driving this remain undefined.  This study explored factors contributing to suicidal thoughts in adolescence (aged 11-15), alongside processes of coping and recovery.  

Methods
We conducted reflexive thematic analysis of semi-structured interviews with nine autistic young people (mean age=21.1) to produce conceptual models of: (i) suicide risk; and (ii) recovery. 

Findings
An over-arching theme described adolescent suicidal thoughts as omnipresent, fluctuating, and unpredictably building to crisis. Self-exploration uncovered multiple meanings and functions of suicidal thoughts. Nested sub-theme 1 described the development of autistic identity. Early experiences of rejection and de-humanisation resulted in existential questioning; self-discovery, neuroaffirming resources, and neurodivergent communities enabled agency and a protective autistic identity. Nested sub-theme 2 described marginalisation and social identity. Harmful school environments, pressure to mask autistic traits and invalidation in health services resulted in suicidal distress and crisis. Critical consciousness and leaving education enabled autonomy, purposeful coping and pursuit of life goals. Living well as an autistic person offered greatest protection, but recurrent setbacks and others’ lack of understanding hindered progress. 

Interpretation
Suicidal thoughts and feelings were shaped by interactions between autistic young people and their environment and marked by epistemic injustice.  Findings resonate with the Integrated Motivational-Volitional model’s emphasis on defeat and entrapment; however, defeat was experienced early, and was pervasive and entrenched, while fluctuations in risk were shaped by harmful environments and neuronormative pressures. Findings further support the COURAGE model of suicide recovery, particularly domains for optimising identity, self-understanding, and meaning in life; however, domains dependent on social acceptance and empowerment were less well-supported, suggesting that opportunities were constrained by broader social and structural barriers. Across both models’ structural factors increased risk and constrained the conditions necessary for autistic people to live meaningful and sustainable lives. Clinicians should prioritise neuroaffirming approaches and resources, but lasting reductions in suicide risk in autistic young people will require structural change, including greater equality of opportunity and an urgent action to reduce the distress of educational environments.

articles.title: Amotivated Solitude: Naming the Space Between Vairagya and Escapism
articles.authors: Pooja Tyagi; Baljeet Kaur
articles.abstract: Recent global data indicate that roughly one in six people worldwide experience loneliness, prompting the World Health Organization to name social disconnection a public health priority. Yet not everyone who prefers solitude over social engagement is lonely, distressed, or withdrawing from life. A growing body of solitude research documents this distinction, but the specific combination addressed here, a preference for solitude that is neither reactively avoidant nor autonomously growth-seeking, remains unnamed. This preference is neither the growth-oriented non-attachment described by the Indian philosophical concept of Vairagya, nor the reactive, affect-driven retreat captured by passive escapism, nor the impairment associated with loneliness or clinical depression, nor the positively-valenced enjoyment described by affinity for aloneness. This paper proposes Amotivated Solitude (Preference) to name this gap: a dispositional or situational preference for solitude that is low in both autonomous, growth-seeking motivation and reactive, anxiety-driven avoidance. Drawing on self-determination theory's amotivation continuum, the solitude-motivation literature, and the developmental construct of unsociability, this paper differentiates the proposed construct from eight neighbouring constructs, addresses the risk of construct proliferation (the jingle-jangle problem) directly, and presents a conceptual map locating the construct along a volition-outcome spectrum. It outlines a research program for construct validation, including qualitative grounding, item development, and psychometric testing against existing non-attachment measures, and closes with limitations and open questions for discussion regarding naming, boundary conditions, and trait versus state framing.

articles.title: Revisiting Cross-Modal Matching in the Light of Luce’s Global Psychophysical Theory
articles.authors: Katharina Naumann; Jürgen Heller
articles.abstract: This study presents a replication of the classical cross-modal matching experiment by J. C. Stevens and Marks (1965, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the USA, 54, 407-411), which examined loudness-to-brightness and brightness-to-loudness mappings.  We extend prior work by complementing traditional group-level analysis with an individual-level examination and by applying the theory of global psychophysics with internal references. This mathematical framework formalizes the underlying mechanisms of cross-modal matching behavior. In matching tasks, the well-documented phenomenon termed the regression effect emerges, wherein the adjusted stimuli gravitate toward mid-level intensities. To model this effect, we implement a novel Bayesian estimation of the global psychophysical model for cross-modal matching. In a sample of seven subjects, including many repetitions at the subject level, the regression effect is observed at both the aggregated and individual levels. The model effectively captures the prevalent nonlinearity in individual matching curves. We discuss the theoretical and methodological implications of these findings and outline directions for future research.

articles.title: Investigating which type of maltreatment has the largest impact on health:  The challenge of measurement error
articles.authors: Milan Zarchev; Henning Tiemeier
articles.abstract: To answer the question of which type of maltreatment has the largest impact on health outcomes, researchers often simultaneously enter multiple maltreatment predictors in a single regression model. However, this approach of mutual adjustment is problematic, as some maltreatment types (e.g. physical neglect) are often measured with more error than others (e.g. physical abuse). Greater measurement error attenuates effect sizes and reduces statistical power to detect associations, implicitly creating the appearance that better measured maltreatment types are more impactful. The attenuation is particularly severe in mutually adjusted models, as maltreatment types tend to correlate with each other. Researchers comparing maltreatment types should routinely report on reliability estimates such as McDonald’s omega and present separately-estimated associations next to the mutually adjusted model.

articles.title: Relationship Microcultures Theory
articles.authors: Maya Rossignac-Milon; Emma S Miller; Lydia Emery; Joshua Conrad Jackson; Eli Finkel
articles.abstract: Just as groups of people form large-scale macro-cultures, close relationship partners construct their own microculture. Dyads invent their own language (the word “muddles” for homemade ceramics), stories (rescuing their cat), rituals (weekly backgammon), morality (conflicts require mutual apologies), identity (activists), and sense of reality (belief in UFOs). We contend that the emergence, development, and maintenance of this co-created microculture predicts key relational and personal outcomes. We introduce Relationship Microcultures Theory (RMT), which complements prevailing relationship theories by examining how particular words and behaviors are interpreted within the history of the specific relationship in which they acquired idiosyncratic meaning, shaping in turn the well-being of the relationship and the individuals involved. In our Microcultural Unit Model, we describe a meta-theory for understanding how particular dyadic interactions become microcultural units (e.g., inside jokes) by acquiring mutual, idiosyncratic, and referential meaning. In our Aggregate Microculture Model, we advance a theory of how more extensive microcultures—those comprising more units, used more frequently, and spanning more life domains—contribute to relational outcomes (e.g., relationship satisfaction and longevity) and personal outcomes (e.g., meaning in life and self-regulatory success). We also theorize that microcultural extensiveness can undermine relational and personal outcomes when mutuality, idiosyncrasy, and referentiality are low. By examining the dyad as a culture in miniature, RMT opens novel research directions for relationship science.

articles.title: Quantifying the relative associations of time of social media use and addictive social media use with emotional distress among U.S. adults
articles.authors: Hyosin Kim; Jakub Helvich; Giselle Lee; Brian Primack
articles.abstract: Both time of social media use (TSMU) and addictive social media use (ASMU) have been associated with depression and anxiety. However, their relative associations with emotional distress remain unclear, and research involving middle-aged and older adults has been limited. We examined associations of TSMU and ASMU with depression and anxiety in a probability-based nationally-representative sample of 1512 U.S. adults aged 30–70 years. Depression and anxiety were measured using the Patient Health Questionnaire-9 and Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7, respectively. TSMU and ASMU, assessed using the Bergen Social Media Addiction Scale, were both operationalized in quartiles to facilitate direct comparison. In separate weighted logistic regression models, both TSMU and ASMU were associated with depression and anxiety. However, when TSMU and ASMU were included in the same models, associations between TSMU and both depression and anxiety became non-significant, whereas associations between ASMU and both outcomes remained strong (p<0.001 for both). Compared with participants in the lowest quartile of ASMU, those in the highest quartile had between 4 and 5 times the odds for depression (adjusted odds ratio [AOR], 4.94; 95% confidence interval [CI], 3.20–7.62), and anxiety (AOR, 4.59; 95% CI, 2.76–7.63), even after adjusting for TSMU. These findings suggest that ASMU may be more strongly associated with depression and anxiety than overall amount of social media use among U.S. adults.

articles.title: Accounts Balanced: The Contingent Role of Rhetoric in Who Survives Political Scandal
articles.authors: Pierce D. Ekstrom; Marti Hope Gonzales; Allison Williams; Elliot Weiner; Rafael Aguilera
articles.abstract: When accused of misconduct in their private or public lives, people choose whether to apologize or to defend their character or reputation. Previous experiments have found that when misconduct is severe or offends outgroup members, transgressors may benefit by defending themselves and denying culpability for wrongdoing. In this study, we explore whether these tendencies can successfully reduce politicians’ accountability for wrongdoing in the context of a U.S. congressional election. We constructed a novel dataset documenting Representatives’ public remarks in response the 1992 House Bank Scandal, during which Representatives from both major parties were accused of misusing funds. Contrary to predictions, conciliatory remarks were not associated with electoral failure among more severe House Bank “offenders.” Consistent with predictions, defensive remarks (refusals) lost their typical association with electoral failure when the incumbent’s party controlled the district. Results suggest that groups may allow their leaders to escape blame for wrongdoing and retain power.

articles.title: Trial After Trial: Temporal Dynamics Reveal a Distinct Computational Phenotype of Chronic Cannabis Use
articles.authors: Samuel Poelker-Wells; Kendra Leigh Seaman; Galston Kok Yi Wong; Francesca Filbey
articles.abstract:
Background: Studies of effort-based decision-making (EBDM) related to chronic cannabis use have yielded inconsistent findings. This variability may reflect the limited ability of behavioral measures alone to distinguish the mechanisms driving observed choices. Computational modeling can help these discrepancies by isolating alterations in valuation, evidence-accumulation, and temporal processes.
Methods: Forty-one individuals who chronically use cannabis (CU) and 45 individuals who do not (NU) completed the Effort Expenditure for Rewards Task (EEfRT).  Drift diffusion, subjective value, and temporal dynamics models were used to characterize latent decision processes of effortful choice. Model-derived parameters were compared between groups and examined in relation to cannabis-use characteristics.
Results: Greater effort allocation via hard-option choice in CU was characterized by less baseline effort avoidance during evidence accumulation and a weaker starting bias toward the easy option, implicating multiple decisional processes. They also showed lower between-participant variability in starting bias and, less definitively, decision caution. Subjective value modeling showed that both groups used similar decision strategies. Incorporating trial progression improved modeling and indicated that greater sustained hard-option choice in CU was related to weaker temporal decline in evidence accumulation and subjective value. Cannabis use characteristics showed no significant associations with latent parameters.
Conclusions:  Adults who use cannabis showed lower effort avoidance both at baseline and during evidence accumulation, greater homogeneity in selected decision processes, and attenuated decline in hard-option valuation. These findings suggest that cannabis-related differences in physical EBDM reflect altered evidence accumulation and temporal stability rather than broad differences in integration of reward, probability, and effort.

articles.title: Nonsuicidal self-injury and approach behavior toward aversive images:  A MouseView.js study
articles.authors: Sarina Rain; Lily Wanlu Martin; Edwin S. Dalmaijer; Thomas Armstrong; Jeremy Gordon Stewart
articles.abstract:
Introduction: Nonsuicidal self-injury (NSSI) is associated with altered responses to self-injury-related cues. However, extant behavioral measures do not capture intentional engagement with stimuli, which may be most clinically relevant to understanding persistent NSSI. 

Methods: We created a novel task in MouseView.js to measure voluntary engagement with NSSI-relevant stimuli using cursor movements. Young adults (N=143) with self-injurious thoughts and/or behaviors histories completed the task and questionnaires assessing NSSI and suicidal ideation (SI) at baseline and 2-, 4- and 6-month follow-ups.

Results: More frequent NSSI and greater SI severity were associated with increased engagement with suicide images (i.e., staged suicide attempts), but not general gore images, across the 10-second viewing period. Greater average engagement with both image types was associated with the presence (versus absence) of past-month NSSI. Greater baseline engagement with both image types prospectively predicted NSSI frequency over follow-ups; however, effects were non-significant when controlling for baseline symptoms.

Conclusion: We provide preliminary evidence that engagement with NSSI-relevant stimuli – measured using cursor movements – may be a concurrent behavioral correlate of NSSI. Effects were most consistent for images depicting self-injury, compared to general gore, suggesting that individuals with NSSI may be especially prone to engaging with content depicting intentional self-directed harm.

articles.title: The Architecture of Academic Safety: Supervisory Communication, the Impostor Phenomenon, and Doctoral Psychological Well-Being—A Mixed-Methods Study"
articles.authors: Varsha singh; Rajnesh meena; Saloni vishwakarma
articles.abstract:
NOTICE: This manuscript is currently under peer review at a journal. This version is the Author's Original Manuscript (AOM) and has not yet undergone formal peer review.

The doctoral journey increases risks for poor psychological well-being and the impostor phenomenon. This mixed-methods study examined how supervisor communication style influences these experiences among PhD scholars. Quantitative data were gathered via an online survey from 90 scholars, alongside qualitative interview data from 20 participants. Quantitative results indicated that scholars generally perceived their supervisors’ communication positively (M = 3.78, SD = 0.42), reported moderate levels of the impostor phenomenon (M = 2.42, SD = 0.99), and demonstrated relatively high psychological well-being (M = 4.26, SD = 0.70). Supervisor communication style was not significantly related to the impostor phenomenon (r = .074, p = .484) but showed a significant positive relationship with psychological well-being (r = .206, p = .049; R² = .043). The impostor phenomenon was negatively, but not significantly, related to well-being (r = -.196, p = .061). Crucially, however, qualitative findings explained this disconnect by revealing that specific, nuanced communication types heavily dictate these experiences. Qualitative findings revealed that instructive clarity, affective support, autonomy, scholarly inclusion, academic recognition, and constructive feedback characterized positive communication, whereas structural ambiguity, inconsistent feedback, intellectual exclusion, systematic invalidation and controlling behaviours induced stress and experienced high imposter phenomenon

articles.title: Personality Differences among Men and Women of Various Sexual Orientations, Including Asexual and Pansexual Individuals
articles.authors: Jakub Fořt; Dominika Benešová; Petr Freudenfeld; Jaroslava Varella Valentova; Jan Havlicek
articles.abstract: Several theoretical approaches explain variance in personality related to sexual orientation. Drawing on the minority stress theory and the gender shift hypothesis, this study explores personality differences across people of various sexual orientations, including underrepresented groups, such as asexual and pansexual individuals. The minority stress theory posits that non-heterosexual individuals experience heightened social stressors, contributing to higher neuroticism. The gender shift hypothesis further suggests that prenatal hormonal influences may lead to sex-atypical development, explaining some personality variation in sexual minorities. Using a large Czech and Slovak sample (N = 6,476), we administered the Big Five Inventory (BFI-10) to heterosexual (N = 2,598), gay/lesbian (N = 1,943), bisexual (N = 1,412), pansexual (N = 389), and asexual (N = 165) cisgender individuals. We found that non-heterosexual men scored higher in neuroticism than heterosexual men, consistent with both the minority stress and gender shift hypotheses. Pansexual and bisexual individuals of either sex were higher in openness to experience than heterosexual individuals, and asexual individuals scored lower in extraversion than same-sex individuals of any other sexual orientation. We recorded mixed results for conscientiousness. No differences were found in levels of agreeableness. Effect sizes of the recorded differences are, except for few, generally small.

articles.title: Made in the Image of the Creator? AI Use in Creative Work Reduces Authenticity, Love and Other Psychological Benefits
articles.authors: Jessica Carson; Paul H.P. Hanel; Wijnand A. P. van Tilburg
articles.abstract: Across psychological, philosophical, and theological traditions, creations have been understood as being “made in the image of their creator”—they reflect the person who made them. The rise of generative artificial intelligence, however, has blurred the throughline between creator and creation. Across three experiments (one pre-registered, U.S. and U.K. samples; N = 651), we examined differences in creator outcomes associated with AI-assisted versus human-only creative work. Compared with human-only work, AI-assisted work was associated with significantly lower self- and identity-relevant indicators, including authenticity, self-creation connection, positive affect, and intrinsic motivation, and with higher levels of the “existential ick” emotions of disgust, guilt, and shame. Additionally, we found that the authenticity gap was statistically mediated by the creators’ perception that their AI-assisted work contains less of their love, above and beyond differences in perceived effort, uniqueness, quality, and expensiveness. We also ruled out effort justification as an alternative explanation. Together, these findings suggest that AI reshapes not only how creative work is produced, but also the extent to which creators experience their work as an authentic expression and extension of themselves.

articles.title: Selflessness, Self-Centeredness, and Mental Health Dynamics in Daily Life
articles.authors: Lucas David; Michaël Dambrun
articles.abstract: Experiences of selflessness and happiness are interconnected in everyday life. Both between-person and within-person variations in selflessness are associated with higher and more stable happiness. However, little is known about the role of selflessness in shaping negative mental health at the experiential level. Moreover, self-centeredness, the second regulatory process proposed by the Self-centeredness/Selflessness Happiness Model (SSHM), has received little empirical attention. This experience sampling study addresses these gaps by examining the dynamic effects of selflessness and self-centeredness, between and within individuals. These effects were assessed on positive and negative mental health, as well as on relationship quality with others and nature. Results reveal distinct yet complementary roles for selflessness and self-centeredness: selflessness fosters and stabilizes mental health, self-centeredness undermines it and introduces greater variability. These findings offer insights into the psychological mechanisms underlying complete mental health and illuminate how these processes shape our connection with the social and natural environment.

articles.title: A Crucial Source of Psychological Certainty in Human Cognition: The Certainty Signature of Central Form
articles.authors: Paul Haward
articles.abstract: Humans often exhibit more certainty than is justified. Drawing on recent work in Form Theory, a theory of conceptual structure, the present paper proposes and tests a novel hypothesis about one important source of psychological certainty. On Form Theory, concepts have a central form: a core structure within each concept that stores a subset of its information, gives that information default influence in cognition, and activates a distinctive set of strong form-generated beliefs. The present paper tests the proposal that psychological certainty is one such form-generated belief. In Experiment 1, participants judged which properties would be present in newly encountered instances of familiar concepts. While they generalized both form and non-form properties to new instances, they reported being certain only for form properties. In Experiment 2, participants showed the same pattern for newly learned concepts. As soon as a property had been encoded as part of a concept’s central form, participants were much more likely to report being certain of its presence in a new instance than when the same property had been introduced in a generic sentence, but not as part of the concept’s central form. These findings help reveal a deep connection between psychological certainty and the structure of human concepts. Further, they suggest that conceptual structure is one important source of psychological certainty and provide a framework for investigating whether strongly held beliefs documented in research on stereotyping, memory, clinical depression, and conflict may sometimes derive from how concepts have been structured.

articles.title: Using natural language processing analysis to investigate daily-life positive autobiographical memories
articles.authors: Christina Haag; Lynn Alison Bueeler; David Bürgin; Michel Philipp; Birgit Kleim
articles.abstract: Recalling positive autobiographical memories (AMs) can improve wellbeing, yet few studies capture these memories as they naturally occur or examine their detailed content. In a sample of 70 community adults, we used ecological momentary assessment to assess naturally occurring positive AMs in daily life. Using the large language model-based Python library BERTopic, we identified eight underlying topics: ‘Friends, partner, family’ (68.42%), ‘Work, study’ (8.33%), ‘Being in nature or the moment, pets’ (5.60%), ‘Family & social events’ (3.69%), ‘Exam success’ (3.96%), ‘Success in sports – self or as a fan’ (3.28%), ‘Outdoor activities and sports’ (3.14%), and ‘School days, studies’ (2.19%). Participants reported vivid, sensory AMs accompanied by positive emotions. Greater AM vividness was systematically associated with greater immediate AM-related happiness, underscoring vividness as a potential amplifier in everyday remembering. By sharing our detailed methodology, code, and anonymized examples, we lay the groundwork for large-scale computational analysis of AMs assessed under the noisy and unstructured conditions of everyday life.

articles.title: Artificial Neutrality: Bias and Omission in Large Language Models’ Descriptions of Urban Wildlife
articles.authors: Sam Gowland; Lauren Scott; djt.vanderlinden@gmail.com; Shaun Lawson
articles.abstract:
Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly prominent AI applications, but they remain vulnerable to bias rooted in their training data. Such bias matters in the context of animals, since LLM outputs can influence human attitudes and behaviours toward wildlife. To explore this, we conducted a word association experiment with human participants (N = 300) and with three LLMs (ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini). Each was asked to provide five keywords for species commonly viewed positively (hedgehogs), negatively (rats), and with mixed attitudes (foxes). Sentiment analysis showed that humans exhibited greater variability, generally reflecting expected
attitudes toward each species. LLMs, by contrast, did not reproduce these distributions. Their responses leaned toward neutral or ecological terms rather than emotive words, diverging from typical human conceptualisations.
Our findings suggest that while LLMs may reduce bias through neutralisation, they risk introducing new distortions, underscoring the need for careful, balanced application in wildlife-related contexts.

articles.title: Structure and function of corpus callosum modified by common variation in the ROBO1 gene
articles.authors: Nea Rinne; Elisa Sahari; Tuija Tolonen; Elísabet Einarsdóttir; Juha Salmitaival; Kimmo Alho; Juha Kere; Patrik Wikman
articles.abstract: The corpus callosum (CC) connects the cerebral hemispheres and enables interhemispheric communication that supports numerous cognitive functions, including reading. ROBO1, a dyslexia susceptibility gene involved in axonal midline crossing, has previously been associated with CC structure, but its relationship with the functional organisation of cerebral reading networks remains unclear. Here, we examined associations between ROBO1 variation, CC structure, reading-related brain function, and reading performance in 178 typically reading adolescents and young adults. Variation across five ROBO1 single nucleotide polymorphisms was summarised using principal component analysis. The resulting PC1 score was examined in relation to fractional anisotropy (FA) and tract count across five CC subdivisions, as well as reading-related activation and functional connectivity in cortical regions connected by these pathways. A greater number of rare alleles across the examined variants was associated with lower FA in the central, middle posterior, and posterior CC. ROBO1 variation was also associated with activation in cortical regions corresponding to the endpoints of the CC tracts, as well as with reading-related functional connectivity between these endpoint regions and clusters in the left temporoparietal cortex and right temporal pole. However, neither ROBO1 variation nor CC structure explained reading performance, suggesting that ROBO1 may contribute to individual differences in the structure and function of interhemispheric language networks even in the absence of measurable behavioural differences.

articles.title: Differential Effects of Task-Context and Stimulus-Category Changes on Recognition Memory: A Replication and Extension of Morse et al. (2023)
articles.authors: Raju Pooja; Pritha Ghosh; Vishnu Sreekumar
articles.abstract: Event segmentation is the process by which ongoing experience is organized into discrete events, with event boundaries marking transitions between successive events. Although contextual changes are thought to trigger event segmentation, different types of contextual change may vary in their effectiveness and their consequences for subsequent memory. In the present study, which is a replication of Morse et al. (2023), albeit with some methodological improvements, we examined whether stimulus-category shifts and task-context shifts produce differential consequences for recognition memory and mnemonic discrimination. Across three experiments using the Mnemonic Similarity Task (MST), event boundaries were instantiated by changes in image category (Experiment 1), encoding task (Experiment 2) or both simultaneously (Experiment 3). Task-context shifts produced reliable behavioral signatures of event segmentation, reflected by an increase in post-boundary encoding response times, and also led to impaired recognition memory for items encountered immediately after a boundary. In contrast, stimulus-category shifts alone produced neither time processing costs nor memory impairments. Critically, combining stimulus-category and task-context changes did not increase recognition-memory impairment beyond those observed for task-context shifts alone. Across all experiments, participants’ ability to discriminate similar lure items from studied targets (lure discrimination) was unaffected by whether the items were experienced close to event boundaries. Our findings suggest that event boundaries capable of impacting memory depend more strongly on changes that require updating of task-goals and control states than on changes in perceptual input alone. Broadly, our results indicate that not all contextual changes are functionally equivalent for event segmentation.

articles.title: Business-size bias in consumer dishonesty: Consumers are less likely to cheat small businesses than big ones
articles.authors: Jareef Martuza; Hallgeir Sjåstad; Helge Thorbjørnsen
articles.abstract: Consumer dishonest behavior—such as return fraud, insurance overclaiming, and retail theft—costs businesses billions of dollars every year. Yet the potential role of organizational features in shaping consumer dishonesty remains unclear. This research examines whether consumers are less likely to cheat small businesses than big ones, and why they might do so. While certain normative theories in philosophy contend that moral transgressions—like dishonesty—are equally wrong regardless of victim identity, we suggest that consumers perceive small businesses as more victim-like than big businesses, which increases the moral cost of cheating small businesses. Supporting this hypothesis, a preliminary study (N = 13,239 businesses) and seven main and seven supplemental studies (N = 10,436) reveal that consumers are less likely to cheat small businesses than big ones, across economic crime surveys, scenario-based, conjoint, and incentive-compatible experiments. Further, consumers perceive small businesses as more vulnerable and moral than big businesses, which mediates lower dishonesty toward small businesses, and increasing perceived vulnerability and morality can causally reduce dishonesty toward big businesses. Thus, beyond incentives, consumer dishonesty is also shaped by victim characteristics. Managers could benefit from pre-empting such victim-based biases by considering business size perceptions when considering policies to deter consumer dishonesty.

articles.title: Uptake, Barriers, and Facilitators of Open Science in Clinical Psychology: Findings from an Exploratory Survey in German-speaking Countries
articles.authors: Anja Christine Feneberg; Jakob Fink-Lamotte; Helen Niemeyer
articles.abstract: Open Science practices (OSP) aim to enhance transparency, reproducibility, and research quality, yet empirical research regarding their uptake in clinical psychology remains scarce. The present survey examined OSP across clinical psychological research, teaching, and psychotherapeutic practice at universities and university clinics in German-speaking countries. Based on responses from 130 participants (M=37.13 ± 9.75 years of age, 61.54% female) preregistration, a-priori sample size planning, and open access publishing were the most commonly reported OSP. Concerns regarding data protection and ethics, time constraints, and fear of mistakes were the most prominent barriers, while access to infrastructure and incentives were the most needed types of support. Teaching activities addressed Open Science topics, whereas implementation in clinical practice remained limited. Overall, the findings highlight the need for field-specific guidelines, institutional support, and aligned incentive structures to foster sustainable adoption of OSP across career-stages and contexts.

articles.title: How Researchers’ Analytical Decisions Impact Brand Price Elasticity Estimates: Insights from A Many-Analyst Study
articles.authors: Oliver Koll; Hannes Datta; Karin Teichmann; koen pauwels; Vahideh Abedi; Joop Adema; Anirban Adhikary; Hamed Aghakhani; Gwen Ahn; Simo Alami Chehboune
articles.abstract: Price elasticities are central empirical measures in marketing, informing pricing, promotion planning, or evaluations of consumer responsiveness. Yet estimates may depend not only on brands, categories, and markets but also on the analytical decisions researchers make in transforming raw purchase data into elasticities. We use a many-analyst design in which 156 independent research teams (RTs) estimate brand price elasticities for 68 meat-substitute country-brand combinations from the same dataset. Each team retained discretion over its analytical approach, including choices concerning modeling, aggregation, fixed effects, control variables, and endogeneity correction. Results show substantial heterogeneity in both choices and estimates. Across 10,415 brand price elasticity estimates, the average is -0.61. However, the variation across the 156 RTs is considerable: the average brand price elasticity per RT ranges from -7.3 to +3.1, with a standard deviation of 0.84. Choices related to time aggregation, fixed effects, time controls, and marketing-mix covariates explain the largest share of variation in reported estimates. Because analytical choices occur in configurations rather than in isolation, we cluster RTs and reveal distinct analytical pathways associated with different patterns of estimates. Our findings contribute to elasticity research by identifying modeling decisions that warrant particular scrutiny and to the open science debate by supporting the call for greater transparency about analytical decisions.

articles.title: To whom should punishment communicate? Children's and adults' perceptions of punishment's message
articles.authors: Young-eun Lee; Sophie Noëlle Charles; Larisa Heiphetz
articles.abstract: Why do people punish? Legal and political theories describing punishment as expressive argue that one of punishment's functions is to communicate information (e.g., which behaviors are unacceptable). While this work emphasizes communicating to transgressors, punishment may also show victims that others take their pain seriously. In two studies, we asked how laypeople perceive the communicative nature of punishment. Study 1 found that adults (n=156), but not 4- to 7-year-old children (n=84), evaluated communicating punishment to transgressors more positively than communicating it to victims. Study 2 (n=188 adults and n=87 children) revealed that adults also evaluated communicating the reason underlying punishment to transgressors more positively than communicating it to victims, whereas 5- to 7-year-old children showed a more balanced evaluation of the two targets. Indeed, children provided more favorable evaluations than did adults of scenarios that did not include transgressors as targets of punishment's message. Together, these findings suggest that adults, but not children, consistently prioritize informing transgressors over informing victims, potentially contributing to social responses to wrongdoing that place insufficient emphasis on victims’ informational and emotional needs.

articles.title: Tone Timing: An Eye-Tracking Study of Dynamic F0 Integration in Spoken Word Recognition
articles.authors: Xin Wang; Bob McMurray
articles.abstract: To recognize words, listeners must map a temporally unfolding auditory input to representations at multiple levels.  Typical accounts argue for immediate and incremental integration of asynchronous acoustic cues, such that each cue is used to partially update phonemic or lexical representations as soon as it arrives, with later cues further modulating those decisions. However, recent studies suggest that incrementality is not universal and fricatives follow a different principle in which early cues are stored in a memory buffer and listeners wait to identify the phoneme until all cues have arrived.  It is unknown why different speech sounds show these differences.  Here, we extend this paradigm to lexical tone, an acoustic/phonetic dimension which extends over a syllable and tracks the dynamics of F0.  In a visual world experiment, we index the relative activation of minimal pairs only differing in Mandarin tones as they change over time to ask whether lexical tone is incrementally integrated or processed in a buffered manner. Our findings first show lexical activation patterns are closely coupled to the timing of pitch contours, supporting the immediate integration of lexical tone.  Therefore, with respect to temporal integration of asynchronous cues, tone is like most segments, though different from fricatives.

articles.title: Development of the Alcohol-Linked Typical Experienced Responses Scale
articles.authors: Kohsuke Yamamoto; Mami Kato; Ryo Eguchi
articles.abstract: Alcohol-related subjective experiences are associated with drinking behavior and alcohol use disorders (AUD) risk. However, existing measures access limited domains, such as alcohol expectancies, emotional reactions, or physiological effects, hindering multidimensional assessment of subjective alcohol experiences. This study developed and validated the Alcohol-Linked Typical Experienced Responses (ALTER) Scale, positive/negative and psychological/physiological responses to alcohol consumption among Japanese adults. Habitual drinkers provided free descriptions of alcohol-related experiences, which, together with findings from previous studies, informed the development of candidate items. Study 1’s exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses supported a five-factor structure: Communication Facilitation, Negative Emotional Arousal, Cognitive Decline, Relaxation Responses, and Physiological Responses. The scale demonstrated acceptable internal consistency and one-month test–retest reliability (Study 2). Study 3 supported construct validity through associations with drinking motives, personality, interoceptive awareness, and problematic drinking, assessed using the Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test. Individuals with higher problematic drinking tendencies reported stronger rewarding and aversive psychological responses, whereas physiological responses did not differ significantly. These findings provide initial evidence for the reliability and construct validity of the ALTER Scale as a multidimensional measure of recalled subjective alcohol experiences, providing a framework for examining individual differences in alcohol responses and AUD-related risk.

articles.title: Usage of Digital Technology and Its linkage with the Development of Life Skills, Mental Health, and Psychological Hardiness among university students
articles.authors: Kadim Lovakumari; Tosendra Dwivedi
articles.abstract:
Background: The pervasive use of digital technology among Indian university students has raised concerns about its implications for life skills, mental health, and psychological hardiness. While moderate use may enhance learning, excessive use is associated with adverse psychological outcomes.
Objective: This study examines (a) prevalence of digital technology usage, (b) differences in life skills, mental health, and psychological hardiness across levels of digital technology usage, and (c) interlinkages among these variables.
Methods: The study adopted a two-phase design. In Phase-1, a Self-constructed Digital Technology Usage Scale was developed and standardized on 1,000 university students from Delhi-NCR. In Phase-2, data were collected from an independent sample of 600 postgraduate university students (300 professional, 300 non-professional) from government and private universities in Delhi, using stratified random sampling (Gender x Stream x University Type). Tools used: (1) Life Skills Assessment Scale (Nair et al., 2010), (2) Mental Health Inventory (Jagdish & Srivastava, 1983), and (3) Psychological Hardiness Scale (Singh, 2008).Analysis: Descriptive statistics, independent-samples t-tests, Pearson correlation, One-way ANOVA, and Multiple Regression were performed using SPSS v26.
Results: Moderate users (2-5 hrs/day) showed significantly higher life skills (M=198.60), mental health (M=158.2) and psychological hardiness (M=105.80) compared to low (<2 hrs) and high (>5 hrs) users (F=8.73 to 10.21, p<.01). Mental health (β=.38) and hardiness (β=.32) significantly predicted life skills.
Keywords: Digital Technology Usage, Life Skills, Mental Health, Psychological Hardiness, University Students

articles.title: Preliminary Evidence on Moral Underpinnings of Rape Victim Blaming in Iran: Replication and Extension of Milesi et al. (2020)
articles.authors: Mazyar Bagherian; Homa Sheibani Asl; Zohreh Hashemi Dezaki; Bahare Bahmani
articles.abstract: According to Moral Foundation Theory, people rely on five intuitive-based foundations in their moral decisions. These foundations are divided into Individualizing foundations (Care and Fairness) and Binding foundations (Loyalty, Authority, and Sanctity). In an attempt to replicate Milesi at al’s (2020) findings in a non-WEIRD and honored context, across three studies, we explored the relationship between Moral Foundation and Acceptance of Modern Myths About Sexual Aggression (AMMSA) with rape victim-blaming. Study 1 showed that Fairness, Authority, and Sanctity foundations were predictive of rape victim-blaming. Study 2 showed that binding foundations predict rape victim-blaming in a preregistered analysis. Our cross-country analyses (Iran, Germany, Spain, and Italy) showed that the effects of binding moral foundations were stronger among Iranian participants than those with less-honored cultures (i.e., Italy, Spain, and Germany). Exploratory analyses revealed no differences in rape victim-blaming among men and women. However, men had higher levels of endorsement of AMMSA than women. Religious individuals had higher levels of rape victim-blaming and AMMSA. Findings are discussed concerning the honored context of Iran’s society.

articles.title: Psychological Functions of Prayer: Findings from a Series of Experiments Comparing Prayer to Self-Talk
articles.authors: Aaron D. Cherniak; Pehr Granqvist; Mario Mikulincer
articles.abstract: Research on spiritual/religious practices has paid insufficient attention to the meaning-making frameworks distinguishing them from secular analogs. In three preregistered experiments, we tested whether increasing the salience of prayer among Jews affected felt security and positive and negative affect (Study 1), prosocial emotions (Study 2), and transcendence (Study 3) more than self-talk or routine-activity primes, and whether religiosity and attachment to God moderated these effects. Participants (n = 277, 209, 241) completed spirituality/religiosity measures and were randomized to reflect on prayer or one of two secular controls before completing outcome measures. Prayer increased felt security and empathic concern beyond both controls, whereas prayer and self-talk raised positive affect similarly above the routine activity; negative affect and personal distress were unaffected. Prayer also produced greater transcendence than the routine control, but not significantly more than self-talk. These effects were largely independent of religiosity, but avoidant attachment to God moderated prayer's effects on negative affect (Study 1) and transcendence (Study 3) in opposite directions. Prayer's benefits thus appear to reflect its relational, God-directed character rather than its self-regulatory function alone, though the specificity varies by outcome, with implications for how theories of religious ritual and spiritually integrated interventions conceptualize its active ingredients.

articles.title: Rational decisions in multi-step environments with few rollouts
articles.authors: Sixing Chen; Kristopher T. Jensen; Marcelo G Mattar
articles.abstract: People routinely make decisions by mentally simulating the potential outcomes of their actions. However, this process appears computationally intractable in real-world situations involving sequences of decisions with exponentially many possible futures. How the brain efficiently evaluates temporally extended decisions despite limited cognitive resources remains a fundamental puzzle. Here we present a mathematical theory showing that for decisions in multi-step environments, the rational strategy is to perform only a few mental simulations, formalized as rollouts. This is because the first rollouts provide substantially more information than later ones despite taking a similar amount of time, so the opportunity cost of additional simulations quickly outweighs their marginal benefit. Our framework demonstrates that this efficiency relies on the correlated reward structure of naturalistic environments, which allows information from one rollout to generalize to many related future paths. This theory also explains why, under resource constraints, many shallow rollouts are preferable to fewer deep ones; why apparently myopic decisions can arise without explicit temporal discounting; and how to relate the dynamics of planning to evidence accumulation models. We validate predictions of our theory in two behavioral experiments, which confirm that humans achieve higher reward rates with few rollouts and dynamically adjust their simulation depth based on available cognitive resources. These findings reveal how the brain balances the depth and breadth of mental simulation to make effective decisions under computational constraints, providing a unifying account of planning that bridges computationally intensive search algorithms in machine learning and the remarkable efficiency of human decision-making.

articles.title: ¡Mira! How Latina Mothers use imperatives to guide children’s participation during play
articles.authors: Reinaldo Cabrera Pérez; Gustavo Carlo; Elizabeth D. Peña
articles.abstract: Maternal imperatives are often treated as a unitary form of directiveness despite serving distinct communicative functions. We examined how Spanish-speaking Latina mothers used imperatives during toy play and whether use varied by site and child gender. Forty-eight mother–child dyads from Mexico (n = 25) and the United States (n = 23) participated in semi-structured play interactions. Maternal imperatives were coded as encouragement, redirection, repetition, or scaffolding. Across 1,430 tokens, scaffolding was most frequent (36.4%), followed by encouragement (25.8%), redirection (23.6%), and repetition (14.3%). Lexical choice was strongly associated with communicative function, indicating systematic form–function patterning. Imperative use was largely similar across sites and child gender, although exploratory analyses identified greater repetition in the United States. Findings show that imperative frequency alone provides an incomplete account of maternal directiveness and underscore the importance of considering the interactional functions of direct linguistic forms.

articles.title: Phoneme overlap analysis of the visual benefit for speech-in-noise perception
articles.authors: John Magnotti; Yue Zhang; Lin Zhu; Yingjia Yu; Michael Beauchamp
articles.abstract:
Seeing the face of the talker improves the intelligibility of speech-in-noise, termed the visual
benefit. The visual benefit is usually measured at the whole-word level, with responses classified
as "correct" or "incorrect". An alternative method measures visual benefit using the phoneme
overlap between stimulus and response. In 55 participants presented with auditory and
audiovisual words, phoneme-overlap analysis estimated 289 different visual benefit values,
compared with only three different values for whole-word analysis. Phoneme-overlap detected a
positive visual benefit in 67% of word-participant pairs, in contrast to 32% for whole-word
analysis. Individual words varied greatly in their phoneme-overlap visual benefit, from 1% to
72%. Variability across words was accurately predicted (r = 0.78) by the phoneme composition
of the word and the visual benefit for untested words could be predicted with a median error of
9%. Measuring the visual benefit for individual phonemes revealed similarly high variability
(1% to 70%) with six phonemes (W, F, V, TH, P, AW) exhibiting visual benefit more than one
standard deviation above the mean. The increased sensitivity of phoneme-overlap analysis
relative to conventional whole-word analysis may provide a useful tool for investigating
audiovisual speech perception in clinical, neuroscience and computer science contexts.

articles.title: Inflated Statistics Lead to Incorrect Inference: How (Not) to Make Cognitive Network Group Comparisons
articles.authors: Chun-Ying Tu; Martin Chodorow; Patricia J. Brooks; Emilia Ezrina; Virginia Valian
articles.abstract: Semantic networks are an increasingly popular method for examining the structure of cognitive representations. We identify a pervasive error in group-level network comparisons. This error, embedded in popular statistical software (SemNeT; Christensen & Kenett, 2023), artificially inflates statistical power by (1) treating bootstrap (re)samples as independent observations and (2) failing to treat the standard deviation of the bootstrapped distribution as a standard error. Study 1 illustrates the problem with a representative study; Study 2 documents the error in 42 published studies that use semantic network analysis. Using verbal fluency data from monolingual (N = 94) and bilingual adults (N = 93), Study 3 demonstrates that, in both naive random walk and correlation-based networks, parametric test statistics improperly become significant and increase in magnitude as the number of bootstrap samples increases, without any change in the underlying data. In contrast, percentile bootstrap confidence intervals based on within-iteration contrasts and permutation tests indicate no reliable group differences (i.e., the confidence intervals include 0, and the observed differences fall within the central 95% of the null distributions). Given the pervasiveness of the inflation error in published research, we suspect that many group differences of semantic organization have been overstated.

articles.title: Robust Measurement of Habits with the Forced-Response Task A Multiverse Analysis
articles.authors: José Juan León; Pablo Martínez-López; Francisco Garre-Frutos; David Luque
articles.abstract: Instrumental behavior reflects a balance between two systems: an outcome-oriented, goal-directed system and a cognitively efficient habit system that gradually gains control with repeated instrumental responding in stable contexts. While overtraining reliably induces habits in animal models, human participants often retain goal-directed control when their performance is assessed using devaluation paradigms. To address this translational gap, the forced-response method has emerged as a promising approach for studying goal-directed and habitual behavior by constraining the time available to respond. This method imposes a dual task in which participants must respond accurately to an instrumental discriminative stimulus at a specific time signaled by a sound. Because the onset of the discriminative stimulus varies across trials, the time available for response preparation is systematically manipulated. Restricting this time can unmask stimulus-driven responses when the goal-directed system has insufficient time to override them. Although the forced-response method has become increasingly popular, its use has also been accompanied by growing flexibility in data analysis, creating a potential “garden of forking paths.” Using four independent datasets, we generated 48 a priori valid preprocessing pipelines to assess variability in two discrete measures of habitual behavior—the proportion of habits and the habit index—as well as their split-half reliability and the proportion of habits as a continuous function of the available response time, modeled using generalized additive models. Results indicated that both habit measures were generally robust across preprocessing pipelines. The proportion of habits was more sensitive to specific preprocessing choices, particularly accuracy and timing-synchrony exclusion criteria, but also showed greater reliability. In all cases, however, the resulting variability was small. Reliability analyses yielded acceptable estimates in most analytic universes. Overall, these findings support the forced-response method as a robust paradigm for studying habit formation and expression in humans.

articles.title: Cognitive Control Neural Correlates of Negative Affective in Psychosis Spectrum Disorders: A Laboratory and Ecological Momentary Assessment Study
articles.authors: Takakuni Suzuki; Margo W Menkes; Maureen Walton; Melvin G McInnis; Jian Kang; Tara A. Niendam; Ivy Fei Tso; Stephan F. Taylor
articles.abstract: Individuals with schizophrenia-spectrum (SZ) and bipolar-spectrum disorders (BD) report experiencing heightened negative affect (NA), which can be operationalized as stable traits and dynamic states. While cognitive control is a potential underlying mechanism, identifying neural underpinning of NA has been challenging. This could be due to the lack of such investigation, but also a comprehensive framework to investigate the association specificity. Data were collected from 105 participants (34 SZ, 34 BD, 37 healthy control [HC]) on the five-factor model of personality traits, cognitive control electroencephalography (EEG), and self-reported mood and contexts via ecological momentary assessment (EMA). Cognitive control indices of EEG were extracted as event-related potentials (ERPs) and time-frequency theta-band activities from three flanker tasks varying in valence (neutral, unpleasant, and pleasant). Participants with SZ and BD generally reported higher NA traits, lower Extraversion, lower Conscientiousness traits, higher Psychoticism, and high average and fluctuation in EMA NA-related experiences than HC participants. Participants with SZ experienced more EMA unpleasant events, were more upset by them, and put more effort into avoiding them. EEG theta-band power from the arrow task was associated mostly with NA-related traits and tendency, and theta-band power from the unpleasant task was associated with EMA unpleasant event occurrence and reactions. ERPs and theta phase activities did not relate to any traits or daily experiences, and no other traits and experiences were related to EEG measures. Cognitive control EEG theta-band power was associated with trait and state NA specifically, potentially reflecting a transdiagnostic indicator of cognitive control and neural mechanism underlying stress-vulnerability in SZ and BD.

articles.title: Form Composition: The Generative Structural Engine of Metaphors in Human Cognition
articles.authors: Paul Haward
articles.abstract: Drawing on Form Theory, a theory of conceptual structure, this paper explores the origins of non-literal meaning in human cognition and proposes a generative structural engine based on each concept’s central form, a unitary structure embedded within every concept we learn, which encodes a compressed subset of each concept’s information and gives that information default influence in cognition. Recent work has found evidence for form composition, a default bias to interpret complex expressions in terms of each concept’s central form. The present paper tests the hypothesis that form composition operates across domain boundaries in a way that immediately generates potential metaphorical meanings. Across four experiments, participants judged interpretations of metaphors as possible if those interpretations involved form-encoded properties, even when the metaphors and the concepts involved were novel. In contrast, they rejected metaphors involving non-form properties as impossible. These findings suggest that form composition enables the spontaneous generation of non-literal meaning. Rather than being a derivative part of composition, metaphor may therefore emerge directly from the underlying structure of concepts and how they naturally combine. The findings have implications for concept learning and other forms of linguistic creativity. They also suggest why humans may possess a persistent bias toward reductive thinking across domains.

articles.title: From Treating to Preventing Distress through Psychological Prehabilitation – A  Novel Theoretical Framework
articles.authors: Michael Baliousis; Lauren Charlotte Heathcote; Chloe Grimmett; Lynn Calman; Christopher Meek; Nima Moghaddam; David Dawson; Mike Rennoldson
articles.abstract:
Background: In cancer prehabilitation, physical components predominate and psychological preparation is often overlooked. Yet up to half of patients develop distress during treatment, which undermines adherence, recovery, and quality of life. Psychological care remains largely reactive and lacks a unifying theoretical framework for prevention. Preventing distress poses three challenges: building resilience; doing so before patients have experienced treatment stressors; and tailoring this to each patient.

Methods: Following conceptual review guidance, we selected theories that address these challenges and integrated them into one framework.

Results: We synthesised five theoretical traditions (stress and resilience, social identity, affective forecasting, stress inoculation, and narrative identity) into four areas for assessment and intervention, framed as questions for the patient. What do I bring? covers beliefs about illness and treatment, coping and emotion regulation, and social support and group memberships. Where am I heading? covers how patients expect treatment to feel, including underestimating their ability to adapt. What do I need? uses stress inoculation to build and rehearse coping, with imagery for stressors that cannot be simulated. Who am I (becoming)? links these through the patient's personal story, from past coping to future recovery. The framework specifies testable mechanisms; for example, limited resources and skewed forecasts may predict distress during treatment. It maps onto universal, targeted, and specialist levels of provision.

Conclusions: The framework provides a theoretical basis for preventing distress through Psychological Prehabilitation for Cancer Treatment. It can guide intervention design, staff training, and evaluation. Research priorities are to test its mechanisms, evaluate it as a complex intervention, and develop brief screening tools that predict future distress.

articles.title: Visuospatial Orienting in Working Memory is Preserved in Adults with ADHD Symptoms
articles.authors: Luísa Superbia-Guimarães; Amy Louise Atkinson; Richard John Allen; Valerie Camos
articles.abstract: People with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) are reported to have pervasive deficits in working memory (WM), yet mechanistic explanations for such deficits are lacking. Research suggests that attentional mechanisms such as reward-based prioritisation and visuospatial orienting are intact in this population (Atkinson et al., 2025; Superbia-Guimarães et al., 2022, 2023). To further examine these mechanisms, we investigated the hypotheses that deficient visuospatial orienting during encoding and maintenance are at the root of WM deficits in adults with ADHD symptoms.  Eighty-four symptomatic participants (Mage = 28.4 years, SD = 4.6) and 107 controls (Mage = 29.4, SD = 4.4) had their symptoms assessed with the Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale. They each took part in one of two experiments involving an item (colour or unfamiliar shape) recognition memory task that incorporated pre- and retro-cues. Across both experiments, we found strong evidence of beneficial pre- and retro-cueing effects upon memory accuracy and reaction time (RT). However, we found no evidence for the expected group differences nor the interaction between symptom status and cueing condition. There was also no evidence for correlations between ADHD symptom scores, recognition accuracy, RT, and cueing benefits. Therefore, attentional mechanisms are unlikely to explain deficits in WM in individuals with symptoms of ADHD.

articles.title: The ontogenesis of socio-affective touch perception: Assessing valence and inferring social relationships from observed tactile interactions.
articles.authors: Louise P Kirsch; Monica Nkele; Adeline Depierreux; Olivier Mascaro
articles.abstract:
Social touch is a powerful communication channel conveying social dispositions and affiliative relationships across the primate lineage. Yet, how social inferences from observed socio-affective touch develop remains poorly understood. Three complementary experiments with 217 children aged 3 to 6 and 144 adults address this gap.
Experiment 1 tested the ability to assess the valence of observed tactile interactions. By age 3, children accurately evaluated a range of positive and negative touch interactions, integrating multiple cues, including the recipient of the touch (object vs. person) and stroke speed—consistent with key properties of skin afferents that process touch. Valence evaluation of observed touch thus emerges early.
Experiments 2a-2b examined children's and adults' ability to infer social bonds from observed touch. Participants watched two actresses: one stroked a character, while the other performed a matched neutral gesture (no touch, or touch at very fast speed). From around age 4, children consistently judged the stroking actress as more likely to be affiliated with the touched character—but only with that specific character, not with a different one. Adults, by contrast, generalized this inference, expecting affiliation between the stroking actress and characters beyond the one she had touched.
These findings reveal a developmental progression in processing observed social touch, from valence detection, to relationship-specific inference, to generalized trait attribution. Thus, observed-touch processing relies not on one unified ability but on a multilevel system with distinct developmental timelines—underscoring touch's central role in social cognition and the need for further research bridging these domains.

articles.title: Gesturing at the Boundary: Can Concurrent Beat Gestures Bias Speech Segmentation?
articles.authors: Huandi Chen; Hans Rutger Bosker
articles.abstract: Beat gestures, rhythmic hand movements that reliably co-occur with prosodically prominent syllables, are one of the most common types of gestures in everyday conversations. Given their coupling to speech prosody, they can influence stress perception and facilitate lexical access. Still, little is known about their contribution to speech segmentation. Recent work has shown that beat gestures conveying distinct rhythms in a precursor (i.e., distal context) can bias the segmentation of subsequently presented acoustically ambiguous speech (Bosker, 2026). However, whether a single beat gesture co-occurring with the ambiguous speech (i.e., proximal context) can similarly shift boundary placement remains unknown. Across two experiments, participants segmented acoustically ambiguous four-syllable sequences (e.g., cry sister nip vs. crisis turnip) while a beat gesture was aligned to either the second or third syllable. Unexpectedly, no reliable effect of gesture placement on segmentation was observed. These findings suggest that isolated beat gestures may not function as reliable independent cues to speech segmentation. Instead, their influence may depend on the broader audiovisual and rhythmic context.

articles.title: An Ethnography of Rituals and Sound Practices among Spiritual-But-Not-Religious Practitioners in Glastonbury
articles.authors: Sotirios Kolios; Kathryn Diane Ford; Aiyana Koka Willard
articles.abstract:
Purpose: Musical sound is common in ritual but has often been treated as part of ritual performance rather than as an object of analysis in its own right. This ethnographic study examines how ritual organisation and musical sound vary across spiritual-but-not-religious (SBNR) practices in Glastonbury, UK, and what these patterns imply for contemporary ritual theory.

Methods: Drawing on ethnographic fieldwork, participant observation, fieldnotes, and reflexive interpretation across community, small-group, and solitary ritual settings, we compared ritual organisation and the use of musical sound across different participatory contexts.

Results: We identified three overlapping ritual categories—community, small-group, and solitary rituals—differing in participation scale, social proximity, ritual authority, and alignment of intention. Across these contexts, three recurring functional dimensions were evident: signalling identity and commitment, strengthening social bonds and spiritual identification, and instrumentality. Musical sound was patterned alongside these dimensions. Instrument-produced sounds, singing, chants, and phonetic vocalisations were used to mark ritual time and space, regulate affect and attention, coordinate participation, and communicate identity and belonging. Their relative prominence varied with ritual scale, social organisation, and perceived purpose.

Conclusion: These findings suggest that ritual is better understood as a multidimensional ritual ecology than through fixed typologies. They also challenge accounts that treat goal demotion or causal opacity as universal features of ritual. Musical sound emerges as a multifunctional ritual facilitator whose acoustic, embodied, and culturally learned properties help practitioners structure, experience, and differentiate ritual life.

articles.title: Adaptive multi-frequency oscillator modeling of coordination recovery during rhythm switching in four-person drumming groups
articles.authors: Bavo Van Kerrebroeck; Alexander Pantelis Demos; Marc Leman; Marcelo Wanderley; Caroline Palmer; Pieter-Jan Maes
articles.abstract: Musical ensemble coordination requires groups to maintain shared timing while adapting to perturbations and changing rhythmic constraints. We developed an adaptive multi-frequency oscillator model of how human quartets recover coordination during switches between binary and ternary meters. The model combines nonlinear harmonic phase coupling, coupling-driven frequency adaptation, and target-directed frequency relaxation within a four-oscillator network, allowing individual tempo adaptation while preserving subgroup-specific coupling within and between dyads. An individual spontaneous production rate dependent resonance term did not reliably improve the model’s prediction for quartet outcomes and was omitted from subsequent analyses. Model parameters were optimized by minimizing discrepancies between empirical and simulated inter-onset intervals, pairwise asynchronies, and cluster-phase dynamics. Simulations reproduced transient destabilization after perturbation cues followed by recovery towards a new coordinated state. Mixed-effects analyses showed that the model fits empirical quartets better than surrogate quartets, indicating sensitivity to genuine human coordination structure and generalization to held-out test data. Optimized parameters revealed condition-specific mechanisms: within-dyad coupling was lower overall in Complex polyrhythms and Binary meter, whereas between-dyad coupling was also lower in Complex rhythms, with a reduction for Ternary meter dyads. Frequency relaxation rates were higher in Complex polyrhythms than Simple isochronous rhythms and in Binary than Ternary meter, suggesting faster target-directed frequency relaxation during polyrhythmic coordination. Stability analyses revealed bounded regions of period and phase synchronization, including Arnold tongue-like entrainment regions shaped by coupling strength, relaxation asymmetry, meter ratio, and the specified harmonic basis. Together, these findings suggest that quartet synchronization depends on a balance between differentiated interpersonal coupling, adaptive frequency regulation, and preservation of distinct rhythmic roles. The model provides an interpretable dynamical framework for understanding how human groups recover and reorganize coordinated behavior under changing rhythmic demands.

articles.title: Gender Differences in Emotional Sharing:   Reconsidering the Role of Traditional Femininity/masculinity
articles.authors: X. Jia; Annet Kleiboer; Karen Holtmaat; Sander L. Koole
articles.abstract: A substantial body of research indicates that men, on average, share emotions less readily than women. The current research examined the extent to which gender differences in traditional femininity and traditional masculinity account for this relationship. In Study 1, 1,500 Dutch adults (938 women and 562 men) completed measurements of emotional sharing (Distress Disclosure Index, DDI; Kahn & Hessling, 2001), gender self-concept (Dutch Gender self-concept Questionnaire, NSIV; Willemsen & Fischer, 1996), and self-stigma towards help-seeking (Self-Stigma of Seeking Help Scale, SSOSH; Vogel et al., 2006). In Study 2, 1,645 Dutch adults (979 women and 666 men) completed measurements of emotional sharing (DDI), gender self-concept (Bem Sex Role Inventory, BSRI; Bem, 1981), and help-seeking intentions (General Help Seeking Questionnaire, GHSQ; Wilson et al., 2005). Gender differences in emotional sharing were consistently partially explained by traditional femininity, but not by traditional masculinity. The same pattern emerged for help-seeking self-stigma (Study 1) and intentions (Study 2). These findings contradict widespread beliefs that traditional masculinity keeps men from disclosing their emotional vulnerabilities and seeking mental healthcare. More generally, the present findings highlight gender self-concept as a valuable theoretical concept in understanding the psychology of emotional sharing.

articles.title: (Un)informed Consent: To What Degree are Research Participants 'Informed' by Common Consent Procedures in Psychology under EU Data Protection Law?
articles.authors: Luisa Jansen; Annika Iris Külpmann; Dara Hallinan; Franziska Boehm; Malte Elson
articles.abstract: There is reason to believe that consent forms in psychological research may routinely not fulfill the requirements for consent outlined in EU data protection law. Where this is the case, the legitimacy of the research conducted may be undermined. However, so far, there is only preliminary data to support the proposition that compliance may not be the norm (Hallinan et al., 2023a). We present the results of a content analysis of a sample of psychological research reports and consent forms used in those studies. We contacted authors of studies published between 2019 and 2021 and asked them to share the corresponding consent materials, resulting in N = 101 sets of papers and consent forms. We evaluated the compliance of consent forms with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and systematically compared the data collected as part of empirical research, as reported in publications, with the details provided in the respective consent forms given to research participants. Results indicate that all consent forms lack essential information for participants, particularly regarding the data controller, the data collected in the study, and participants' legal rights, even when studies involve collecting sensitive data (n = 58). We discuss the shortcomings and present ways forward for psychological researchers to facilitate both the sharing of research data and the protection of their participants’ privacy, when enabling participants to make the consent they give actually informed.

articles.title: Exploring the Role of Transportation and Narrative Persuasion in Historical Virtual Reality from a Democratic Education Perspective
articles.authors: Lea Frentzel-Beyme; Hannah Decker; Nicole Krämer
articles.abstract: Virtual  reality  (VR)  is  increasingly  used  in  history  education  to  enable  immersive  engagement  with  the  past.  Although  these  applications  may  stimulate  interest  and  emotional  involvement, concerns have been raised about their potential to hinder critical reflection and foster  uncritical  acceptance  of  story-consistent  beliefs.  Drawing  on  the  transportation-imagery  model,  the  present  study  (N  =  106)  investigates  the  correlations  between  transportation  (i.e.,  narrative  immersion)  in  the  history-related  VR  application  Anne  Frank  House  VR  and  users’  emotional  responses,  knowledge,  and  story-consistent  political  beliefs.  Special  attention  is  paid  to  the  role  of  users’  political  orientation.  The  results  indicate  that  transportation is positively correlated with emotional responses and story-consistent beliefs (e.g., support for refugees) but not with factual or perceived knowledge. These findings point to the persuasive potential and educational opportunities offered by VR for history education. Although VR may not convey knowledge, it may foster engagement with socially and politically relevant topics.

articles.title: Attention Fragmentation: Toward a Formal Construct Definition, a Differentiated Nomological Network, and a Research Agenda for Scale Development
articles.authors: Diksha Sharma; Pooja Tyagi
articles.abstract: The proliferation of notification-driven, multi-device digital environments has produced widespread everyday experiences of scattered, discontinuous focus. Researchers and commentators frequently label this experience “attention fragmentation” (AF), yet the term is used loosely in the literature and has not been formally distinguished from adjacent constructs such as distraction, multitasking, attention span, task-switching, mind-wandering, and smartphone addiction/compulsive use. No dedicated, psychometrically validated scale for AF currently exists; where researchers have needed to quantify AF, they have relied on proxy measures built for other purposes — most recently a reverse-scored trait-mindfulness scale (Bayaskar & Sharma, 2026). This manuscript (a) proposes a formal operational definition of AF grounded in the interruption and attentional-control literatures, (b) systematically differentiates AF from six related constructs and the instruments used to measure them, (c) documents a genuine, current, and specific measurement gap, (d) proposes a tentative five-dimensional structure to guide item generation, and (e) outlines a three-phase empirical program: item development, exploratory factor analysis, and confirmatory factor analysis with convergent, discriminant, and incremental validity testing for developing and validating an Attention Fragmentation Scale (AFS). This manuscript reports no new empirical data; it establishes the conceptual and methodological foundation for the validation studies that follow.

articles.title: Discussing Racial Demographic Change Online: Constructive Discourse Is Prevalent, Rewarded, and Propagated
articles.authors: Jonathan Doriscar; Anika Wilsnack; Tessa Charlesworth
articles.abstract: Racial demographic change is transforming the United States away from a White majority, a shift that can make concerns about group status especially salient. Public responses increasingly unfold in online video comment spaces, which are often perceived as ubiquitously hostile and toxic. Using 14 years of YouTube and TikTok comments (N = 101,103) responding to 106 high-engagement videos, we operationalize two discourse-feature indices: destructive features (e.g., toxicity and identity attacks) and constructive features (e.g., compassion and curiosity).
