Goals in Focus (GiF) is a novel cognitive–behavioural intervention targeting a comprehensive set of mechanisms implicated in motivational negative symptoms and reduced goal-directed behaviour. This single-blind, randomised controlled pilot trial examined the feasibility, safety, and acceptability of GiF. Thirty Participants with schizophrenia-spectrum disorders and at least moderate motivational negative symptoms were randomised to receive either up to 24 GiF sessions over six months or a waitlist control condition. Blinded assessments were conducted at baseline and six months post-randomisation (T1). Feasibility was evaluated against prespecified criteria for recruitment, eligibility, consent, retention, data completeness, attrition, and treatment exposure. Safety and acceptability were assessed through adverse event monitoring and satisfaction ratings alongside qualitative feedback, respectively. Preliminary efficacy was examined using with the motivational negative symptoms subscale of the Brief Negative Symptom Scale as the primary outcome and ecological momentary assessment (EMA) of goal pursuit mechanisms. All feasibility criteria were met except for treatment exposure. GiF was safe and well accepted. The baseline-adjusted effect on motivational negative symptoms at T1 was small and imprecise (b = 0.94, 95% CI [−3.17, 5.05]), compatible with both improvement and deterioration. EMA outcomes showed more promising signals of improvement. Overall, GiF appears to be feasible safe and well accepted although refinements to treatment exposure are warranted before progressing to a definitive efficacy trial.

articles_hidden.title: Eye Tracking and NLP: A Survey and an Outlook
articles_hidden.authors: Yevgeni Berzak; David Robert Reich; Omer Shubi; Lena A. Jäger
articles_hidden.abstract: With the rise of LLMs, NLP has been redefining itself as a field of study, with an increasing interest shift towards areas such as NLP for science, model analysis, human-centered AI and user-facing applications. As part of this transformation, in recent years, a new area of NLP which combines text processing with eye movements in reading has been emerging. Recent work has demonstrated that this area has a strong potential for driving innovation in NLP and enhancing its scientific and societal impact. In this survey, we characterize the main streams of work on the intersection of eye tracking for reading and NLP, provide critical commentary on promises and challenges, and identify key open directions that can guide future work in this area.

articles_hidden.title: Identifying people with psychotic illnesses who could reduce or discontinue antipsychotic medications with a lower risk of relapse: a scoping review
articles_hidden.authors: Anna Liguori; Sarah Markham; Elen Williams; Firoza Davies; Anna Ferguson Montague; Alexandra Burton; Natalie Shoham
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Psychotic disorders can confer a substantial illness burden. Whilst Antipsychotic Medications (APMs) are effective in preventing relapse, they are associated with significant adverse effects, leading some patients to consider APM dose reduction or discontinuation.
Aim: We aimed to synthesise evidence on factors associated with relapse vs no relapse following APM dose reduction or discontinuation in patients with psychotic disorders. 
Methods: We searched Embase, PsycINFO, PubMed, CINAHL and grey literature sources with no date restrictions and followed PRISMA guidelines. We included evidence sources which reported on factors associated with relapse/ no relapse following APM dose reduction or discontinuation in patients with a psychotic disorder, or tools to identify patients with a lower risk of relapse. We consulted our Lived Experience Advisory Panel (LEAP) throughout the review process.
Results: 69 studies met our inclusion criteria. 60 reported empirical evidence on factors associated with relapse/ no relapse, while 8 sources provided expert opinion or guideline-based recommendations and 1 source included both empirical results and expert opinion. We identified 62 independent factors across sociodemographic, illness, treatment, and biological domains. No factor had sufficiently consistent evidence to support its use as a reliable predictor of relapse. Factors reported in expert opinion pieces and guidelines largely aligned with those in empirical studies.
Conclusions: While factors affecting relapse risk following APM dose reduction or discontinuation are increasingly being researched, current evidence does not support any specific factor as a predictor of successful APM dose reduction or discontinuation. Nevertheless, several potentially promising factors warrant further investigation.

articles_hidden.title: Tuning in: how interoception shapes body image across early adolescence
articles_hidden.authors: Mariana Von Mohr; Rosie Donaghy; Vivien Ainley; Abigail Agyemang; Manos Tsakiris
articles_hidden.abstract: Early adolescence is a critical time marked by dynamic changes in physiology, appearance and social environment. These changes are also reflected in how adolescents perceive themselves, in-cluding their bodies. The transition from pre-pubertal through pubertal stages allows us to con-sider the development of the self from the perspective of how body perception, both from within and from the outside, changes. While research in adults and post-puberty adolescents suggests that lower interoceptive accuracy is associated with greater body image concerns, how these fac-tors interact during puberty remains unknown. We tested a sample of 181 girls (aged 10-14 years), spanning from pre-puberty to post-puberty, on measures of interoceptive accuracy and behavioural and self-report measures of body image. Lower interoceptive accuracy predicted greater body image dissatisfaction. Moreover, this relationship was moderated by puberty stage, showing that the protective effect of higher interoceptive accuracy against body image dissatis-faction was stronger during more advanced stages of puberty. Our findings show that interocep-tive influences extend from the basic multisensory integration to conscious attitudes about our body during a critical developmental period, highlighting the positive role that better interocep-tion can play in mental health.

articles_hidden.title: Uncorrected publication bias distorts the spindle-memory link: Comment on Chen et al (2024) “Sleep spindles consolidate declarative memory with tags: A meta-analysis of adult data”
articles_hidden.authors: Péter Przemyslaw Ujma
articles_hidden.abstract: The recent meta-analyis by Chen et al (2024) investigates the link between sleep spindles and the consolidation of tagged declarative memory traces and reports substantial publication bias. The present commentary discusses the significance of publication bias in the literature of the cognitive neuroscience of sleep spindles. Using the dataset published by the original authors, it is demonstrated that with adequate controls for publication bias, the link between sleep spindles and memory consolidation is greatly diminished or absent, in line with the pattern seen in other recent meta-analyses. Large samples, transparent and standardized analysis strategies, and strict controls for publication bias in meta-analyses are essential to ensure replicability in the cognitive neuroscience of sleep spindles.

articles_hidden.title: Associations between adverse childhood experiences, parent-child and peer attachment relationships, and daily-life self-harm in adolescents
articles_hidden.authors: Julie Janssens; Ginette Lafit; Eva De Corte; Robin Achterhof; Karlijn Susanna Francisca Maria Hermans; Anu Pauliina Hiekkaranta; Inez Myin-Germeys; Olivia J Kirtley
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objective: Adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) are associated with self-harm, but it remains unclear whether they are differentially associated with self-harm thoughts and behaviours and which factors may attenuate these associations. We investigated associations between ACEs and lifetime and daily-life self-harm thoughts and behaviours in adolescents, and whether paternal, maternal, or peer attachment relationship quality moderated these associations. Additionally, we explored associations with specific types of ACEs.
Method: N = 1014 adolescents (mean age = 14.05 years, SD = 1.91; 66.66% female) were recruited from the general population through schools across Flanders, Belgium. Retrospective questionnaires assessed ACEs, lifetime self-harm thoughts and behaviours, and paternal, maternal, and peer attachment relationship quality. Experience Sampling Methodology (ESM) assessed daily-life self-harm thoughts and behaviours ten times per day for six days.
Results: Greater exposure to ACEs was associated with lifetime self-harm and with greater odds of reporting self-harm thoughts and behaviours in daily life, but not with the intensity of daily-life self-harm thoughts when present. Maternal attachment relationship quality attenuated the associations between ACEs and lifetime self-harm and between ACEs and daily-life thought intensity, but did not moderate the occurrence of daily-life self-harm thoughts or behaviours. Paternal and peer attachment relationship quality did not moderate these associations. Exploratory analyses indicated variation across ACE types, with sexual victimization showing the most consistent associations across lifetime and daily-life self-harm outcomes.
Conclusions: Findings are consistent with conceptualizing ACEs as background vulnerability factors within the pre-motivational phase of the IMV model and suggest that maternal attachment relationship quality may attenuate some associations between ACEs and adolescent self-harm. Distinguishing between the occurrence and intensity of self-harm thoughts in daily life may help clarify how childhood adversity relates to self-harm.

articles_hidden.title: Causal Strength Under Structure Uncertainty
articles_hidden.authors: Björn Meder; Magda Osman; Simon Stephan; Michael R. Waldmann
articles_hidden.abstract: How should a learner estimate the strength of a causal influence when it is uncertain whether the causal relation exists? We address this question using the framework of Bayesian causal induction. Existing accounts have primarily focused either on inference about causal structure or on estimation of causal strength under an assumed structure. We propose structure-averaged causal strength as a method for estimating causal strength under structure uncertainty. By averaging causal strength across alternative structures according to their posterior probabilities, the account provides a strength estimate that reflects uncertainty about both whether a causal relation exists and how strong it is. Normatively, our analyses clarify how causal strength should be estimated when the existence of the causal relation itself remains uncertain. Empirically, structure-averaged strength provides accurate predictions of human judgments of causal influence across a broad set of published studies, suggesting that human causal judgments reflect uncertainty about both causal strength and causal structure. Together, our analyses show how inferences about causal structure shape judgments of causal strength under uncertainty.

articles_hidden.title: The ‘stickiness’ of disgust: Testing the hypothesis of disgust intractability in the context of instrumental reversal learning.
articles_hidden.authors: Emily Bagley; Camilla Nord
articles_hidden.abstract: Discrete emotion theories conceptualise fear and disgust as distinct emotions. This notion is supported by the finding that Pavlovian disgust conditioning is more resistant to extinction than fear conditioning—disgust may be ‘stickier’ than fear. Dimensional emotion theories challenge this, suggesting that categorical differences between emotions reflect variations along shared dimensions of valence and arousal. Reinforcement learning assumes a dimensional framework: assuming that learning from negative events depends on an outcome’s valence and arousal. Here, using a novel online reversal learning task and modelling framework (n = 340), we show that instrumental punishment learning is not ‘outcome agnostic’. Emotion-learning differs from points-based learning, and disgust-learning is uniquely ‘sticky’, altering perseverative error-rate, lose-shift probability, and a model-based ‘stickiness’ parameter, relative to other types of learning. This suggests that whilst some features of learning are shared between emotions, disgust has a distinct behavioural profile, with implications for emotion science and computational psychiatry.

articles_hidden.title: From Prediction Accuracy to Prediction Use: A Monitoring-Centered Framework for Interactive Sport Expertise
articles_hidden.authors: Yingzhi Lu; Mengkai Luan; Xiaoran Gao; Wenzi Wang; Chen Yiheng; Chenglin Zhou
articles_hidden.abstract: Action anticipation is widely recognized as a cornerstone of expert performance in interactive sport. Decades of research have shown that skilled performers predict upcoming actions more accurately than less-skilled performers by extracting kinematic cues and integrating them with contextual information. This literature has provided a powerful account of how anticipatory predictions are formed. Yet, interactive sport rarely ends when a prediction is generated, because opponents continue to move, sensory evidence changes, contextual priors may mislead, and performers must determine whether an initial prediction remains useful for action. In this narrative review, we argue that the field should move beyond anticipation accuracy toward the adaptive use of anticipation during unfolding interaction. Drawing on sport expertise research, predictive-processing accounts, performance-monitoring theory, observed-action error studies, and sport-specific neurophysiological evidence, we propose a monitoring-centered framework for interactive sport expertise. In this framework, anticipation generates probabilistic reference states, monitoring evaluates whether these states remain aligned with unfolding input, and functional discrepancy processing determines whether mismatch matters for action goals, affordances, and motor plans. We further argue that discrepancy processing is graded and functionally meaningful rather than binary. From this perspective, expert performers may not only predict better; they may also detect diagnostic mismatch more selectively, tolerate irrelevant variability, and couple action-relevant discrepancy information with sport-specific motor preparation and adjustment. The framework yields testable predictions for assessment, training, and future research on expert performance in sport.

articles_hidden.title: When Vision Disagrees with Language: Private and Population-Level Color Knowledge  in Red–Green Dichromacy
articles_hidden.authors: Jiahui Lu; Ziyi Xiong; Peijun Yuan; Xiaoying Wang; Yanchao Bi
articles_hidden.abstract: Human concepts are shaped by two distinct information sources: private sensorimotor experience and socially transmitted knowledge mainly conveyed through language in an abstract symbolic form. Because information geometry in these sources is largely aligned, their relative contributions to conceptual representation are difficult to disentangle. We exploit a group-level dissociation, in which the alignment between sensory color geometry and population-level language structure diverges systematically (red–green dichromacy vs. trichromacy), and a model-level dissociation (object-color geometry derived from large language models vs. from image-based sensory models), to disentangle vision and language contributions to object knowledge. Sensory color geometry differed behaviorally and neurally between dichromats and trichromats, yet behavioral object-color representations converged across groups and corresponded robustly with language-derived geometry. LadATL consistently expressed language-derived geometry across tasks and groups, whereas LpFG showed a group-dependent representational profile in the chromatic-object task: trichromats showed relatively greater correspondence with sensory-derived geometry, whereas dichromats retained correspondence with both geometries. Dichromats also showed stronger intrinsic connectivity of LadATL with LpFG and EVC. These findings reveal how the brain flexibly draws on sensory evidence and socially transmitted knowledge to maintain population-aligned conceptual representations across heterogeneous sensory experiences.

articles_hidden.title: Correspondence Is Not Mechanism: A Construct-Validity Audit of Implicit Egotism
articles_hidden.authors: Simon Bibby
articles_hidden.abstract: People like the letters of their own names a little more than other letters, and the digits of their own birthdays a little more than other digits. From those small laboratory preferences, a research programme has inferred that people are disproportionately drawn to places, partners, occupations, and purchases carrying their own letters, names, or numbers, and that unconscious self-association is what draws them. This article develops a seven-question diagnostic standard for evaluating whether evidence linking a laboratory effect to real-world outcomes identifies the proposed mechanism or only a correspondence. The standard is applied in a paper-by-paper audit of implicit egotism. Both preferences have laboratory support, although the name-letter effect is more extensively replicated. The extension claims audited here lack comparable evidence that specifically identifies the proposed mechanism. Across the archival, field, and corpus literature audited here, the designs cannot separate implicit egotism from marriage within ethnic groups, cohort effects, and family lineage, and where randomisation removes those confounds, awareness of the cue, ordinary similarity, attention and social distance remain. Where reanalysis has applied corrected baselines, many of the original effects have reduced or disappeared, and where correspondence survives, unconscious self-association has not been identified as its source. The strongest residual archival finding, examined as a limiting case, does not isolate the mechanism either. The audit therefore offers a revised evidential assessment of one programme and a diagnostic standard applicable to other laboratory-to-real-world mechanism claims. In the laboratory the phenomenon is robust. Outside it, the evidence does not yet show that it shapes the choices people make.

articles_hidden.title: Norms for Emotional Valence and Polarity for 3,596 French Words: Implications for Lexical Processing
articles_hidden.authors: Aurélie Garrone; Maximiliano A. Wilson; Georges Chedid; Christophe Bedetti; Guillaume T. Vallet; Simona Maria Brambati; Maxime Montembeault
articles_hidden.abstract: Language and emotion are closely interconnected, with words carrying affective properties, such as emotional valence, ranging from negative to positive with a neutral midpoint, and emotional polarity, which reflects the absolute distance from that midpoint. Although norms for emotional valence and polarity exist in many languages, they remain limited for French, particularly Québec French. We therefore aim to 1) develop norms for emotional valence and emotional polarity in a set of 3,596 highly characterized French words taken from the French Lexicon Project (Ferrand et al., 2010); and 2) assess the influence of valence and polarity on lexical decision times in a word recognition task. A group of 351 French-speaking participants from Quebec took part in an online valence rating task and rated words on a 0-100 scale based on their emotional content. Descriptive norms for valence and polarity (mean, standard deviation) were then prepared for each word and are available open access on lexique.org. Both emotional valence and polarity were found to be significant predictors of lexical decision time. In particular, positive words were significantly associated with faster lexical decision times, compared to neutral and negative words. Our study provides novel standardized norms of emotional valence and polarity for Québec French, supporting research at the intersection of language and emotion in an understudied linguistic context, and helps shed some light onto the role of affective dimensions of language in word processing.

articles_hidden.title: Mapping Cannabis Use and Environmental Availability in a Sample of Black Young Adults: A Descriptive Geolocation Analysis
articles_hidden.authors: P. Priscilla Lui; Zachary Willett; Nia Ashley Jones; Kevin Michael King; LaTrice Montgomery
articles_hidden.abstract: Black young adults report higher rates of cannabis use and associated problems, relative to national averages. Yet the environmental contexts contributing to these disparities remain poorly understood. Physical availability of cannabis, indicated by proximity and density of licensed retail vendors, is a robust determinant of typical use, and cannabis vendors are concentrated in neighborhoods with greater proportions of Black residents. Existing research has relied largely on area-level data, limiting insight into where and in what environmental contexts individuals use cannabis in their daily life. This descriptive study used baseline and daily diary data from 181 Black young adults (Mage = 24.03; 43.6% women, 16.6% non-binary gender identity; 56.4% non-students) from the Greater Seattle-Tacoma Area, Washington, one of the first American states to legalize recreational cannabis. Geolocation data on participants' residences and cannabis use occasions were collected and linked to Washington State Liquor and Cannabis Board vendor records. Participants lived near cannabis availability (median 62 vendors within a 10-mile radius; median 0.81 miles to the nearest vendor). Across recorded use occasions over two weekend days, over half occurred at home (59.62%), when participants were alone (66.43%), and most commonly in the evening between 8:00-10:00 pm. Findings offer individual-level evidence of high cannabis retail availability among Black young adults in an urban area, characterize the situational contexts of their use in daily life, and lay the foundation for future research on environmental and personal risk factors driving cannabis-related outcomes in this population.

articles_hidden.title: Evaluating AI-Assisted Psychoeducational Report Writing: A Framework for Utility, Equity, and Defensibility
articles_hidden.authors: Adam Lockwood
articles_hidden.abstract: Psychoeducational reports translate assessment data into decisions about eligibility, services, and instruction, yet research documents persistent problems with their clarity, data-linkage, and usefulness to families and educators (Hale & Brown-Chidsey, 2023; Hite, 2026). Generative artificial intelligence (AI) has entered report writing, and early studies describe its adoption and effects on report quality (Farmer, Lockwood, Floyd, & Sisco, 2025; Lockwood, Farmer et al., 2025). School psychology lacks a structured way to determine when AI assistance is useful, equitable, and defensible and when it introduces risk. This conceptual article proposes a framework organized around three domains: utility, equity, and legal and ethical defensibility. Utility concerns whether reports help intended users understand and act on findings. Equity concerns whether reports improve access while avoiding bias, deficit framing, and unsupported cultural assumptions. Legal and ethical defensibility concerns whether reports preserve practitioner judgment, protect student information, and remain consistent with special education law and professional ethics. The framework considers both where AI is used in a report and the specific task it performs. It supports distinguishing lower-risk from higher-risk uses and informs a proposed risk-stratification system and decision pathway. Implications for practice, training, governance, and research across school psychology are discussed.

articles_hidden.title: De-Pathologizing Student Distress: Policy Lessons from Finland for Global Higher Education Governance
articles_hidden.authors: Nicholas Rowe
articles_hidden.abstract:
Higher education student mental health remains misunderstood and inadequately prioritized by
university leadership and policy bodies. Extending a foundational Finnish study across ten
countries (US, Canada, UK, Ireland, Netherlands, Norway, Finland, Germany, South Korea,
Australia), the baseline findings transpose with remarkable statistical consistency. Diagnosable
poor mental health averages 33.07% (21.97% severe) versus 33.0%/31% in Finland, while
postgraduate distress reaches 40.87% (40.0% predicted in Finland). Student distress doubles the
national average rate (16.02%), and suicide ideation averages 13.87% (mirroring Finland's
12.4–13.2%), with severe distress surpassing military veteran and professional benchmarks. As
arguably the largest and worst-affected cohort, student distress accounts for 388,100 lost lifeyears across these ten nations, driving multi-million treatment costs even at 30% utilization.
Despite being contended to fail to protect students, current policies continue to rely on reactive
individualizing counseling that frames structural distress as personal vulnerability attributed to
student failures in lifestyle and self-care. Furthermore, paternalistic "young person" narratives
misclassify mature cohorts, masking root causes inherent to the academic environment. The
study further shows that while poor mental health and suicide ideation seem virtually identical
and age-related for 18–25 year old students and non-students, the rates of older postgraduate
students are significantly different, showing almost double rates of incidence in both categories.
By empirically validating these cross-national realities, this review supports Finnish student
union demands for European Union health programmes to prioritize student mental health,
providing governance bodies across all jurisdictions with a robust foundation for systemic
structural reform and a non-judicial duty of care.

articles_hidden.title: The AI roles for education framework: Developing evidence-based educational technology in the age of generative AI
articles_hidden.authors: Laura Allen; Caitlin Mills; Angela Stewart; Melina Uncapher; Blair Lehman; Sherry Lachman; Marisa Peczuh
articles_hidden.abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) has made it possible to build almost any kind of educational technology, but this flexibility has outpaced the conceptual infrastructure needed to build it well. As a result, there is little evidence or agreement about which types of AI are effectively supporting education and which are not. We argue that this uncertainty stems in part from treating "AI" as a monolith. Debating whether AI is helpful or harmful without specifying what role it is playing, for whom, and toward what end has produced a fragmented evidence base that cannot effectively guide research, design, or policy. To address this, we introduce the AI Roles for Education Framework, which identifies Cognitive Extender, Assessor, Social Partner, Environment, and Orchestrator as canonical roles AI can occupy in educational technology. Each role is grounded in distinct theoretical traditions that shape its constraints and risks. We suggest that specifying a role is a theoretical and practical commitment that determines what a system should do, how it should be built and validated, what counts as success, and where it is likely to fail. The framework is designed to serve researchers, designers, engineers, and educators by anchoring design and evaluation decisions from the outset and providing an analytic lens for making sense of contradictory findings in existing work.

articles_hidden.title: Measuring What Matters: Development of the TRACE Measure (Trauma, Resilience and Adversity in Cultural Experiences)
articles_hidden.authors: Jessica Pryce; Yaacov Petscher; Sarah O'Dell; Chelsey Bowman; Stephanie Curenton-Jolly
articles_hidden.abstract:
Purpose
The Adverse Childhood Experiences (ACE) framework has been instrumental in understanding the long-term effects of childhood adversity but has been critiqued for its limited attention to cultural context and resilience. This study introduces and pilots the TRACE measure (Trauma, Resilience, and Adversity in Cultural Experiences), a culturally informed extension of ACE that integrates traditional adversity indicators, culturally specific adversities, and resilience factors within a single framework. The purpose of this study was to examine the preliminary psychometric properties and structural validity of the TRACE measure.

Methods
The TRACE measure was administered to parents (N = 122) of kindergarten students participating in a longitudinal literacy project across eight elementary schools. The instrument included three domains: traditional ACE items, culturally informed ACE (C-ACE) items, and culturally informed resilience (C-Resilience) items. Confirmatory factor analyses (CFA) using weighted least squares estimation (WLSMV) were conducted to evaluate dimensionality and model fit. Competing models, including correlated factors and bifactor structures, were compared. Reliability was assessed using coefficient omega (ω).

Results
Item-level CFAs demonstrated good model fit and strong reliability for both ACE (ω = .95) and C-ACE (ω = .93) domains, with acceptable reliability for C-Resilience (ω = .78). The correlated factors model showed poor fit, whereas bifactor models demonstrated improved fit, supporting a general adversity factor (G-ACE) alongside domain-specific factors. The general factor accounted for approximately 55%–59% of the common variance among adversity indicators. A moderate inverse relationship between adversity and resilience was observed (r ≈ −.50), indicating that these constructs remain distinct.

Conclusions
Findings provide support for the TRACE measure as a psychometrically viable and conceptually meaningful extension of the ACE framework. By integrating culturally informed adversity and resilience within a single instrument, TRACE offers a more comprehensive and contextual approach to assessing childhood experiences. This framework has implications for research, practice, and policy by supporting more culturally responsive and asset-based approaches to understanding and addressing childhood adversity.

Keywords: Adverse Childhood Experiences, Resilience, Cultural Contexts, Psychometrics, Trauma

articles_hidden.title: Youth Perspectives on Physical Activity Promotion in a Statewide 4-H Youth Development System
articles_hidden.authors: Denver M. Y. Brown; Amirhossein Ghanaatian; Peter Stoepker; Judith Sempa; Zaira Sandoval; Sarah Maass; Doina Caragea
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Cooperative Extension’s youth development program, 4-H, offers community-based infrastructure that may support physical activity (PA) promotion, particularly among rural youth, but youth perspectives on its role remain understudied. This study characterized youth perceptions of (1) how Kansas 4-H currently supports PA and (2) what additional PA opportunities the organization could offer. 
Methods: We analyzed responses to two open-ended items from a cross-sectional online survey of Kansas 4-H youth in Grades 3–12. Question-specific topic guides were developed through large language model (LLM)–assisted topic discovery and domain-expert finalization. Responses were coded by multiple open-weight LLMs, with human review of disagreement and quality-control cases. Exploratory subgroup analyses examined differences by rurality, gender, and grade.
Results: Among 710 respondents (52.5% female, 68.9% rural), the current-support and desired-opportunity items yielded 692 and 464 usable responses, respectively. Current supports most often involved livestock and animal care (40.0%), games, sports, and active recreation (35.4%), and hands-on projects, service, and active work (10.4%). Desired opportunities centered on sports and active recreation (29.5%); walking, running, hiking, and cycling (25.6%); and outdoor, adventure, and nature activities (9.5%). Subgroup differences were observed for livestock/animal care (rural vs urban: +10.2 percentage points), shooting sports/archery (male vs female: +5.4), and games/sports/active recreation (Grade 12 vs Grade 3: -14.0; all p≤.05).
Conclusions: Findings support a layered approach that integrates PA more intentionally into existing 4-H programming, while expanding opportunities responsive to youth interests and local resources. Community-engaged co-design can help translate these priorities into feasible programming across 4-H settings.

articles_hidden.title: Effects of a Mobile Recovery Support App on Substance Use and Related Consequences Among Adults Seeking to Maintain Sobriety: A Randomized Controlled Trial
articles_hidden.authors: Joseph LaBrie; Bradley M. Trager; Weizhou Tang; Oliver Hatch; Kelsey Armstrong
articles_hidden.abstract: Objective: This study evaluated whether Pink Cloud, a mobile recovery support application, improves substance use outcomes among adults seeking to maintain sobriety. Method: Participants were 1,209 adults who reported abstaining from alcohol and other drugs for at least 72 hours. Participants were randomized to receive access to Pink Cloud or to an active control condition. Outcomes included the number of days participants used alcohol and/or drugs and the number of alcohol- and/or drug-related consequences experienced during the past 30 days (1-month follow-up) and the past 60 days (3-month follow-up). Hurdle models were conducted to examine condition differences in the likelihood of reporting any use or consequences and, among participants reporting each outcome, the number of days used or consequences experienced. Results: Across follow-up, participants assigned to Pink Cloud were significantly less likely than control participants to report any alcohol/drug-related consequences (OR = 0.75). Sensitivity analyses indicated that, at 1 month, Pink Cloud participants were significantly less likely to report any alcohol/drug use (OR = 0.77) and, among those who used, reported significantly fewer days of use (IRR = 0.79). They were also significantly less likely to report any alcohol/drug-related consequences at 1 month (OR = 0.72). Conclusion: Findings provide preliminary evidence that Pink Cloud may offer support for maintaining sobriety. Future research should determine whether mobile recovery support tools, such as Pink Cloud, can provide more sustained benefits when integrated with formal treatment, continuing care, and peer-based recovery support.

articles_hidden.title: The ordinary concept of intelligence is inclusive but hierarchical
articles_hidden.authors: carlotta pavese; Paul Henne
articles_hidden.abstract: A scientist solves a difficult problem. A footballer makes a decisive play. People may judge both intelligent, but are they equally inclined to infer that each person is intelligent? Across eight experiments and three supplementary experiments (N = 6,979), we found they were not. People attributed intelligence to practitioners of intellectual and embodied activities, but they were more inclined to infer that a practitioner was intelligent when they practiced an intellectual rather than an embodied activity—even when the practitioner was described as intelligent at that activity. We found no evidence that this asymmetry differed between human and artificial agents. People were also more inclined to generalize intelligence than skillfulness across activities. These findings suggest the ordinary concept of intelligence is inclusive but hierarchical: people attribute intelligence to practitioners of intellectual and embodied activities but are more inclined to infer that practitioners of intellectual activities are intelligent.

articles_hidden.title: Family-Specific Dynamics Between Parenting and Preschoolers’ Self-Regulation: Evidence from 100-Day Daily Diary Data
articles_hidden.authors: Dian Yu; Lauren G. Bailes; Jaely DeLeon; Juliana Marie Agnolet
articles_hidden.abstract: Current research supports that parenting practice contributes to individual differences in preschoolers’ self-regulation (SR). Dynamic systems theory suggests that the link between parenting and child SR may be bidirectional and family-specific. Taking a dynamic systems perspective, this study examined the daily bidirectional link between parenting practices and preschoolers’ SR and the family-specific holistic dynamic patterns. Thirty-nine families took part in a 100-day daily diary study in the United States. Using dynamic structural equation modeling, we examined the autoregressive and cross-lagged effects of daily parental responsiveness, negative reactivity, and child self-regulation. Autoregressive and cross-lagged effects were estimated as random slopes, allowing the dynamic effects to vary from family to family. On average, parental responsiveness predicted future SR, and SR predicted future negative reactivity. Significant heterogeneity was identified, indicating that the bidirectional links between parenting and SR were family-specific. Considering autoregressive and cross-lagged effects holistically, all families showed a tendency to return to their equilibrium states, defined by their personal means of responsiveness, negative reactivity, and SR. Among the 39 families, 19 families had a mutually influential connection between negative reactivity and SR, and one family had a mutually influential connection between responsiveness and SR. The rest of the families did not show a mutually influential pattern between parenting and child SR. The findings highlighted the importance of considering heterogeneity in the holistic within-family processes. The effectiveness of future interventions should be considered family-specifically and as changes in family dynamic patterns.

articles_hidden.title: Measuring a dreaming population: multilevel temporal organization in 75,000 dream reports
articles_hidden.authors: Alexander V. Lebedev
articles_hidden.abstract:
Dream reports exhibit reproducible organization at multiple scales. We analyzed >75,000 reports from four platforms: 30,241 reports by 5,524 Dreamseer users and ~45,000 from DreamBank, Reddit r/Dreams, and the Sleep and Dream Database. Within reports, emotional valence declined from beginning to end. Forward and reversed trajectories were distinguishable in all five corpus-language samples with a screening instrument (AUC 0.647–0.667) and four of five after sentence-level rescoring with the primary sentiment model.

The effect survived contributor-level inference and seven controls for ending-related material. Shuffling sentence order eliminated the mean descent while preserving lexical content, localizing the effect to sequence. Matched first-person waking accounts, fiction, and encyclopedic prose also declined, showing that downward movement is not dream-specific. However, on the endpoint estimand, Dreamseer and DreamBank declined more strongly than waking narratives (all q < .001); after standardization by within-document sentence-valence dispersion, they also exceeded all three human comparators (9/9 contrasts, q ≤ .018), with approximately two- to five-fold greater descent. Separation was less consistent for whole-trajectory slope. The hypothesized failure of emotional resolution at the ending was unsupported: the difference was concentrated earlier, with dreams beginning near neutral and then declining.

At population scale, Friday reports were lighter than Monday reports in English (β = +0.024, p = .008), but this did not replicate in Russian, was uncorrected, and partly reflected who reported. Nightmare-content variance increased before 12 downturns (Kendall’s τ = +0.236), surviving four of five surrogate tests but not a window-length block bootstrap; autocorrelation did not increase. We treat this as a prospective hypothesis, not evidence of critical slowing down. Low intrinsic dimension and a percolating semantic “continent” also appeared in matched non-dream prose, whereas non-narrative prose fell outside the connectivity range shared by all narrative corpora.

Weekly affect and content showed no robust entrainment to market, media, search, attention, or cultural indicators, constraining detectable direct societal coupling at this temporal resolution. At COVID-19 onset, explicit pandemic vocabulary increased ninefold (+4.68 percentage points), exceeding all 44 placebo-in-time cutoffs (empirical p = .022), showing that the stream could register a major societal event.

Together, these findings demonstrate collective structure without sustained interpersonal synchrony. Macroscopic organization emerged despite absent average-night convergence and a thin unexplained tail of unusually cohesive nights, while trajectory, calendar, variance, and event-related observables operated through partly independent channels.

articles_hidden.title: Rescripting suicidal mental imagery in young people: A pilot study of feasibility, acceptability and safety
articles_hidden.authors: Lianne Schmaal; Georgie Paulik; Zamantha Munoz; Laura van Velzen; Pemma Davies; Martin Mitrevski; Eleanor Bailey; Phoebe Gleeson; Lisa Incerti; Samantha Galea
articles_hidden.abstract: Suicidal mental imagery – vivid, intrusive mental images of suicide or death - is common among young people experiencing suicidal ideation and may increase risk of suicidal behaviour, yet interventions directly targeting these images are lacking. We conducted a single-arm pilot study evaluating the feasibility, acceptability and safety of a brief, therapist delivered imagery rescripting intervention targeting action-facilitating suicidal mental imagery in help-seeking young people aged 16–25 years with mood disorders and current or recent suicidal ideation. Fourteen participants were recruited; 12 were eligible for the intervention and 11 (92%) completed treatment and follow-up. The recruitment target (N=25) was not met, largely due to service disruptions and clinician capacity constraints. Acceptability and safety criteria were met: 73% reported that sessions were not distressing, none felt less safe following treatment, and no participant showed increased suicidal ideation from baseline to follow-up. Two serious adverse events occurred but were judged unrelated to the intervention. Exploratory analyses showed reductions in suicidal-image frequency, realness, compellingness, intrusiveness and distress, alongside a 52% reduction in suicidal ideation severity. Our pilot study indicates that directly rescripting action-facilitating suicidal mental imagery showed encouraging short-term safety and acceptability signals in young people, supporting evaluation in a larger randomised controlled trial.

articles_hidden.title: Recovering Within-Family Lagged Effects of the Discordant Sibling Random Intercept Cross Lagged Panel Model on Sibling Panels
articles_hidden.authors: Yongseok Lee; Robert Duncan; Kristine Marceau
articles_hidden.abstract: The Discordant Sibling Random-Intercept Cross-Lagged Panel Model (DS RI-CLPM) integrates the sibling-comparison design with the Random Intercept-Cross Lagged Panel Model (RI-CLPM) to separate shared family-level confounding from sibling-specific processes, and stable heterogeneity from within-child dynamics. Despite its empirical work, its performance relative to conventional longitudinal models remains untested. Using Monte-Carlo simulations, we compared the DS RI-CLPM against a wave-specific discordant sibling model, CLPM, and RI-CLPM, evaluating relative bias and root mean squared errors (RMSE). The results showed that the DS RI-CLPM generally recovered the within-family cross-lagged effect and standard errors across most manipulated conditions. However, it exhibited substantial bias and higher RMSE when unmeasured child-level time-varying confounding was present. Thus, the DS RI-CLPM is effective for examining sibling-specific within-family cross-lagged effects while controlling for stable or family-shared confounders, but it is insufficient when unmeasured child-specific time varying confounding is plausible.

articles_hidden.title: File drawer report: Testing for spontaneously perceived joint affordances in an object-based compatibility task
articles_hidden.authors: Shaheed Azaad; Simon Laham; Natalie Sebanz
articles_hidden.abstract: Evidence from joint action research suggests that a suite of spontaneous cognitive and perceptual processes underpins our ability to coordinate with others. We tested whether people spontaneously perceive affordances (or action possibilities) for the dyad when a co-actor is present. To test this hypothesis, we asked participants to complete an object-based response time task either alone (individual condition) or while seated next to a partner who completed the complementary task (joint condition). Participants in both conditions made unimanual go/no-go keypresses to objects that afforded either a bimanual (e.g., a laundry hamper) or unimanual (e.g., a bucket) grasp. In total, we conducted seven experiments (total N =293). An initial experiment revealed an affordance × task interaction effect on response times, such that responses to bimanually graspable objects were faster in the joint than in the individual condition. However, several follow-up experiments failed to replicate this finding, providing no overall evidence for spontaneously perceived joint affordances.

articles_hidden.title: Missing Pretest–Posttest Correlations in Pretest–Posttest–Control Group Designs:  A Practical Trade-Off for Meta-Analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Lucas Wilhelm Liebenow; Valentin Emslander; Thorben Jansen; Oliver Lüdtke
articles_hidden.abstract: Pretest–posttest–control group (PPC) effect sizes incorporate baseline information but require the pretest–posttest correlation for sampling-variance estimation, which is frequently unavailable in primary studies. This creates a practical trade-off: retaining baseline information requires an assumption about repeated-measures dependence, whereas using posttest-only effect sizes avoids this requirement but discards available baseline information. The present study used a simulation to evaluate whether missing correlations can be replaced by constant assumed values while maintaining acceptable variance calibration, and complemented the simulation with reanalyses of three published meta-analyses to illustrate the consequences for meta-analytic effects. Across 2,160 design conditions, we examined the sampling variances of two pretest-informed estimators (dppc1  and dppc2). Performance was evaluated in terms of coverage of nominal 95% confidence intervals and standard-error ratios. Across the fixed-correlation conditions, coverage declined from .97 to .83 for dppc1 and from .97 to .79 for dppc2 as the assumed correlation increased from .20 to .80, with corresponding standard-error ratios declining from 1.31 to 0.70 and from 1.32 to 0.68. Misspecification was asymmetric: overestimating the true correlation produced anti-conservative standard errors and undercoverage, whereas underestimating it generally produced conservative inference. Across the empirical examples, pooled PPC estimates were comparatively stable across correlation assumptions, whereas ignoring baseline information produced larger shifts in several pooled effects.  Based on these findings, we provide practical guidelines for handling missing pretest–posttest correlations, emphasizing a hierarchical use of study-specific information, external evidence, and transparent sensitivity analyses when constant assumptions are required. An accompanying Shiny app supports these analyses: https://lliebenow.shinyapps.io/ppc-rho-sensitivity-explorer/.

articles_hidden.title: Potential Agency in the Absence of Actual Motor Control? Ownership-dependent Judgments in the Rubber Hand Illusion
articles_hidden.authors: Hélène Vanborren; Fleur Touzard; Matthew Longo; Loïc Paul Heurley; Brouillet Thibaut
articles_hidden.abstract: We define potential agency as the explicit judgment that one could have made an artificial hand move had one intended to do so. We asked whether participants would report potential agency for an artificial hand they had no means of controlling, and how such reports varied with body ownership. In a within-subject static rubber hand illusion (RHI) paradigm, 104 participants received synchronous and asynchronous visuo-tactile stimulation while their real hand remained hidden; neither the real nor the artificial hand moved, and no sensory consequences of voluntary action were available. After each induction, participants rated ownership of the artificial hand and potential agency towards it; proprioceptive drift was also measured. Synchronous stimulation produced the expected RHI pattern, with higher ownership and greater proprioceptive drift than asynchronous stimulation. Potential agency ratings were also higher following synchronous stimulation. Across conditions, ownership was positively associated with potential agency, but this association was stronger under synchronous stimulation. In the synchronous condition, ownership accounted for 56% of the variance in potential agency. Critically, on the −3 to +3 scales, the model-estimated probability of positive endorsement (mean potential agency rating ≥ +1) increased from 10% at ownership 0 to 88% at +3. Reanalysis of a comparable static RHI dataset showed a convergent ownership-dependent pattern. These findings extend the study of the ownership–agency relationship beyond executed actions and their sensory consequences: even in the absence of actual motor control, experienced ownership was closely related to whether the artificial hand was judged to be available for voluntary movement.

articles_hidden.title: Bodily Rhythms Bias Temporal Decisions Through Dissociable Neural Processes
articles_hidden.authors: Amir Jahanian Najafabadi; Srishti Mittal; Kayser Christoph
articles_hidden.abstract: Being able to judge time accurately is central to behavior. Yet, judgements of time are shaped by factors such as attention and arousal, and hence our physiology. We studied the relation between cardiac and respiratory states and categorical judgements of sub-second intervals in humans. We asked whether these states relate to specific biases in time judgements and how they reflect in neurophysiological (EEG) signals. Thirty participants categorized tones of 450 to 600 ms duration as short or long, while we recorded 128-channel EEG, ECG, and respiration. Participants' reaction times were linked to cardiac and respiratory rates as well as respiratory phase. Systematic biases in interval categorization were predicted by heart rate and respiration rate. The physiological variables were not predictive of response accuracy, hence reflecting biases in time judgments rather than being tied to sensory precision. We then used multivariate EEG analysis to dissect neurophysiological signals related to interval duration and participants’ choice and modelled the influence of the physiological states on these. The respiration phase was linked to multiple EEG signals during a trial, while heart rate was predictive of choice-related signals carried by EEG components shortly before the response. This shows that cardiorespiratory states are systematically associated with the transformation of temporal information into categorical decisions, supporting an embodied account of time perception in which time perception fluctuates with ongoing physiological states.

articles_hidden.title: No convincing evidence for a mediated effect of childhood trauma on alexithymia among patients with depression: A reevaluation of Zhou et al. (2026)
articles_hidden.authors: Kimmo Sorjonen; Bo Melin; Marika Melin
articles_hidden.abstract: Using the covariance matrix reported by Zhou et al., we reexamined the evidence underlying their proposed mediation model linking childhood trauma and alexithymia in individuals with depression. Our analyses show that the same covariance structure is equally compatible with a conceptually distinct latent-variable framework that does not require the directional pathway advanced in the original study. In this competing model, self-reported childhood trauma, sleep disturbances, anhedonia, and alexithymia are viewed as manifestations of a broader latent factor, core self-evaluation. The findings highlight a general challenge in the interpretation of observational data: the same pattern of associations may often be accounted for by multiple theoretically plausible models. Consequently, correlational evidence alone offers limited justification for privileging one explanatory account over others. Consideration of alternative models should therefore constitute a standard component of efforts to infer psychological mechanisms from observational findings.

articles_hidden.title: Assessing Person-Specific Symptom Networks From Brief Narratives: Development and Initial Evaluation of the Narrative-to-Network (N2N) Approach
articles_hidden.authors: Felix Vogel; Carla Paulus; Julian Reichert; Jonas Tesarz; Stefanie Jungmann
articles_hidden.abstract: Person-specific symptom networks formalize which problems characterize an individual and how those problems are perceived to influence one another, making them increasingly relevant for individualized case conceptualization, treatment planning, and personalized psychotherapy. However, existing approaches typically rely on structured causal assessment or intensive longitudinal data, both of which can increase assessment burden. We developed and initially evaluated the Narrative-to-Network (N2N) framework for deriving directed person-specific networks from brief spoken narratives in which individuals describe their psychological difficulties and perceived relations among them in their own words. Following a development phase (N = 22), an independent evaluation sample (N = 50) completed a narrative assessment and a Perceived Causal Networks (PECAN) assessment. Narratives lasted approximately three minutes. Manual coding showed relatively high agreement for node identification (Dice = .76) and edge direction conditional on a shared relation (agreement = .81), with lower agreement for edge presence (Dice = .62). Narrative-derived and PECAN networks showed partial but incomplete convergence (mean Jaccard = .29). Most problems identified in narratives were also identified through PECAN (62.6%), whereas only 36.7% of PECAN problems appeared in the corresponding narratives. Despite containing substantially fewer problems and relations, narrative-derived networks were perceived as highly representative; among participants with complete ratings (n = 39), mean representativeness scores were 33.26 for narrative-derived networks and 34.10 for regulated PECAN networks, with no statistically significant difference (p = .527). Narrative node count was positively associated with psychological distress both concurrently (ρ = .34) and at follow-up (ρ = .40). These findings provide initial evidence that structured person-specific symptom networks can be reproducibly derived from brief prompted spoken narratives and may offer an economical, complementary representation of individuals’ difficulties.

articles_hidden.title: AI Mindset – An Empirically Tested Theoretical Framework on the Psychological Factors Shaping AI Competence and AI Use
articles_hidden.authors: Shuyan Feng; Martin J. Koch; Astrid Carolus
articles_hidden.abstract:
Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a powerful tool in the educational sector. Research
examining the factors that facilitate its practical application by teachers has increased
substantially. Although empirical studies highlight the importance of psychological factors in
shaping engagement with AI technologies, the systematic integration of cognitive, emotional,
and motivational variables into AI use research remains fragmented. To advance the
psychological foundation, the present study proposed and empirically tested a model for AI
Mindset, conceptualised based on prior psychological and social-cognitive theories. The AI
Mindset framework posits a triadic structure, comprising dispositional factors, contextual and
situational characteristics, and technology-related appraisals, to explain teachers’ use of AI.
Structural equation modelling of 224 teachers revealed that AI Mindset variables significantly
predict pedagogical AI competence and AI use. Specifically, dispositional factors of openness
and need for relatedness associated with AI use indirectly through pedagogical AI
competence. Contextual and social facilitations of habit demonstrated the strongest direct
effect on AI use and indirect effect via competence. In terms of technology-related appraisals,
fear showed a complex pattern, with a positive direct effect on AI use but a negative indirect
effect through AI competence. The effect of effort expectancy was fully mediated by
competence, whereas hedonic motivation exerted a direct positive effect on AI use. In sum, by
introducing and empirically testing the AI Mindset framework, the present study integrates a
psychological perspective into the AI use research, provides a foundation for understanding
AI-related use patterns, and informs professional development and AI technology design.

articles_hidden.title: Beyond Rules of Thumb: Empirical Sample Size Requirements for Detecting Institutional Effects in the context of Therapist Effects
articles_hidden.authors: Juan Segundo Pena Loray; Björn S. Siepe; Miriam Ina Hehlmann; Anne-Katharina Deisenhofer; Robin Anno Wester; Julian Rubel
articles_hidden.abstract: Objective: Multilevel modelling of therapist effects (TE) and institutional effects (IE) is standard in psychotherapy research, yet empirical sample-size guidance is scarce for TE and virtually absent for IE. Existing recommendations rely on rules of thumb from two-level designs that vary widely across sources and do not extend to three-level structures. We aimed to provide empirically derived design recommendations for reliably detecting TE and IE in three-level psychotherapy studies. Methods: We conducted a fully factorial Monte Carlo simulation crossing six design factors: true TE, true IE, patient allocation (balanced vs. unbalanced), patients per therapist, therapists per institution, and number of institutions. This yielded 52,488 unique conditions, each with 1,000 replications. For every condition we fitted a three-level random-intercept model and derived parametric bootstrap 95% confidence intervals for both intraclass correlations, evaluating bias, RMSE, coverage, and statistical power at three pre-registered thresholds. Results: Detecting TE was feasible across a wide range of realistic designs, requiring as few as 10 to 40 total therapists for moderate effects (TE ≥ 0.05). Detecting IE, in contrast, was strongly constrained by the number of institutions: no design with fewer than four institutions reached 80% power at the primary threshold, and adequate detection of small to moderate IE (≤ 0.20) required at least five institutions with substantial within-institution sampling. Conclusion: Reliably detecting IE imposes qualitatively different design requirements than TE, particularly regarding the minimum number of institutions. We provide cutoff tables and a Shiny application to support empirically informed sample-size decisions.

articles_hidden.title: Understanding Creativity in Human–AI Collaboration:  How Cognitive Strategies and Student Profiles Relate to Students’ Creativity
articles_hidden.authors: Kim van Broekhoven; Marian Hickendorff
articles_hidden.abstract: Creativity is widely recognized as a critical competency for addressing the complex challenges of the twenty-first century. At the same time, Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is transforming how students learn, think, and solve problems in higher education. In human-AI collaboration, this study first identified students’ cognitive strategies in GenAI-supported contexts, and examined the relationship between the cognitive strategy used and the creativity (i.e., originality and quality) of each idea. Second, this study identified latent profiles of students’ cognitive strategy use, and their relationship with creativity. Using a novel process-oriented theoretical framework and a combination of deductive and inductive analyses, six cognitive strategies were identified: repeat, unmediated, experiential, conceptual combination, semantic, and assumption reversal. A laboratory-based observational study involving 146 undergraduate students showed that constructive cognitive strategies (conceptual combination and semantic) were more frequently associated with highly original ideas than active cognitive strategies (unmediated and experiential), whereas no differences were found for idea quality. Furthermore, latent profile analysis identified four distinct profiles of human–AI collaboration: Largely Independent Thinkers, AI-Constructive Combiners, AI-Balanced Thinkers, and AI-Reliant Reproducers. Although the profiles did not differ in their average originality, they differed significantly in their average quality. Students classified as AI-Constructive Combiners, AI-Balanced Thinkers, and AI-Reliant Reproducers produced ideas of higher quality than the Largely Independent Thinkers. These findings demonstrate that the way students cognitively engage with GenAI shapes their creativity and provide insights for fostering effective human–AI collaboration in higher education.

articles_hidden.title: Packaging Psychological Theory: A New Standard for Reusable Computational Models
articles_hidden.authors: Kyra Evers; Lourens Waldorp; Eiko I Fried; Fred Hasselman; Denny Borsboom
articles_hidden.abstract: Psychological theories are increasingly expressed as computational models to improve their rigour, robustness, and testability. Yet in the absence of shared standards for distributing such models, researchers often rely on idiosyncratic code formats. This creates large heterogeneity in the accessibility, quality, and intelligibility of models, making implementations difficult to reproduce, interpret, or extend. As a consequence, computational models are rarely reused, creating a vast space of isolated models with little effort towards theoretical integration. To address this challenge, we propose a new standard: computational models representing psychological theory should be distributed as software packages (e.g., in R, Python, or Julia). Packaged models should be openly available and licensed for reuse, documented and tested, checked by automated workflows, and preserved with a persistent identifier. Unlike static code archives, packages are tools made for users, with a familiar and engaging interface. Their format accommodates different programming languages, modelling frameworks, and stages of model development, giving authors substantial flexibility in how models are formalized and implemented. We illustrate the packaging standard with affectOU, an example R package implementing a psychological theory of affect dynamics. Our proposed standard draws on established infrastructure and best practices from software engineering to improve model quality and reproducibility. Adopting this standard would lower the cost of verifying and reusing computational models for authors, reviewers, and readers alike. In our view, improving model reusability is not optional but essential for cumulative progress in psychological theory.

articles_hidden.title: Crossmodal Congruency Affects Sensitivity but not Speed in Auditory–Tactile Go/NoGo Tasks
articles_hidden.authors: Andrea Andonovska; Ben Godde
articles_hidden.abstract: Crossmodal congruency and interference influence perception and action depending on modality, congruency, and task constraints. This study investigated auditory–tactile interactions using a Go/NoGo paradigm to dissociate effects on response speed (reaction time, RT) and perceptual sensitivity (d’). Participants performed a frequency discrimination task in which high- and low-frequency auditory tones (1000 vs. 500 Hz) and tactile vibrations (100 vs. 70 Hz) served as Go and NoGo signals across five conditions: unimodal auditory (A0), unimodal tactile (T0), auditory targets with tactile distractors (At), tactile targets with auditory distractors (Ta), and a combined condition (AT). In the crossmodal conditions, participants attended one modality while ignoring the other, and distractors were either response-congruent (both stimuli signaled the same response) or response-incongruent (the two modalities signaled different responses). Modality significantly affected performance, yielding particularly slow RTs and reduced d’ in the tactile-target condition containing auditory distractors (Ta). Crossmodal congruency robustly altered sensitivity, showing higher d’ for congruent than incongruent trials, particularly for tactile targets, but did not reliably influence RT. No evidence for multisensory facilitation emerged in the combined condition. These findings reveal a dissociation between speed and sensitivity in auditory–tactile processing, consistent with accounts where crossmodal congruency primarily limits or enhances the quality of perceptual evidence.

articles_hidden.title: Capturing the Hostile Attribution Bias through Conditional Reasoning Tasks: The Hostile Reasoning Test as an Indirect Measure of Aggressiveness
articles_hidden.authors: Paul Bacher; Manuel Becker; Fabian Hölzenbein; Hannes Krahl; Karl Christoph Klauer; Sarah Teige-Mocigemba
articles_hidden.abstract: The Hostile Attribution Bias is considered a central component of aggressiveness. It is thought to be a rather impulsive mechanism which justifies (reactive) aggressive behavior as logical and reasonable. Therefore, reasoning tasks may provide an unobtrusive means to make the hostile attribution bias accessible to measurement. In this manuscript, we developed such a task, the Hostile Reasoning Test (HRT), and assessed its psychometric properties. In three studies, we found that the HRT is reliable, shows convergent and discriminant validity for a male (Study 1, N=206) and female (Study 3, N=207) sample, and demonstrates incremental validity beyond self-reported aggressiveness in predicting reactive aggressive behavior (Study 2, N=78). The present results indicate that reasoning tasks such as the HRT are a promising complement to self-report measures, in particular if the more reactive and impulsive aspects of aggressiveness are of interest.

articles_hidden.title: Stronger together? Examining the buffering effects of same-ethnicity partners on experiences of discrimination among sexual minority men of color
articles_hidden.authors: Paolo Aldrin Palma; Shayna Skakoon-Sparling; Joel Michel Le Forestier; Terri Haochuan Zhang; Jane Cao; Aki Gormezano; Tin D. Vo; Milada Dvorakova; Joseph Cox; Nathan Lachowsky
articles_hidden.abstract: Group membership and social connections play important roles in protecting people from stigmatized groups against the effects of discrimination on mental health. However, because people can belong to many groups, they may find themselves in situations where they experience stigmatization from others with whom they also share a stigmatized identity. We examine these intersectional experiences with a subsample of sexual minority men of color from a larger cohort study focused on sexual minority men’s health and wellbeing in Canada’s three largest cities (N = 314, nvisits = 725). We examine (i) whether experiences of racism from other sexual minority men and homophobia from other people of color affects the types of partners people seek out and (ii) whether having partners from a similar ethnoracial background protects against the effects of discrimination on mental health. We found that neither racism from other sexual minority men (including sexual racism) nor homophobia from people of color affected whom participants sought out as sexual partners. Having more partners of the same ethnoracial background had mixed protective effects. The effects of racism from sexual minority men (but not sexual racism) on mental health were attenuated among participants who reported more ethnoracial ingroup partners. However,  having more partners exacerbated the effects of homophobia from other people of color. These effects were limited to partners of the same race or ethnicity, and not to partners of color in general. These findings highlight the importance of attending to intraminority intersectional experiences and nuances of the effects of group membership across different forms of stigma.

articles_hidden.title: How Meaning Shapes a Rule: Neural Signatures of Morphological Learning and Generalization
articles_hidden.authors: Marianne Azar; Alec Marantz
articles_hidden.abstract: Rule generalization is one of the most useful tools our mind uses to facilitate learning. In language, we apply it to connect what words mean to what they are made of, such as their suffixes. This is a morphosemantic relation, and it helps us process words we already know and easily acquire new words by composing their meaning. How is this relation acquired, and how does it manifest into generalization for understanding new words? In this study, we investigated the brain basis of these questions through an English-based artificial language study, where learners read sentences to learn a suffix-meaning relation of new words like “thinkle”. Words were either meaningful (places or things) or had no clear meaning. Each suffix family had majority and minority meaning words that participants had to keep track of for testing. For meaningful words in training, we found that higher performance scores predicted higher selective engagement in the left inferior frontal gyrus, specifically the pars triangularis and pars opercularis. In testing, both learned and generalized words, both increased lateral prefrontal cortex engagement. Meanwhile, words with no clear meaning had a much more diffuse brain engagement, recruiting bilateral temporoparietal regions. This resembles the processing of abstract words from previous literature. We found no difference between majority and minority meaning words, especially with the variance in participants’ performance strategies, but found differences in what predicted significant brain activity based on strategy difference. This study grounds itself in the reality of word and affixal semantics with previous research on language learning and universals. Ultimately, it lends a learning paradigm that resembles natural language learning across many languages to carefully investigate its brain basis, while addressing an understudied aspect of rule generalization: ambiguity.

articles_hidden.title: Word Learning Seasons: Climate Effects on Early Vocabulary in Monolingual and Bilingual Children
articles_hidden.authors: Laia Fibla; Krista Byers-Heinlein
articles_hidden.abstract: Children’s vocabularies reflect the dynamic worlds they inhabit, yet traditional models of language acquisition treat environmental influences as static. This study reveals how seasonal variations in weather systematically influence early vocabulary composition. Three studies involving 16–30 months old monolinguals and bilinguals (total N = 1294), examine how climate conditions affect word learning using parent-reported vocabulary checklists. Children in cold-weather regions (Wisconsin, Montreal) produced significantly more winter-related words compared to peers in milder climates (Texas, Florida), while seasonal analyses showed that within populations, winter word acquisition and knowledge peaked in the coldest months and declined during the warmest months. This pattern was most pronounced in older children, and in bilinguals with greater language exposure. Our research shows how children’s language systems adapt to environmental variations, advancing our understanding of language acquisition as a responsive process shaped by continuous interactions between cognitive development, language exposure, and the changing environmental landscape children navigate.

articles_hidden.title: The Emergence of a Distinction between Things and Stuff
articles_hidden.authors: Vivian C. Paulun; Sanghee Song; Elizabeth Spelke
articles_hidden.abstract: Solid objects typically move as cohesive, bounded bodies; they do not split apart, spread, or divide. Yet, non-solid substances, like sand, do. Adults hold distinct expectations for solid objects and non-solid substances, or things and stuff. But when does this distinction emerge in development? Here, we asked whether infants expect sand to be non-cohesive. We familiarized 4-to-6- and 13-to-15-month-old infants with videos of a solid object or non-solid sand. Subsequent test events showed the object or sand falling onto a wedge and either splitting into two pieces or piles or moving cohesively on one side of the wedge. Infants in both age groups looked longer when the solid object unexpectedly split apart, confirming robust cohesion expectations. Yet, for granular substances, infants showed no equivalent preference—neither expecting stuff to be cohesive nor to be non-cohesive. These findings suggest that cohesion expectations develop along different trajectories for things and stuff.

articles_hidden.title: Does internalized homonegativity lower sexual satisfaction? A longitudinal assessment among gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men (GBM) in Canada's three largest cities
articles_hidden.authors: Sarah Meora Kowall; Paolo Aldrin Palma; Shayna Skakoon-Sparling; Terri Haochuan Zhang; Aki Gormezano; Jérémy Lelièvre; Darell H.S. Tan; Daniel Grace; Trevor Adam Hart
articles_hidden.abstract:
Purpose: Internalized homonegativity is associated with lower sexual satisfaction among gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men (GBM). Though internalized homonegativity is commonly seen as an antecedent to lower sexual satisfaction, existing research tends to be cross-sectional, limiting our ability to make causal inferences. This has important implications for GBM sexual health and clinical interventions. The goal of this study is to examine the longitudinal associations between internalized homonegativity and sexual satisfaction.

Methods: We analyzed data from a longitudinal study of GBM in Vancouver, Toronto and Montreal, Canada (N = 1307). Using a random-intercept cross-lagged panel model (RI-CLPM), we analyzed data from baseline up to two years of follow-up to model the within-person changes in internalized homonegativity and sexual satisfaction. The RI-CLPM allowed us to account for the stable differences between individuals that may inflate correlations, thus allowing for a stronger estimate of within-person variation over time.

Results: There were no cross-lagged associations between internalized homonegativity and sexual satisfaction, but there were significant random-intercept associations such that participants who scored higher on internalized homonegativity tended to score lower on sexual satisfaction.

Conclusion: Our findings suggest that cross-sectional associations in past research  are likely due to stable between-person differences and that internalized homonegativity and sexual satisfaction may be independent processes. From a clinical perspective, internalized homonegativity may be useful in identifying potential issues with sexual (dis)satisfaction, but reducing internalized homonegativity may not be sufficient in alleviating these challenges.

articles_hidden.title: In-Person Contemplative Dyad Meditation to Increase Mindfulness, Connection, and Well-Being in Young Adults:  A Small Randomized Controlled Trial
articles_hidden.authors: Vera U. Ludwig; Jenny Wey; Mahir Sudad; Boris Bornemann; Elaina Lin; Scott Rennie; Mironel de Wilde; Michael Platt
articles_hidden.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: This study tested whether in-person Contemplative Dyad Meditation (CDM) can help young adults connect and improve well-being. In CDM, two individuals take turns sharing present-moment experiences while the other listens non-judgmentally. CDM was compared to an active social comparison condition, Fast Friends (FF), and a no-intervention group (NI).
METHODS: This preregistered, randomized controlled trial enrolled 119 participants aged 18–35 (82% women, 1% non-binary, 17% men). Participants were assigned to CDM, FF, or NI. CDM participants received a meditation training followed by up to six in-person practice sessions over two weeks, whereas FF participants completed up to six structured in-person conversations. Primary intervention-level outcomes—assessed before and after the entire intervention—included self-reported mindfulness, thriving, and loneliness. The primary session-level outcome—assessed before and after each exercise—was closeness. Secondary and exploratory outcomes included intervention-level measures of affect, depression, anxiety, social anxiety, self-compassion, and empathy, as well as session-level measures of affect and heart rate. Analyses were per-protocol, supplemented by a conservative, complete-case intention-to-treat analysis. 
RESULTS: CDM significantly increased mindfulness compared to both FF and NI, but no effects were found for thriving or loneliness. Lower baseline mindfulness was associated with greater increases in mindfulness following CDM. Both CDM and FF increased momentary closeness from before to after the respective practices. Regarding secondary intervention-level outcomes, CDM increased overall positive affect after the intervention period, whereas no effects emerged for the remaining measures or for FF. However, modest statistical power warrants caution in interpreting null findings. At the session-level, both CDM and FF increased momentary positive affect after the practices, while FF additionally reduced momentary negative affect. Exploratory analyses indicated that CDM, but not FF, was associated with reduced heart rate following the exercises, consistent with reduced emotional arousal. Intention-to-treat analyses showed broadly similar patterns of results, although mindfulness effects no longer survived correction for multiple comparisons.
CONCLUSIONS: We provide initial evidence that CDM can increase mindfulness, positive affect, and social connection in young adults, whereas FF showed benefits primarily for social connection. Exploratory analyses suggested distinct physiological correlates across conditions. CDM involved a higher time investment due to the initial meditation training, potentially affecting comparability. Both CDM and FF may be beneficial for improving social connection, while operating through partly different mechanisms. Given the small sample size and lack of long-term follow-up, further research is needed.

articles_hidden.title: Associations between dark triad traits and affective and cognitive theory of mind
articles_hidden.authors: Lucy Hampson; Caitlin Hill; Kacie Hoyles; Ellie Hunstone; Gareth Richards
articles_hidden.abstract: The dark triad comprises three socially aversive personality traits: Machiavellianism, subclinical psychopathy, and subclinical narcissism. Theory of Mind (ToM) involves ability to infer thoughts and beliefs (socio-cognitive component) and attribute emotional states to others (socio-perceptual component). With conflicting findings in the literature, we utilised a cross-sectional online survey to examine correlations between dark triad traits and ToM.
