The project combines developmental (epi)genomic mapping of the human brain, genomic analyses of trans-syndromal phenotypes, exposome-wide environmental assessment, and Artificial Intelligence-based modelling to identify predictive and actionable markers of mental health trajectories of young people. By harmonizing multimodal data from existing population-based cohorts and by establishing the first international, trans-syndromal clinical cohort of help-seeking young people, Youth-GEMs is generating biologically informed polygenic and exposomic scores, cell-type-specific regulatory annotations, and interpretable machine-learning models. Continuous engagement with young people, clinicians, and stakeholders ensures that findings translate into tools for early detection, monitoring, and personalized intervention. Together, these efforts aim to advance mechanistic understandings of youth mental health, improve prediction of emerging illness, and support the development of evidence-based, developmentally sensitive approaches to prevention and care.

articles_hidden.title: Maternal Emotional Experiences During Everyday Infant Soothing: Within- and Between-Person Predictors from an Ecological Momentary Assessment Study
articles_hidden.authors: Sarvenaz Oloomi; Alexis Hernandez; Alexa Monachino; Irene Tung; Lauren C Shuffrey; Santiago Morales
articles_hidden.abstract: Infant crying and mothers’ efforts to soothe their infants are highly emotional experiences that shape parent–infant co-regulation and bonding. Despite the importance of this process, relatively little research has examined how mothers feel when they soothe their infants, especially with real-time, ecologically-relevant measures. In this study, we collected ecological momentary assessment (EMA) in a geographically representative sample between September 2022 and September 2025 for up to 14 days to capture mothers’ (N = 250; Mage = 33.2 years, range = 19–45, 51.5% Hispanic/Latinx) emotional experiences during soothing interactions with their infants (Mage = 9.4 months, range = 3–23 months; 52.8% female; 57% Hispanic/Latinx). Mothers also completed questionnaires about their distress (anxiety, depression, and stress) symptoms and their infant’s temperamental negative affectivity. Within-person analyses revealed that maternal positive affect decreased and negative affect increased as soothing became longer and more difficult. Between-person analyses indicated that higher infant negative affectivity and greater maternal distress were associated with mothers reporting more negative emotions while soothing, whereas more positive maternal emotions were related to less maternal distress. Results were present while accounting for mothers’ mood while completing the survey, soothing difficulty and duration, infant age and sex, and socioeconomic factors. These findings highlight that soothing can be a particularly challenging and emotional experience for mothers high in distress symptoms and those with infants high in temperamental negative affectivity, pointing to the need for targeted interventions within this population that support maternal emotion regulation and parent-infant interaction quality.

articles_hidden.title: More effort, more variability, but greater relative precision: Distributional modeling of effort-performance coupling
articles_hidden.authors: Lukas Hack; Katja Rewitz; Silas Wagner; Wanja Wolff
articles_hidden.abstract: Ratings of perceived exertion (RPE) are widely used to prescribe exercise intensities. When used this way, researchers and practitioners may implicitly or explicitly rely on assumptions about the coupling between perceived effort and performance. These assumptions refer to two dimensions: the average shape of how effort translates to performance and the variability of performance across effort levels. Straightforwardly, effort-performance coupling can be thought of as linear, with constant variability across the intensity spectrum. However, classic psychophysical scaling laws (e.g., Fechner’s law) and motor control research (e.g., signal-dependent noise) predict that such coupling is non-linear, with intensity-contingent increases in variability. These assumptions are rarely made explicit and have not been jointly tested. To address this, we fitted and compared theory-driven Bayesian multilevel models reflecting distinct assumptions about the mean and the variability structure, using leave-one-out cross-validation for model selection. Data were collected from 101 climbers performing an isometric handgrip task with effort prescribed using a RPE 1-10 scale. We found robust evidence for a heteroscedastic variability structure, with a systematic increase in absolute force variability with prescribed RPE. Additionally, we found modest evidence favoring an exponential mean shape over a linear mean shape, suggesting that force increases disproportionately with effort. These effects were gender unspecific and are broadly consistent with Fechner’s psychophysical law and signal-dependent noise theory. Together, these findings suggest that a direct translation from effort to performance systematically misrepresents the actual relationship. Instead, practitioners and researchers should expect a disproportionate increase in performance with increasing absolute performance variability.

articles_hidden.title: A School-Based Intergenerational Engagement Program to Improve Older Adults’ Cognitive, Health and Social Outcomes: A Pilot Randomised Controlled Trial.
articles_hidden.authors: Anna Krzeczkowska; William J. McGeown; Alan J. Gow; Louise A. Brown Nicholls
articles_hidden.abstract: High quality evidence on the potential health benefits of intergenerational engagement (IE) for older adults, particularly using relatively moderate exposure, is limited. This pilot randomised controlled trial (RCT) evaluated the impact of a school-based IE intervention designed to engage healthy older adults in real-world activities and provide multimodal (cognitive, social, physical) engagement. Additionally, feasibility of the program was evaluated. The sample comprised 36 participants (29 females, 7 males), aged 60-80 years, who had been randomised to the intervention or a wait-list control group. Intervention participants assisted primary (elementary) school teachers in supporting children’s (4-8 yrs) reading, writing, and numeracy for 8 hours per week over six months, with data collected at baseline and 3- and 6-month follow-up sessions. The intervention was found to be generally feasible and was associated with significant improvements in: cognition (working memory, episodic memory, auditory verbal learning); daytime functioning (staying awake/alert); attitudes towards children; and sense of generative achievement (helping the younger generation). Benefits were typically observed at 3 months and maintained at 6 months. Moderate intensity participation in this school-based IE intervention therefore shows preliminary efficacy as a multimodal health promotion initiative for older adults. Minor intervention modification and full-scale assessment is now warranted.

articles_hidden.title: Navigating consumer uncertainty: Curiosity and individual differences in exploratory consumer behavior
articles_hidden.authors: Collin Kather; David M. Lydon-Staley
articles_hidden.abstract: Consumers differ not only in whether they explore marketplaces, but also in how they explore them. We examined whether multidimensional curiosity helps explain two forms of exploratory consumer behavior: exploratory acquisition of products and exploratory information seeking. Across two independent samples of adults (Study 1, N=461; Study 2, N=337), participants completed measures of six curiosity dimensions and exploratory consumer behavior. Stress tolerance was uniquely associated with greater exploratory acquisition in both studies after accounting for the other curiosity dimensions. Covert social curiosity was uniquely associated with greater exploratory information seeking in both studies. Associations between thrill seeking and acquisition and between overt social curiosity and information seeking emerged in Study 1 but did not replicate in Study 2. Joyous exploration and deprivation sensitivity showed bivariate associations with exploratory behavior but did not explain unique variance consistently. These findings indicate that a multidimensional curiosity framework provides a more differentiated account of the psychological heterogeneity underlying how consumers navigate uncertain marketplaces.

articles_hidden.title: Context-specific adaptation of cognitive processing in changing virtual environments
articles_hidden.authors: Ulrike Senftleben; Daniel Zeidler; Stefan Scherbaum; Matthew McGinity; Caroline Surrey
articles_hidden.abstract: Human cognition is sensitive to context cues, as indicated by the context-specific proportion congruency (CSPC) effect. This effect demonstrates that individuals implicitly adapt their cognitive processing to contextual cues that predict the likelihood of conflict. However, CSPC paradigms typically rely on simple, two-dimensional context cues, raising questions about their validity for complex, real-life environments. In this preregistered study, we examined whether CSPC effects emerge in three-dimensional, naturalistic contexts delivered via virtual reality (VR). We presented a numerical Stroop task in two virtual environments—a forest and an office—alternating on a trial-by-trial basis. Unbeknownst to participants, each environment was paired with either a high (80%; mostly congruent/MC context) or low (20%; mostly incongruent/MI context) proportion of incongruent trials (counter-balanced). Our results show the typical CSPC effect: reduced response time differences between incongruent and congruent trials in the MI environment relative to the MC environment. This finding indicates that context-dependent adjustments of cognitive processing extend to complex, semantically meaningful virtual environments. This supports the ecological validity of CSPC learning and highlights the importance of context cues in real-life cognitive processing. Further, our study highlights how VR opens up new avenues for studying context-dependent cognition beyond conventional laboratory stimuli.

articles_hidden.title: Robust Measurement of Habits with the Forced-Response Task A Multiverse Analysis
articles_hidden.authors: José Juan León; Pablo Martínez-López; Francisco Garre-Frutos; David Luque
articles_hidden.abstract: Instrumental behavior reflects a balance between two systems: an outcome-oriented, goal-directed system and a cognitively efficient habit system that gradually gains control with repeated instrumental responding in stable contexts. While overtraining reliably induces habits in animal models, human participants often retain goal-directed control when their performance is assessed using devaluation paradigms. To address this translational gap, the forced-response method has emerged as a promising approach for studying goal-directed and habitual behavior by constraining the time available to respond. This method imposes a dual task in which participants must respond accurately to an instrumental discriminative stimulus at a specific time signaled by a sound. Because the onset of the discriminative stimulus varies across trials, the time available for response preparation is systematically manipulated. Restricting this time can unmask stimulus-driven responses when the goal-directed system has insufficient time to override them. Although the forced-response method has become increasingly popular, its use has also been accompanied by growing flexibility in data analysis, creating a potential “garden of forking paths.” Using four independent datasets, we generated 48 a priori valid preprocessing pipelines to assess variability in two discrete measures of habitual behavior—the proportion of habits and the habit index—as well as their split-half reliability and the proportion of habits as a continuous function of the available response time, modeled using generalized additive models. Results indicated that both habit measures were generally robust across preprocessing pipelines. The proportion of habits was more sensitive to specific preprocessing choices, particularly accuracy and timing-synchrony exclusion criteria, but also showed greater reliability. In all cases, however, the resulting variability was small. Reliability analyses yielded acceptable estimates in most analytic universes. Overall, these findings support the forced-response method as a robust paradigm for studying habit formation and expression in humans.

articles_hidden.title: Preregistration Publication Consistency – A Study of Psychological Research Published by Authors from German-Speaking Institutions
articles_hidden.authors: Lena Hahn; Kai Sassenberg
articles_hidden.abstract: Preregistrations aim at reducing researchers' degrees of freedom. This goal is only reached if researchers adhere to them or at least transparently report deviations. The popularity of preregistration in psychology has increased, and so has research on preregistration publication consistency. However, previous research investigated preregistered publications in specific samples (e.g., a single journal, a restricted research area). Thus, generalizability of previous results is limited. To avoid this limitation, we scrutinize preregistration publication consistency in psychology by coding a diverse sample of journal publications and preregistrations from 2021 to 2024 drawn from a database of all empirical publications by psychologists with affiliations to institutions in German-speaking countries. We analyzed three aspects critical to researchers’ degrees of freedom in confirmatory research: the preregistered hypotheses, the sample size, and the exclusion criteria. Consistent with previous research, our results show that deviations are common, with roughly half of the sample having inconsistencies in at least two of the aforementioned aspects. Additionally, preregistration publication consistency was neither related to journal reputation (i.e., Journal Impact Factor and Transparency and Openness Promotion Factor) nor time (i.e., preregistration and publication year). We discuss implications of our findings for reporting preregistration deviations.

articles_hidden.title: Attachment-Informed Leadership (AIL):  A New Leadership Framework based on Attachment Theory and Social Neuroscience
articles_hidden.authors: Pascal Vrticka; Jonathan Wolf-Phillips
articles_hidden.abstract: Leadership research has catalogued many styles, among them transformational, authentic and servant leadership, but has offered few accounts of the regulatory mechanisms through which leader-follower relationships operate. We propose that attachment, understood through social neuroscience, supplies one such mechanism. Humans regulate environmental demands relationally, and attachment organises this social regulation of a finite bioenergetic budget under challenge. When followers face threat, dependence or uncertainty, this relationship can come to serve attachment functions, and the leader's reliability as a security provider bears on how much of followers' regulatory resources remains available for work. Building on the Social Neuroscience of Human Attachment (SoNeAt), we develop an attachment-informed leadership (AIL) framework spanning social allostasis, attachment and caregiving, predictive regulation and biobehavioural synchrony. We position AIL relative to evolutionary accounts of leadership and derive nine propositions that distinguish attachment processes from exchange, trust and identification, measurable from self-report to physiology and brain activity.

articles_hidden.title: Differential Effects of Self-centeredness and Selflessness: A Six-Month Longitudinal Study Across Mental, Relational, and Ecological Domains
articles_hidden.authors: Lucas David; Michaël Dambrun
articles_hidden.abstract: The Self-centeredness/Selflessness Happiness Model (SSHM) posits two complementary modes of self-based psychological functioning, selflessness and self-centeredness, relevant across multiple subfields of psychology. Shaped by developmental, social and cultural influences, selflessness and self-centeredness differentially forecast multiple variables from individual mental health to ecological concerns and behaviors. Addressing the largely correlational nature of prior evidence on the model, we conducted a two-wave longitudinal study over six months (N = 316) to test the middle-term prospective effects of selflessness and self-centeredness on mental health, relationship quality, and ecological orientation. Controlling for autoregressive stability and within-wave covariation, cross-lagged panel models indicated that selflessness prospectively predicted higher positive mental health and lower negative mental health and ecoanxiety. By contrast, self-centeredness predicted lower positive mental health, relationship quality and relationship with nature, and higher negative mental health. Additional findings revealed the mutual inhibition between the two dispositions. These findings extend cross-sectional research on the SSHM by demonstrating medium-term prospective associations and by positioning selflessness and self-centeredness as transdisciplinary predictors of holistic forms of health spanning intrapersonal, interpersonal, and ecological domains.

articles_hidden.title: Improving Brain-Behaviour Causality with Neurofeedback
articles_hidden.authors: Theo Ferreira Marins; Michal Ramot; Aurelio Cortese; Ranganatha Sitaram; Guilherme Wood
articles_hidden.abstract: A robust and reliable causal mapping of human brain function requires ruling out multiple sources of bias and confounding. New standards for causal inference suggest that the causal evidence provided by traditional methods, such as lesion mapping and non-invasive brain stimulation, may have critical gaps. Based on recent evidence, we discuss how brain-behaviour causality has been assessed in humans with well-established tools, and the extent to which emerging techniques, such as neurofeedback, provide additional insights. Finally, we introduce the Causal-Neurofeedback, a unifying framework based on functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) that dictates experimental and analytical choices designed to address new standards for causality with high granularity. This framework consists of manipulating fine-grained neural signatures and adopting key experimental and analytical control strategies to improve causal robustness. We conclude by discussing the potential of neurofeedback, through this framework, to provide robust causal evidence across diverse experimental contexts.

articles_hidden.title: Pluralism within limits: How to make the idea of multiple NCC kinds useful
articles_hidden.authors: Lukas Kob; Tomas Marvan
articles_hidden.abstract: Recently, several authors have argued that the current impasse in consciousness science supports a pluralistic interpretation: the view that seemingly contradictory findings may both be valid because consciousness can be brought about in different ways, each sufficient to generate conscious experience. We analyze different versions of pluralism to determine under what conditions it offers a viable interpretation of consciousness science. We argue that viable pluralism requires a two-factor framework distinguishing general consciousness factors (mechanisms rendering contents conscious) from content encoding itself. Moreover, NCC kinds must be finite in number and systematically ordered to enable a unified scientific model. While pluralism enables testable hypotheses, significant ontological tensions arise: how can consciousness constitute a unified natural kind if realized by fundamentally distinct NCC kinds? Drawing on philosophy of science, we propose an alternative interpretation in terms of scientific rather than natural kinds. Our goal is not to advocate for pluralism, but rather, to critically examine its viability and implications. Based on this, we urge the field to engage more explicitly with the foundational assumptions that shape consciousness research.

articles_hidden.title: From Morality to the Plate: Moral Foundations, Food Neophobia, and Sustainability Preferences
articles_hidden.authors: Giovanni Telesca; Marika Rullo; Carol Coricelli
articles_hidden.abstract: The present study examined whether moral foundations and food neophobia are associated with sustainable food choices and support for food-related sustainability policies in a sample of 296 Italian adults. Food neophobia (FN), a stable psychological tendency to refuse new foods, has been associated with reduced dietary variety and lower consumption of plant-based alternatives. Moral foundations (MFs) shape individuals' pre-reflective sensitivities to different moral orientations and have been linked to pro-environmental attitudes and food-related behaviors. Drawing on Moral Foundations Theory (MFT), we hypothesized that binding and individualizing foundations would differentially predict FN and, through it, sustainable food outcomes. Binding MFs (i.e., oriented toward purity and ingroup preservation) may function as dispositional antecedents of FN, as individuals who strongly endorse these concerns are likely to perceive novel foods as potential sources of contamination or threats to cultural and group identity. Conversely, individualizing MFs (i.e., oriented toward care and fairness) may reduce such avoidance by fostering openness toward foods associated with reduced harm and environmental benefit. Results showed that binding MFs were associated with higher FN, whereas individualizing MFs were negatively associated with it. FN was negatively associated with liking for plant-based foods and consumption frequency, as well as with policy support. FN fully mediated the associations between moral foundations and affective and behavioral indicators of sustainable food consumption and partially mediated the effects of MFs on policy support. These findings suggest that FN may be a key psychological pathway through which moral sensitivities translate into sustainable dietary choices and policy preferences.

articles_hidden.title: Semantic Interference in Blocked-Cyclic Word Production with Different Stimulus Types, Tasks, and Response Modalities
articles_hidden.authors: Stefan Wöhner; Andreas Widmann; Sophia Forchner; Erich Schröger; Jörg D. Jescheniak
articles_hidden.abstract: Theories of word production rely heavily on semantic context effects. For example, when pictures are named repeatedly and sorted by semantic category, it takes longer to name them than when they are named in an intermixed manner. Wöhner et al. (2021) found that semantic interference in blocked-cyclic naming was approximately three times greater for sounds (e.g., barking) than for pictures (e.g., a dog). This study explored possible reasons for this differential interference pattern. When the stimuli were presented briefly, the differential interference was replicated, ruling out the possibility that it results from a large overlap between stimulus processing and phonological response preparation. When the sounds and pictures were replaced with spoken and written words that the participants translated into their second language, the size of the interference was similar, showing that the differential pattern does not result from different stimulus modalities (auditory vs. visual). When participants typed their responses, the differential interference was replicated again, showing that it does not depend on a certain response modality (spoken vs. written). Additionally, pupil dilation data suggest that sounds, compared with pictures, may activate additional representations that contribute to the interference. Overall, the data imply that semantic interference in word production is shaped by early, stimulus-specific, perceptual and semantic “lead-in” processes that precede lexical selection. More attention should be given to these early processes in word production research.

articles_hidden.title: Evaluating biomarkers and prediction models: predictive utility analysis with E2P Simulator
articles_hidden.authors: Povilas Karvelis; Daniel Felsky; Anissa Abi-Dargham; Guillermo Horga; Andreea Andreea
articles_hidden.abstract: Precision psychiatry aims to identify biomarkers and develop prediction models to improve diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment selection. Despite extensive research, translating findings into clinically useful tools remains challenging. Here we argue that one important contributor to this translational gap is a pervasive misalignment between routine statistical analytic practices and the requirements for real-world decision making. To help address this, we introduce predictive utility analysis: a statistical workflow for estimating the practical significance of biomarkers and prediction models by accounting for outcome base rates and measurement reliability. Starting from effect size or model performance estimates, the workflow simulates expected real-world performance in a target population and summarizes it across complementary metrics including positive and negative predictive value, Precision-Recall AUC, and Net Benefit. Analogous to how power analysis is used for determining the conditions needed to achieve statistical significance, predictive utility analysis can help determine the conditions needed to achieve practical significance. We implement and illustrate this workflow using E2P Simulator, a recently developed open-source web tool that makes predictive utility analysis accessible through interactive simulations and publication-ready visualizations. We demonstrate its application using specific examples in three key areas: diagnostic (depression, Alzheimer’s disease), treatment response (antidepressants), and risk (suicide attempts and psychosis onset) prediction, highlighting conditions under which we may expect clinically meaningful advances. While we focus on translational challenges in psychiatry, the workflow and tools presented here address general statistical challenges and are broadly applicable across biomedical and behavioral sciences.

articles_hidden.title: Heritability is not destiny
articles_hidden.authors: Emma Meaburn; Mahitab Elgamal; Qidong Song; Michael Thomas
articles_hidden.abstract:
High heritability estimates for behavioural traits such as cognitive ability and educational attainment are often misinterpreted as showing these traits are resistant to environmental intervention. However, heritability describes sources of variation within a population, not how outcomes would change under alternative environments - the counterfactual relevant to education policy.

We illustrate this using a computational model of English past-tense acquisition, an established model of experience-dependent cognitive development. In an artificial neural network, simulated genetic influences were implemented through a polygenic architecture affecting neurocomputational parameters, while environmental variation reflected differences in the richness of linguistic input. By varying these influences, we generated populations with low or high trait heritability and compared their responses to (a) behavioural interventions and (b) improvements in environmental quality.

Population intervention effects depended on how strongly adverse environments had constrained prior development, rather than heritability. Gene x environment interactions were small and only appeared in high heritability populations – environments worked similarly for all genotypes. Improving environmental quality across cohorts benefited populations similarly regardless of trait heritability. To test an exemplar policy counterfactual, interventions were targeted to reduce achievement gaps: prior performance was more effective for targeting intervention than environmental disadvantage or polygenic scores.

These findings support the view that heritability is not destiny. Because cognitive development is plastic and experience-dependent, environmental change can improve outcomes across genotypes. The policy relevance of genetics lies not in predicting immutable outcomes, but in identifying where intervention can be most effective. Genetics is not about destiny, it is about opportunity.

articles_hidden.title: Environmental and social context are associated with emotional states and their dynamics
articles_hidden.authors: Florencia Altschuler; Christophe Gauld; Enric Vilajosana; Cecilia González Campo; Pamela Chavarría-Elizondo; Víctor De la Peña-Arteaga; Asier Juaneda-Seguí; Ignacio Martínez-Zalacaín; VIktor Jirsa; Pierpaolo Sorrentino
articles_hidden.abstract: Emotional states fluctuate with everyday context, but contextual influences can operate at markedly different temporal scales and magnitudes. We examined the longitudinal effects of two naturalistic contextual exposures - daily weather (precipitation and temperature) and the COVID-19 lockdown-  on emotional states assessed using ecological momentary assessment (EMA) in a university-based cohort in Barcelona, Spain, comprising up to 25,724 observations from 156 participants. Lockdown analyses were restricted to the subset of participants with observations both during and outside the lockdown period (n=45). Participants completed daily smartphone-based assessments of happiness, anxiety, muscular tension, worry, and avoidance over six months. Within-participant fixed-effects models showed that greater precipitation was associated with lower happiness and higher anxiety, muscular tension, and avoidance, whereas temperature showed no significant associations with any of these outcomes. In contrast, lockdown was associated with a broad shift toward lower happiness and higher negative emotional states and with greater day-to-day variability in happiness, anxiety, muscular tension, and avoidance. These findings illustrate how low-magnitude environmental variation and large-scale social disruption can be detected within the same real-world EMA framework, with the latter affecting both emotional states and short-term dynamics.

articles_hidden.title: Does the Creature of Habit Scale capture general habit tendencies? Lessons from anorexia nervosa.
articles_hidden.authors: Caroline Monica Harbison; Sanne de Wit; Joseph Wonderlich; Caroline Touzeau; Alexandra Muratore; Hilde Geurts; Joanna Steinglass; Karin Foerde
articles_hidden.abstract: The Creature of Habit Scale (COHS) was designed to assess general habit tendencies, with Automaticity and Routine subscales assessing distinct features of habits. However, the Automaticity subscale is composed predominantly of eating-related items, raising questions about the scale’s construct and content validity. To evaluate this, COHS scores were compared between individuals with anorexia nervosa, restricting subtype (ANr; n = 35) and controls (n = 26), and associations with eating disorder habit strength (Self-Report Habit Index) and psychopathology (Eating Disorder Examination Questionnaire; Three-Factor Eating Questionnaire) were examined. Automaticity scores were significantly lower in ANr than controls (W = 192, p < .001). Within ANr, Automaticity was negatively associated with eating disorder severity (B = -2.74, p < .001) and eating-related habits (B = −4.18, p < .001). Automaticity was positively associated with TFEQ Disinhibition across groups (B = 0.39, p < .001) and, within ANr, negatively associated with TFEQ Restraint (B = -0.21, p = .012). The Automaticity subscale of the COHS may primarily reflect disinhibited eating rather than general habitual tendencies, challenging its construct and content validity and suggesting caution in its use as a general habit measure in eating disorders and across populations.

articles_hidden.title: The Case Against the Design Hierarchy in Psychological Network Analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Adela-Maria Isvoranu
articles_hidden.abstract: The network perspective conceptualizes psychological phenomena as systems of interacting components, placing dynamics at the center of explanation. This has justified criticism of studies that use cross-sectional networks to claim within-person dynamics, uniquely identified causal mechanisms, or effective intervention targets. In the current methodological climate, however, an implicit design hierarchy has emerged in which cross-sectional design is itself treated as the objection. In an audit of 157 papers across three journals, 65% of 127 eligible papers named cross-sectional design as a limitation and 68% recommended longitudinal research as a remedy. Such a hierarchy mischaracterizes designs operating at different temporal scales: they estimate different structures rather than progressively better answers to one question. Cross-sectional networks can distinguish conditional from marginal associations, characterize the conditional-association structure, support measurement development, identify patterns for replication, and generate constrained hypotheses, particularly when measures represent characteristic tendencies or experiences over a defined period. Longitudinal and intensive longitudinal designs are not automatic upgrades over cross-sectional designs; their evidential value depends on temporal resolution, lag selection, measurement quality, model assumptions, and the distinction between group-average and person-specific inference. Designs should therefore be judged by alignment of question, measurement, model, and claims—not by position in an assumed hierarchy.

articles_hidden.title: Examining the Relations Between Self-Construal, Culture, and Cognitive Dissonance Using the Induced-Compliance Paradigm
articles_hidden.authors: Tim Figureau; Daniel Priolo; Willem W. A. Sleegers; Kenneth G DeMarree; Omid Ghasemi; Amélie Gourdon-Kanhukamwe; Maxime Mauduy; Asil Ali Özdoğru; Robert M Ross; Bjørn Sætrevik
articles_hidden.abstract: Cognitive dissonance, traditionally conceptualized as a fundamental psychological process involving discomfort from inconsistent cognitions, may vary across cultures. These variations could be attributed to self-construal, or how individuals define themselves in relation to others. Although previous cross-cultural research has predominantly used the free-choice paradigm, significant concerns have been raised regarding its procedural validity and the robustness of its findings. To address this issue, this registered report presents secondary analyses of a large-scale international dataset. We investigated the moderating role of cultural variables on dissonance effects within the induced-compliance paradigm across 18 countries (N = 3,804). We hypothesized that dissonance effects would be stronger for participants with higher individual-level self-construal scores (H1), in more individualistic countries (H2), and in countries with higher country-level self-construal scores (H3). Our results did not support these hypotheses, suggesting that cultural moderation may not generalize to the induced-compliance paradigm. We discuss the necessity of reassessing the procedure’s reliability and clarifying the theoretical role of choice.

articles_hidden.title: Chronometric Normalization for BYOD Digital Assessments: Separating Hardware Latency from Cognitive Fluency
articles_hidden.authors: Eudald Correig Fraga; Carlos García Sancho; Marc Colomer Canyelles; Brian Butterworth
articles_hidden.abstract:
The transition to digital, Bring-Your-Own-Device (BYOD) environments has vastly expanded the scale and accessibility of psychological and educational testing. However, unstandardized
hardware introduces systematic mechanical latencies that contaminate timed cognitive performance, leading to measurement error and possible diagnostic misclassification. Furthermore, naive device-specific normalization strategies are inadequate, as they inadvertently suppress meaningful sociodemographic variance that inherently correlates with device ownership. To address this methodological gap, we introduce a chronometric normalization framework designed to isolate and remove hardware-driven latency without altering underlying cognitive capacity. The model leverages a brief motor task to estimate individual mechanical delay and calibrates this correction against a device-minimal, untimed cognitive task that is substantially less sensitive to hardware speed. This anchors the calibration so that real between-group differences in ability are retained. We demonstrate the framework’s practical utility using data from COSMOS, a large-scale dyscalculia screening battery administered to 54,538 students across 910 schools using the hardware available at each school. Results indicate that while trackpad users initially exhibited severe, artifactual underperformance on timed fluency tasks, the chronometric correction successfully neutralized this hardware penalty. By realigning score distributions while preserving structural
demographic differences, this open-source method ensures that subsequent norming and diagnostic decisions reflect true cognitive architecture rather than the mechanical limitations of the user’s interface.

articles_hidden.title: Mathematical modelling of interactive tapping reveals tap intervals as strongest predictor of subsequent tap timing
articles_hidden.authors: Shane Mannion; Ivana Konvalinka
articles_hidden.abstract:
Successful interpersonal rhythmic coordination requires people to continuously adapt both the
timing and tempo of their actions to one another. Classical error-correction models distinguish these
processes as phase and period correction, typically modeling them as responses to instantaneous and
cumulative asynchrony, respectively. These models were developed mostly for sensorimotor synchro-
nisation to an external pacing signal, rather than interactive interpersonal coordination where both
partners adapt. It thus remains unknown which temporal information people actually use to adapt
their behaviour to one another. We show, using a bounded generalised least-squares framework and
joint finger-tapping data obtained from both bidirectional (reciprocal) and unidirectional (leader-
follower) interactions, that the previous inter-tap interval (ITI) of a partner is a better predictor for
an individual’s next ITI than either cumulative or instantaneous asynchrony. We argue that this
predictor is not only the strongest from a modelling perspective, but also the most parsimonious
from a theoretical point of view. Our results support these claims and show that the partner’s
previous ITI provides a less endogenous predictor of adaptation, addressing a long-standing issue in
models of tapping behaviour.

articles_hidden.title: Introspection and Difficulties in Documenting Subjective Experiences of Meditation
articles_hidden.authors: Ndabenhle Siphesihle Mthembu
articles_hidden.abstract: Introspective research into subjective experiences of meditation is constrained by an inability to document meditative experiences in a manner that addresses their irreducible qualities. Meditators' integration attempts are negatively affected due to this methodological gap. Thus, more responsive documentation methods need to be developed within introspective research. This paper theorizes that documentation failure in introspective research stems from a fundamental linguistic flaw embedded in how pre-linguistic felt-significance relates to downstream documentation methods. During a subjective meditative event, an experience possesses felt-meaning, defined as the direct perception of a quantity of meaning within the event itself. This felt-meaning is pre-linguistic and serves as the raw material out of which expressed meaning—the formal linguistic description—is constructed. The primary cause of documentation difficulty arises when pre-linguistic events are perceived to be devoid of felt-significance. When an experience presents no identifiable pattern from which to construct a linguistic description, generating expressed meaning becomes increasingly difficult, exposing a hard limit of language itself.

articles_hidden.title: Emotion Recognition From AI-Generated and Human Faces: Performance, Mental Health, and Demographic Diversity
articles_hidden.authors: Matthew J Vowels; Laura Marika Vowels
articles_hidden.abstract:
Facial emotion-recognition tasks are widely used to investigate social-cognitive differences across mental health conditions, but their
scientific value depends on the faces used to measure performance. Established photographic databases are difficult and expensive to
expand, and many provide little ethnic diversity. AI-generated faces offer a more representative, flexible, and scalable alternative,
provided they capture the same clinically relevant individual differences as photographs of human faces. We compared 161
photorealistic AI-generated faces with 72 images from FACES, an established human-photograph set. Prolific participants contributed
83,206 valid trials; 77,238 trials covering the six shared emotions entered the primary comparison (accuracy \textit{n} = 1,047; response
time \textit{n} = 1,046). AI-diverse expressions were recognised more accurately (89.12\% vs.\ 81.72\%) and faster (2.29 vs.\ 2.64 s) than
FACES expressions, while AI-diverse and AI-White performance did not differ significantly. The AI task retained the individual differences needed for research: lower accuracy on both sources was associated most consistently with psychotic-like experiences and obsessive-compulsive symptoms, with magnitudes aligned with previous literature. AI-diverse and FACES accuracy correlated at \textit{r} = .56, and corrected split-half reliability was .70 and .60, respectively. Women were more accurate than men; participant ethnicity was unrelated to performance. Higher AI accuracy indicates that the expressions were clear; it does not show general psychometric superiority, possibly because very easy items can compress differences among high performers. The combination of clear expressions, comparable symptom sensitivity, and broader representation shows that generative AI can modernise a core social-cognition research tool while making stimulus design more controllable, expandable, and shareable.

articles_hidden.title: Cognitive Probe Framework: From Passive Reading to Active Probing
articles_hidden.authors: YUTing Sun; Zewei Yu
articles_hidden.abstract:
Natural language processing systems are strong readers. Given text, they can classify, extract, and generate. Yet a fraud investigator assessing a suspicious borrower, an AI tutor helping a student who answers incorrectly, and a brand manager studying consumer perceptions face a different problem. The central question is not what a text says, but what the system should ask to reveal how a person thinks. NLP has spent decades improving the ability to answer questions, while the systematic design of questions remains underdeveloped.
This paper introduces the Cognitive Probe Framework (CPF), a general computational framework that actively presents structured semantic stimuli, or probes, to elicit responses from a human cognitive subject. CPF represents the responses as structured cognitive vectors and uses those representations to generate steering options. The framework supports the probing, interpretation, and bounded intervention of cognitive states through a closed-loop process with three stages: Probing, Modeling, and Steering.
CPF is organized as a four-level family. CPF serves as the general framework at L0. Eight specialized branches occupy L1: the Adversarial, Heuristic, Linking, Stress, Consensus, Foresight, Elicitation, and Metacognitive Cognitive Probe Frameworks, abbreviated ACPF, HCPF, LCPF, SCPF, CCPF, FCPF, ECPF, and MCPF. Each branch contains specialized probe tools at L2 and can support applications at L3. The family spans individual, organizational, market, and societal levels. MCPF is the only inward-facing branch: it uses reflective questions to examine a person's awareness of their own cognitive processes, addressing a structural blind spot left by the seven outward-facing branches.
Beyond its technical architecture, CPF describes a dual mechanism for cognitive augmentation. Expertise augmentation externalizes memory, amplifies weak cues, and directs attention, reducing cognitive load and unstable judgment under pressure. Learning scaffolding makes expert reasoning visible, traceable, and reproducible, accelerating skill acquisition by novices. Grounded in situation awareness, distributed cognition, and cognitive apprenticeship, CPF is positioned not only as a framework that uses NLP but also as a paradigm for bridging limits in human cognition and the complexity of real-world decisions.
The paper also introduces Probe Ethics as a meta-layer constraining the entire framework. It establishes transparency, reversibility, and human judgment as three governing principles and addresses risks that arise when AI is used in social settings, including cognitive manipulation, power asymmetry, cultural bias, and automation bias.
As a vision and position paper, this work defines the scope, family structure, core concepts, design principles, and research roadmap of CPF. It does not claim that all branches are empirically validated. Its aim is to move NLP from passive text reading toward active, accountable cognitive probing.

articles_hidden.title: When do intentions predict action? The temporal dynamics of the intention–action gap
articles_hidden.authors: Peiyuan Zhang; Luisa Leonelli; Yijun Lin; Wei Ji Ma
articles_hidden.abstract: Procrastination is defined as voluntarily delaying an intended course of action, yet the gap between intention and action is rarely measured directly, and little is known about how it unfolds over time. We gave 127 adults seven days to complete 180 units of a self-paced online reading task and recorded the timestamp of every completed unit. Before the task began, 67 of them reported how many units they intended to complete on each of the seven days, so that intended and actual work were expressed in the same units on the same days. Among those who finished, work was concentrated 0.59 days later than intended, although the day people finished did not differ from the day they had planned. The gap widened through Day 4, stopped growing on Day 5, and narrowed over the final two days. Intentions predicted when people started but not when they finished, and their influence faded after the first half of the task. Trait procrastination showed the opposite pattern, predicting actual but not intended work and shaping the timing of work throughout the task, most strongly in the middle.

articles_hidden.title: Formal Properties of Spontaneous Figure Drawings are Associated with Contemporaneous Affective State
articles_hidden.authors: Jake Hooper; Jennifer Mitlehner; Margaret E. Sereno
articles_hidden.abstract: Does the way a person draws reveal how they feel? Expressionist theory proposes that affect leaves traces in the formal properties of art, yet existing evidence relies largely on exceptional artists or on drawings created to depict a specified emotion. Adult participants completed a spontaneous figure drawing and reported their current affective state. Each drawing was quantified using two complementary approaches: (1) rater-coded formal elements and (2) computational image statistics. The resulting set of 40 drawing features was reduced to 9 interpretable components. Controlling for drawing time and artistic skill, these drawing components explained meaningful variance in affect, with the strongest and most robust associations emerging for negative affect. Critically, human ratings and computational image features each captured unique information not accounted for by the other, and these effects were observed in ordinary, untrained participants who were never instructed to communicate emotion. Spontaneous figure drawings thus appear to contain recoverable signatures of contemporaneous affective state embedded in their formal structure, independent of artistic skill. These findings position everyday drawing as an accessible, information-rich, and compact behavioral window into affect and provide a reproducible framework for quantifying how emotion is externalized in visual form.

articles_hidden.title: Drawn to Belong, but Not Just Anywhere: Identity Complexity, Uncertainty, and the Allure of Extremist Groups
articles_hidden.authors: Michelle Blaya-Burgo; Michael A. Hogg
articles_hidden.abstract: People often identify with radical groups before engaging in violence, yet the psychosocial processes that make these groups appealing warrant closer examination. Across two studies, we examined whether identity complexity moderated the relationship between self-uncertainty and positive attitudes toward and willingness to join radical groups. In Study 1 (N = 164), we experimentally manipulated identity complexity and self-uncertainty. Contrary to our hypotheses, neither manipulation nor their interaction significantly predicted attitudes toward or willingness to join a hypothetical radical group. Given the sample limitations and the limited effectiveness of the uncertainty prime, Study 2 (N = 259) provided a more rigorous test by manipulating identity complexity while examining naturally occurring self-uncertainty. Again, identity complexity and its interaction with self-uncertainty did not predict either outcome. However, higher self-uncertainty was associated with greater willingness to join the radical group, whereas younger age and greater identity centrality (but not complexity) predicted more positive attitudes toward and greater willingness to join it. These findings suggest that the prominence of a specific identity, rather than the complexity of one's broader identity structure, may be more relevant to understanding openness to radical groups and may inform identity-based approaches to prevention and countering violent extremism and deradicalization efforts.

articles_hidden.title: More Than Use and Cheating: A Developmental Study of High School Students’ Meaning- Making About AI
articles_hidden.authors: Gabriel Velez; Aubrie Robinson; Larry Zhiming Xu; Sahil Bagai
articles_hidden.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has become increasingly embedded in adolescents’ educational experiences, yet little research has examined how young people make sense of AI and its implications for their development. Guided by the Phenomenological Variant of Ecological Systems Theory (PVEST), this qualitative study explored how high school students understand AI in education and how those understandings relate to their identities as students. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 18 students from 11 U.S. high schools and analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis. Students commonly framed AI as a neutral tool whose value depended on how it was used. They described their own AI use as supporting learning and coping with academic stress while characterizing peers’ use as more likely to involve cheating. Participants also expressed fears about dependency, diminished learning, and future employment. Finally, they perceived AI as altering learning processes and contributing to mistrust and distance in student– teacher relationships. Findings highlight AI as a developmental and relational phenomenon rooted in identity processes central to adolescence.

articles_hidden.title: Integrating conflicting visual 3D shape cues
articles_hidden.authors: Jovan Kemp; Fulvio Domini
articles_hidden.abstract: How does the visual system handle discrepant estimates of depth from conflicting visual cues? One possibility is that less reliable cues are suppressed in favor of cues that are more likely to produce veridical depth estimates. This can be accomplished by a statistically robust implementation of the Bayesian framework for cue integration. However, suppression relies on the assumption that individual cues generally produce consistent depth estimates, an assumption that may not hold. Alternatively, the cues may be integrated via a vector summation, as proposed by the Intrinsic Constraint theory, regardless of whether they conflict. Using an absolute depth judgment task and a two-interval forced-choice (2-IFC) task, we evaluate cue integration for a range of cue-conflict ratios. Participants were shown 3D corrugated surfaces with depths specified by a set ratio of the binocular disparity cue and monocular cues composed of texture and shading. In the depth judgement task, participants adjusted the depth of the 3D surface until it matched the target depth specified by a 2D reference. Discrimination thresholds measured from the component cues in isolation were additionally used to parameterize the Bayesian robust model. The results showed the matched depth systematically varied with the cue-conflict ratio. The vector summation model produced a better fit to the data than the Bayesian robust model. In the second task, participants performed a 2-IFC task discriminating between surfaces with the same cue-conflict ratio. The discrimination thresholds extracted from this task were again better predicted by the vector summation model. These results indicate that cues are integrated directly rather than through statistically robust mechanisms, challenging the dominant Bayesian account of cue integration.

articles_hidden.title: The relationship between numerosity and the Fourier power spectrum of dot arrays
articles_hidden.authors: Joonkoo Park; Shimin Hu; Ruoyu Yuan
articles_hidden.abstract: This technical note presents mathematical derivations that establish the relationship between numerosity and the Fourier power spectrum of dot arrays, a standard stimulus in biological and psychological research in numerosity perception (e.g., DeWind et al. (2015); Park and Huber (2022). We derive a closed-form solution for the radially averaged power spectrum of images depicting arrays of identical dots as a function of dot number, radius, spacing, and spatial frequency. We also demonstrate that an unconventional distillation of the Fourier coefficients, as done in Paul et al. (2022), reveals an artifactual relationship between that metric and numerosity.

articles_hidden.title: Representations of Change Support Object Individuation in Infancy
articles_hidden.authors: Peter Mazalik; Justin Halberda
articles_hidden.abstract:
“One can never step in the same river twice, for it is not the same river and he is not the same man.” This ancient puzzle by Heraclitus highlights that the world, and ourselves, are constantly changing. But to raise these puzzles, one must engage the concept of CHANGE. Developmental research shows that even infants represent highly abstract notions, including objects, agents, cause, and number. Here, we ask whether they also represent CHANGE.

We adapted the individuation paradigm pioneered by Xu and Carey (1996), in which two objects emerge sequentially from behind an occluder, preventing spatiotemporal cues about the number of objects. Infants must instead rely on contrastive featural/kind information. Prior work shows that before 12 months, infants fail to individuate objects differing in basic-level category (e.g., duck vs. truck), but succeed with broader distinctions (e.g., object vs. agent).

Here we show that infants can use the contrast between a continuously changing object and a static object to infer the number of entities present. This effect cannot be
explained by saliency alone, as infants’ longer looking at unexpected outcomes differs
from any preference for the more salient changing object, and is striking in light of
reports that infants at this age fail to individuate objects by color alone (Leslie, 1998).
Representing change opens a new avenue for research: What types of change are
encoded? Over what timescales? Embedded in which cognitive systems? By 8 months,
infants already appreciate change as a core property of the world.

articles_hidden.title: Does confidence indicate face-identity matching accuracy for own-race and other-race faces?
articles_hidden.authors: Geraldine Jeckeln; ALICE O'TOOLE
articles_hidden.abstract: Confidence reliably indicates face-matching accuracy for same-race faces. However, it is unclear whether this holds for other-race faces. We examined the confidence-accuracy relationship for same- and other-race faces in Caucasian and African American participants. To eliminate response bias in observers’ confidence-scale use, we measured confidence using a confidence forced-choice task, rather than with confidence ratings. Participants completed two consecutive face-matching trials and selected the trial on which they felt more confident. Results showed an other-race effect for face-matching accuracy, but not for the confidence-accuracy relationship. We also examined whether comparative-trial difficulty predicted confidence decisions. For African American participants, difficulty predicted confidence for same- and other-race decisions. For Caucasian participants, difficulty predicted confidence for same-, but not other-race, decisions. Confidence predicted accuracy for same- and other-race faces, with difficulty consistently guiding confidence for same-race faces. These findings enhance our understanding of how confidence decisions are formed and guide cross-race identification decisions.

articles_hidden.title: Research practices and transparency in Slovak social sciences: A national analysis based on random sampling of publications (2013-2022)
articles_hidden.authors: Marcel Martončik; Ivan Ropovik; Peter Babincak; Gabriel Baník; Jaroslava Bočanová; Denisa Fedáková; Richard Gamrát; Samar Issmailová; Klára Kačmariková; Pavol Kačmár
articles_hidden.abstract: The credibility of the social sciences has been increasingly questioned, with concerns centering on limited transparency, replicability, questionable research practices, and incomplete reporting. Most evidence on these problems comes from self-report surveys, which are subject to recall and self-presentation biases. Analyzing the published literature offers a complementary approach that reveals what the scientific record contains. In this study, we examined the research, reporting, and transparency practices of Slovak social science literature published between 2013 and 2022. We coded a stratified random sample of 998 articles from two national registries and Scopus. For each record, we extracted methodological, statistical, bibliometric, and transparency-related characteristics, and applied granularity-related inconsistency of means (GRIM) tests to assess the internal coherence of reported results. Open science practices were rare and showed little improvement over the decade: data were shared in 5.0% of empirical studies, code in 4.1%, only one study was preregistered, and none was published as a Registered Report. More consequentially, standard reporting was frequently incomplete: sample size justification was present in 12.3% of applicable studies, effect sizes and confidence intervals accompanied all analyses in 32.0% and 7.1% studies, respectively, and reliability evidence and missing data handling were often absent. Among studies reporting sufficient detail for GRIM testing, 19.4% of assessed values were inconsistent, and 30% of these studies contained at least 25% inconsistent values. The findings suggest that the credibility of this literature is constrained primarily by insufficient reporting standards. Reforms should prioritize complete methodological reporting, with more demanding open science practices to follow.

articles_hidden.title: Beyond Scalar Choice: Foraging as a Policy Framework for Decision Neuroscience
articles_hidden.authors: Zahra Rezaei; Juan F. Ramirez-Villegas; Ian Q Whishaw; rob sutherland; Majid H Mohajerani
articles_hidden.abstract:
Foraging is a fundamental form of decision-making, requiring animals to search, evaluate resources,
allocate effort, manage risk, and coordinate behavior. Much of foraging neuroscience reduces this
behavior to scalar choice, using reward magnitude, delay, effort, risk, or opportunity cost to explain
whether an animal stays or leaves, accepts or rejects, harvests or switches. We argue that this
approach leaves a defining feature of foraging underdeveloped. Animals do not simply compare
values at isolated decision points. They implement policies that organize state-dependent patterns
of approach, inspection, consumption, transport, withdrawal, persistence, and disengagement over
time. Here we propose a policy-centered perspective in which the primary explanatory unit is the
mapping from internal and external states onto an organized repertoire of actions. This framework
retains the normative strengths of optimal foraging theory while broadening the interpretation of
departures from its predictions. Apparent suboptimality may reveal hidden costs, latent state variables,
or changes in policy organization rather than a simple failure of valuation. This perspective
also reframes the neural problem. Understanding foraging as policy points to a distributed neural
basis that integrates valuation, spatial memory, action selection, risk regulation, and behavioral
sequencing. By shifting the unit of analysis from scalar choice to policy organization, foraging provides
a principled bridge across behavioral ecology, decision neuroscience, reinforcement learning,
and research on artificial agents.

articles_hidden.title: What's The Function? Eigenfunctions Shaping (Non)Parametric Growth Curves
articles_hidden.authors: Suryadyuti Baral; Emilio Ferrer
articles_hidden.abstract:
Growth Curve Models (GCMs) are central tools for analyzing longitudinal data in psychology and are estimated under the Multilevel Modeling (MLM) or the Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) frameworks. Despite their flexibility, both approaches require researchers to predefine functional forms or loadings, aiding interpretation but risking model misspecification. We propose functional principal component analysis (FPCA) as a nonparametric extension of these models, where estimated eigenfunctions can inform the functions used in MLMs and the loadings in SEMs.
     
We evaluate FPCA’s ability to recover underlying functional structure in longitudinal data and assess its robustness to violations of key assumptions, including orthonormality of data generating functions and independence of random effects. Sample size and time points are varied to reflect realistic intensive and sparse longitudinal designs. FPCA is fit to training data, and the resulting eigenfunctions inform GCM loadings evaluated on held-out test data. Results show that FPCA accurately recovers generating functions under orthonormal conditions, with improved estimation under higher sample sizes and larger number of time points. GCMs informed by eigenfunctions show good fit and parameter recovery when assumptions are met. An empirical illustration demonstrates how FPCA can uncover functional patterns and guide model specification. Indeed, FPCA can be a valuable nonparametric complement to conventional longitudinal models.

articles_hidden.title: Does internalized homonegativity lower sexual satisfaction? A longitudinal assessment among gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men (GBM) in Canada's three largest cities
articles_hidden.authors: Sarah Meora Kowall; Paolo Aldrin Palma; Shayna Skakoon-Sparling; Terri Haochuan Zhang; Aki Gormezano; Jérémy Lelièvre; Daniel Grace; Trevor Adam Hart
articles_hidden.abstract:
Purpose: Internalized homonegativity is associated with lower sexual satisfaction among gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men (GBM). Though internalized homonegativity is commonly seen as an antecedent to lower sexual satisfaction, existing research tends to be cross-sectional, limiting our ability to make causal inferences. This has important implications for GBM sexual health and clinical interventions. The goal of this study is to examine the longitudinal associations between internalized homonegativity and sexual satisfaction.

Methods: We analyzed data from a longitudinal study of GBM in Vancouver, Toronto and Montreal, Canada (N = 1307). Using a random-intercept cross-lagged panel model (RI-CLPM), we analyzed data from baseline up to two years of follow-up to model the within-person changes between internalized homonegativity and sexual satisfaction. The RI-CLPM allows us to account for the stable, trait-like differences between individuals that may inflate correlations, thus allowing for a stronger estimate of within-person variation over time.

Results: Although there were no cross-lagged associations between internalized homonegativity and sexual satisfaction, we found that participants who scored higher on internalized homonegativity also tended to score lower on sexual satisfaction after accounting for within-person variation, suggesting these effects are due to stable between-person differences.

Conclusion: Cross-sectional associations are likely due to stable between-person differences affecting both outcomes, suggesting that internalized homonegativity and sexual satisfaction are independent processes. From a clinical perspective, internalized homonegativity may be useful in identifying potential issues with sexual well-being, but reducing internalized homonegativity may not be sufficient in alleviating these outcomes.

articles_hidden.title: Mental Health Literacy Across Psychology Students and Large Language Models
articles_hidden.authors: Eileen Richter; Konrad Schöniger; Maya Schulze; Luisa Frede; Korbinian Moeller; Ronny Redlich; Markus Spitzer
articles_hidden.abstract:
Mental health misconceptions are widespread, yet it remains unclear how accurately psychology students distinguish such misconceptions from evidence-based information, whether this differs across stages of psychology education, and how their performance compares with that of large language models (LLMs). 
We evaluated the accuracy of 150 psychology students, including 70 first-semester and 80 more advanced students, in classifying 15 mental health myths and 15 facts. Additionally, we used Chat GPT-5.4, Claude Sonnet 4.5, DeepSeek V3.2, and GLM-5 to classify the same statements across 80 independent runs per statement and model. 
Students classified mental health myths more accurately than facts, and advanced students outperformed first-semester students in classifying both statement types (myths: 87.7% vs. 75.2%; facts: 69.3% vs. 55.4%). A binomial generalized linear mixed-effects model indicated that group differences in classification accuracy varied between myths and facts. LLMs generally showed higher accuracy than both student groups in classifying statements, although performance varied substantially across models, particularly for facts. Item-level analyses revealed partly distinct error patterns: students and LLMs struggled with some of the same facts, whereas they also showed relative advantages on specific statements. 
These findings suggest that mental health literacy differs significantly across stages of psychology education and that, although current LLMs perform strongly on this classification task, some item-specific errors recurred across repeated runs. Examining which misconceptions and facts remain difficult may help identify specific gaps in both psychology education and AI-generated mental health information.

articles_hidden.title: Questionable mediated effect of self-efficacy on depressive symptoms among college students: A reassessment of Desai and Lueke (2026)
articles_hidden.authors: Kimmo Sorjonen; Bo Melin; Marika Melin
articles_hidden.abstract: Using the covariance matrix reported by Desai and Lueke, we conducted a reanalysis of the evidence supporting their mediation framework relating generalized self-efficacy to depressive symptoms in college students. We demonstrate that the observed pattern of covariation can be represented equally well by a theoretically different latent-variable model that does not assume the directional sequence proposed in the original investigation. In this alternative specification, generalized self-efficacy, perceived stress, college maladjustment, and depressive symptoms are conceptualized as indicators of a broader latent construct, core self-evaluation. These findings illustrate a fundamental limitation of observational research: identical covariance structures can often be explained by multiple competing models. Consequently, correlational data alone provide limited grounds for favoring one theoretical interpretation over alternative explanations. Consideration of rival models should therefore be a routine part of efforts to draw conclusions about psychological processes and mechanisms.

articles_hidden.title: Cultural Models of Everyday Love in Contemporary Spain: A Mixed-Methods Cultural Consensus Study
articles_hidden.authors: Saida Heshmati; Jaymes Paolo Rombaoa; Lindy Williams; Dana Hussein; Carmen Goicoechea; Andrew Villamil; Catalina LeeAnn Oselio; Saina Salamati; Corey Abramson; Martín Sánchez-Jankowski
articles_hidden.abstract: Love can emerge through moments and interactions in our daily lives, varying across different cultural contexts. Using a sequential mixed-method approach guided by Cultural Consensus Theory (CCT; Romney et al., 1986), we examined the shared agreement on which daily life experiences evoke loving feelings in Spanish culture across two studies. In Study 1, we conducted semi-structured interviews (n = 54), two-person group interviews (n = 6), and focus groups (3–5 participants; n = 40) to explore how love manifests across different relationships in daily life in Spain. Through qualitative thematic analysis, we identified recurring experiences, centering around explicit affection, instrumental support and dependable care, quality time, and thoughtful, attentive actions. This analysis informed the development of the 61-item Felt Love Questionnaire for Spain (FLQ-Spain), which collects everyday experiences with the potential to make people feel loved within the Spanish context. In Study 2, we administered the FLQ-Spain to a representative sample of Spaniards (N = 502) to assess how likely these experiences are to elicit loving feelings in the Spanish culture. Results from cognitive psychometric analysis revealed a shared agreement in the responses. ‘Highly likely’ loving eliciting experiences were characterized by support and dependability, sharing quality time, and explicit expressions of love—and particularly so within close ties such as family, partners, and friends. Results also showed that controlling or possessive behaviors from romantic partners or familial ties were unlikely to elicit love. This investigation contributes to the understanding of the shared beliefs in love in everyday life based on the perspectives of Spanish culture.

articles_hidden.title: Rhythm of Thought: Tracing the Dynamics of Deliberation in Reasoning
articles_hidden.authors: Jérémie Beucler; Wim De Neys
articles_hidden.abstract: When an intuitive answer is uncertain, people are thought to engage in further reasoning. But what people actually do during this additional thinking, how it unfolds over time, and why it sometimes leads to better answers remain unclear. We scored think-aloud protocols with large language models to track, moment by moment, four possible functions of deliberation (generating candidate responses, justifying them, controlling intuitive responses, and regulating cognitive effort), together with expressed confidence. Deliberation showed a clear temporal organization: generation dominated early, whereas justification, control, and regulation became increasingly prominent as reasoning progressed. Correct responses involved more justification, control, and regulation than biased responses, and these evolving dynamics predicted accuracy for out-of-sample participants and items. Confidence and deliberation also showed reciprocal lagged associations: lower confidence predicted further generation, justification, and control, whereas regulation predicted subsequent increases in confidence. Deliberation, then, appears to involve not a single act of "thinking harder," but an evolving interplay of reasoning processes whose organization is linked to whether reasoning succeeds.

articles_hidden.title: A randomised controlled trial of Detour: a multi-component app-based intervention for youth smoking cessation
articles_hidden.authors: Suhaavi Kochhar; Hanneke Scholten; Maartje Luijten
articles_hidden.abstract: Cigarette smoking is a leading cause of preventable death, and adolescents and young adults (AYA) report the highest levels of smoking across age groups. Yet, quitting before 30 years can reduce most health risks attached to smoking. Unfortunately, there is a paucity of effective interventions catering to AYAs specifically. In the present pre-registered randomised controlled trial, we tested the efficacy of Detour, a multi-component app-based intervention, against a digital self-help brochure (N = 613; Mage = 20.9 years). The intervention period was five weeks long with one pre-quit week and four post-quit weeks. Quit day was on the first day of the second intervention week. Participants filled questionnaires at the start and end of the intervention, as well as three and six months later. The primary cessation outcome was 14-day point prevalence of smoking at 6-month follow-up. Secondary cessation outcomes included smoking prevalence at post-test and 3-month follow up, and weekly smoking at all time points. Contrary to our hypotheses, the Detour group did not report higher abstinence rates than the brochure group at any time points. Unexpectedly, the Detour group reported higher weekly smoking levels than the brochure group at all time points. These results could potentially be attributed to the comparison of Detour with an active control group, and technical limitations of the Detour app. Future studies can consider having an additional inactive control group to tease out general intervention effects and designing simpler interventions with a special focus on functionality and technological smoothness.

articles_hidden.title: Newborn infants show neural sensitivity to changes in auditorily presented numerical information
articles_hidden.authors: Kaisa Lohvansuu; Jarmo Hamalainen; Tiina Parviainen; Hanna-Maija Lapinkero; Daniel Ansari; Bert De Smedt; Minna Torppa; Tuire Koponen
articles_hidden.abstract: Human infants are assumed to be born with an innate understanding of quantities—a number sense— that enables them to detect non-symbolic number differences, for example, between sets of objects. This early ability has been found to be a predictor of later math skills. The assumption of innateness is based largely on studies in infants at 6 months of age or older and using visual stimuli with large numerosities, or in studies lacking statistical power. Using EEG, we studied pre-attentive discrimination for auditorily presented non-verbal numerical and non-numerical magnitudes of sleeping newborns (N = 104) to investigate whether the newborn auditory system is discriminating the number of sequentially presented sounds. The results showed that the 2-part repeated standard sound was discriminated from 3-part deviating sound and from 1-part deviating sound. As also the responses to 3-part sound differed from the responses of the same stimulus presented alone as a control, these results suggest that the difference between 2-part repeated sound and 3-part deviant sound is not merely due to physical features of the stimuli but reflects processing of numerosity. These results suggest that newborn infants are able to pre-attentively process at least some differences in the number of stimuli supporting the view of innateness of numerical magnitude discrimination. As the earlier evidence for innateness in newborns is limited, our study utilising small numerosities and auditory modality instead of vision—given the confounds in visual paradigms—offers complementary results on the innate brain processing on numerical information.

articles_hidden.title: Better data, better policy: Distinguishing income poverty and financial stress may promote better temporal decision-making
articles_hidden.authors: Eike Kofi Buabang; Sarah Ashcroft-Jones; Kai Ruggeri
articles_hidden.abstract: The poverty trap is a cycle in which financial hardship is reinforced through short-sighted choices. To design effective policy, it is important to identify who is at risk of falling into it. Yet different measures of poverty may not identify the same people as at risk. This study tested whether subjective financial stress is associated with intertemporal choice over and above income poverty, and whether financial literacy moderates these effects. Across seven countries (N = 1,497; Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Slovenia, Spain, the UK, and the US), financial stress was associated with more present-oriented choices in five of seven countries on a temporal discounting task and in five of seven countries on a windfall allocation task. By contrast, income poverty showed no reliable association, and financial literacy did not consistently moderate either relationship. These findings suggest that identifying who is at risk of the poverty trap requires capturing lived financial reality, not just income brackets, and that financial education may offer little to individuals whose short-sighted choices reflect constraint rather than comprehension. Policy makers are encouraged to review how poverty is defined for targeting purposes, and to prioritise policies that expand financial resources over those that assume the problem is a lack of knowledge or planning.

articles_hidden.title: Evolutionary Theory Makes Predictions About Cognition Beyond Rational Optimization
articles_hidden.authors: Cameron Turner; Thomas L. Griffiths
articles_hidden.abstract: Evolution by natural selection produces the appearance of design in minds, brains, and behavior. While rational models of cognition are usually considered to be consistent with evolution, they are rarely derived from distinctively evolutionary assumptions. Bayesian modeling, reinforcement learning, rational analysis, and resource rational analysis all postulate optimization objectives of coherence in information use or maximization of expected value, potentially under resource constraints. However, cognition is performed by an individual within a lineage where success is determined by the persistence of the lineage across generations. Here, we present a signal detection model that shows how this distinctly evolutionary objective produces predictions that depart from those of rational models. We find that the source of environmental uncertainty determines cognitive design, with weak priors being favored in environments dominated by change. This ensures offspring vary so that some profit against novel challenges, and is favored even at the expense of accurate decision making. Cognitive structure should reflect stable environmental trends, but in fluctuating environments selection strips structure away to release behavioral diversity. We highlight that evolution maximizes the geometric mean number of offspring over generations, an objective that recurs across optimization problems where outcomes accumulate sequentially, including in finance, control engineering, and information theory.

articles_hidden.title: Maladaptive Personality Traits and Statement Validity Assessment. Mapping DSM-5 Trait Domains and Facets onto Lying, Suggestibility, and Autobiographical Memory Quality
