articles_hidden.authors: Elsa Gewehr; Merle Hurtmanns; Johannes Zimmermann
articles_hidden.abstract: Statement validity assessment (SVA) requires experts to weigh a witness’s personality when judging motives for deception, expectable statement quality, and suggestibility. We propose the maladaptive trait model of the Alternative DSM-5 Model for Personality Disorders as a common language for these steps and test its expectations with low-stakes paradigms at the domain and facet level. In a German community sample (N = 258), we administered the Personality Inventory for DSM-5 Short Form, a matrix cheating task, the Lying in Everyday Situations scale, an online Gudjonsson Suggestibility Scale, and self-ratings of memory quality and imagery vividness. We report correlations between all 5 domains and 25 facets with all criteria, with confidence intervals, false-discovery-rate correction, and Bayes factors. Self-reported lying was positively related to Antagonism and Disinhibition, with motive-specific patterns; contrary to preregistration, so was Negative Affectivity. Memory clarity and imagery vividness were related to Detachment, Negative Affectivity, and several of their facets. No trait was related to behavioral dishonesty or suggestibility; Bayes factors mostly favored the null. Facets improved cross-validated prediction where they diverged from their domain. For SVA, the results support using antagonistic and self-protective profiles in motive analysis and lowering expectations of detail and vividness for detached and depressive witnesses.

articles_hidden.title: Why do suicide rates increase in the spring and decrease in the fall? Insights from Canadian suicide rate and death rate data spanning 2010 to 2020
articles_hidden.authors: James Christopher Wiley
articles_hidden.abstract: In 1952, the psychiatrist Erwin Stengel hypothesized that suicide becomes rarer in times when the value of life within a society is lower, when death is more common. In Canada, suicide rates and death rates present with consistent seasonality between years, fluctuating inversely with one another. However, the typical pre-pandemic seasonality seen in death rates was broken during the first year of the COVID-19 pandemic, as a consequence of inordinate deaths occurring at an odd time of year. This offers a unique opportunity to observe whether suicide rates were inversely disrupted. The present study models weekly Canadian suicide rates using death rates, from time series data spanning 2010 to 2019. Results indicate that suicide rates decrease on average by 0.27 standard deviations per 1 standard deviation increase in the death rate. This model is then used to predict 2020 suicide rates, using 2020 death rates. Predictions account for 11.6% of the variation in actual 2020 suicide rates. Furthermore, actual 2020 suicide rates display a negative disruption at the same time as the 2020 death rate positive disruption, and this suicide rate disruption is mimicked by our model predictions. Overall, results are interpreted as being favorable towards Stengel’s theory. As alternative interpretation, we suggest that non-suicide-related deaths preferentially remove potential suicides from the population. Overall analysis suggests that elevated death rates during colder seasons are driven by increases in cardiovascular disease (e.g., heart attacks) and communicable disease transmission relative to warmer seasons, resulting in suppressed suicide rates.

articles_hidden.title: Perceived punitive consequences and adolescent violent crime: The moderating role of socio-legal legitimacy in a Brazilian birth cohort
articles_hidden.authors: Andreas Bauer; Justice Tankebe; Thaís Martins-Silva; Alicia Matijasevich; Aluísio J. D. Barros; Iná Santos; Luciana Tovo Rodrigues; Joseph Murray
articles_hidden.abstract: Research on legitimacy and crime is dominated by cross-sectional evidence from high-income countries. Furthermore, less is known about how legitimacy and deterrence jointly shape adolescent violence in fragile institutional contexts. Using longitudinal data from the 2004 Pelotas Birth Cohort Study in Brazil (n = 1,510), a population-based, prospective longitudinal study, we examine whether perceived punitive consequences and three legitimacy dimensions — regarding the police, the law, and the social system — are associated with violent crime at ages 15 and 18. Higher perceived punitive consequences and more positive perceptions of legitimacy across all domains were associated with lower odds of violent crime at age 15, whereas only police legitimacy and perceived punitive consequences were associated with lower odds of violent crime at age 18. Legitimacy of the law and of the social system moderated the association between perceived punitive consequences and violent crime at age 15, with negative associations strongest among adolescents who viewed institutions as less legitimate. These findings suggest that legitimacy is multidimensional and that both normative and instrumental processes jointly shape adolescent violence in high-violence contexts.

articles_hidden.title: Post-selection Inference in Multiverse Meta-Analysis: The PIMMA Framework
articles_hidden.authors: Matteo Manente; Livio Finos; Gianmarco Altoè; Filippo Gambarota
articles_hidden.abstract: Meta-analyses, like primary studies, are affected by researcher degrees of freedom: researchers must decide which studies to include, how to compute effect sizes, and which statistical models to use. Different reasonable choices can lead to different results, making multiverse meta-analysis a useful tool for assessing robustness across alternative specifications. However, multiverse meta-analysis also introduces a multiple-testing problem. Current inferential approaches mainly provide a global test, which can establish that at least one specification differs from the null but cannot identify which individual specifications do so while accounting for multiplicity across the full multiverse. We introduce Post-selection Inference in Multiverse Meta-Analysis (PIMMA), which allows inference on individual specifications while controlling the Family-Wise Error Rate (FWER) and accounting for their dependence. In practical terms, PIMMA shows which results remain statistically significant after accounting for multiplicity across all reasonable analytical choices. In simulations, the specification-level test adequately controlled Type I error, with power comparable to robust variance estimation in scenarios where both methods maintained appropriate Type I error control. In an application to meta-analyses of Cognitive Behavioral Therapy efficacy for adult depression, 297 of 336 unique meta-analytic analyses remained significant after step-down max-T adjustment for multiple testing, accounting for dependence among analyses. PIMMA therefore extends multiverse meta-analysis from a global assessment of whether any effect is present to specification-level inference, allowing researchers to evaluate robustness across specifications and identify which individual results remain significant under appropriate error control.

articles_hidden.title: Memory experiences under psychedelics – an exploratory prospective online study
articles_hidden.authors: Samuli Kangaslampi; Kim PC Kuypers
articles_hidden.abstract:
Rationale

Case reports and early clinical research suggest classic psychedelics can occasion intense recall and processing of autobiographical memories. Such memory experiences have seen very little study more recently, although they may hold importance for both therapeutic effects and potential iatrogenic harms.

Objectives

This prospective, exploratory study aimed to assess 1) the extent and content of memory experiences in naturalistic psychedelic use, as well as their associations with 2) elements of set and setting, 3) emotional breakthroughs and psychological insights, and 4) longer-term changes in well-being and later subjective evaluations of the experience.

Methods

English-speaking adults (N = 66, Mage = 34.91, 60.1% male) planning to take a classic psychedelic were assessed online before, 1-3 days, and 3-5 weeks after taking the psychedelic with self-report instruments.

Results

On average, participants spent around a quarter of their psychedelic experience recalling past events, although variance was high. Positive and recent memories were most commonly recalled. Four in ten participants recalled usually avoided memories, nearly half potentially traumatic experiences, and a quarter memories of events they had never recalled before. Memory experiences, especially recalling avoided memories, were associated with more emotional breakthroughs and psychological insights and higher evaluations of the experience as useful, but did not predict changes in well-being.

Conclusions

Recalling past events of one’s life may form a major, largely neglected element of many psychedelic experiences and be associated with therapeutic processes. Recalling apparent memories never remembered before under psychedelics may be more common than previously thought and needs careful study and consideration.

articles_hidden.title: The Experimental Study of Habitual Behavior in Humans: A Review of the Validity of Current Protocols
articles_hidden.authors: Pablo Martínez-López; Francisco Garre-Frutos; Miguel A. Vadillo; David Luque
articles_hidden.abstract: Although habits play a key role across psychological science, current laboratory methods may limit our understanding of these behaviors. The dual‑system framework defines habits as context-triggered, outcome‑insensitive responses that emerge gradually with repeated instrumental training. Many human experimental paradigms have been developed to test this characterization of habits. However, most of them fail to provide clear evidence of habit formation, suggesting a gap between habit theory and existing methodologies. We systematically review evidence on the construct validity of fourteen paradigms in which training amount was manipulated. We also reanalyze publicly available datasets from studies using these paradigms to assess the psychometric reliability of their measures. Paradigms that mirror classical approaches derived from habit theory have consistently failed to induce habits, whereas recent approaches have revealed training effects. However, these novel paradigms often rely on broader operationalizations that substantially diverge from traditional definitions. Among the paradigms reviewed, the forced‑response task stands out as capable of inducing habitual behavior while providing a narrowly operationalized measure with reliability estimates ranging from .74 to .83. Finally, we argue that strengthening the credibility of the field will require greater attention to the psychometric properties of habit measures, including precise operationalization, reliability, and systematic validity testing.

articles_hidden.title: How Long Do Refutational Text Effects Last? Evidence From a Six-Month Follow-Up Study of Misconceptions in Psychology
articles_hidden.authors: Elena Varea; Silvia Guerrero; Paula Barrios; Ileana Enesco
articles_hidden.abstract: This work analyzes the effectiveness of refutational texts in correcting misconceptions in psychology and the stability of that change. To this end, it focuses on two variables: the level of engagement with the texts and the specific nature of different myths. The prevalence of misconceptions in the fields of developmental psychology and educational psychology was assessed, and the three most widespread misconceptions, related to adolescence, educational videos, and learning styles, were identified. Using a pre-test/post-test design with a six-month follow-up and an equivalent control group, the study compared reading refutational texts (R) with reading plus producing a summary (RS). A total of 328 psychology students participated and the rejection of the three misconceptions was assessed one week after the intervention and six months later. At Post-test I both intervention groups showed significantly higher probabilities of rejecting all three misconceptions than the control group, with stronger immediate effects observed in the RS condition. At Post-test II, six months later, these effects were attenuated, although rejection remained above baseline levels. The learning styles misconception, which was considered to involve a deeper conceptual framework, showed the greatest resistance to long-term change. Overall, refutational texts promoted conceptual change, but their effects were not fully stable over time and differ between misconceptions, highlighting the need for interventions to be repeated and tailored to each type of myth.

articles_hidden.title: Altered Self-Other Distinction in Motor and Cognitive Domains in Individuals with Borderline Personality Disorder: Evidence from a Multi-Site Behavioral Study
articles_hidden.authors: Ekaterina Pronizius; Celine De Meulemeester; Nita Bislimi; Sarah Kathryn Fineberg; Ingmar Heinig; Martin Horký; Inga Niedtfeld; Magdalena Helísková; Pavla Horká Linhartová; Thea M McAfee
articles_hidden.abstract: Self–other distinction (SOD), defined as the ability to separate self- from other-related mental representations, has been proposed as a core mechanism in borderline personality disorder (BPD), yet experimental evidence remains limited. In this preregistered, multicenter study (Austria, Belgium, Czechia, Germany, USA), we assessed motor SOD (Automatic Imitation Inhibition Task, AIT) and cognitive SOD (Visual Perspective-Taking, VPT) in 290 adults (131 BPD, 159 healthy controls), alongside a Stroop-based inhibitory control task. Overall, individuals with BPD showed slower and less accurate performance across tasks. In the AIT, BPD exhibited reduced motor SOD relative to healthy controls, reflected in increased imitative interference. These effects were robust to covariate adjustment and not explained by demographic or clinical factors. In the BPD sample, symptom severity was neither associated with motor SOD performance nor interindividual differences in self-reported childhood maltreatment. In the VPT task, the BPD group showed greater egocentric bias than controls, with effects varying depending on covariate inclusion (e.g., ADHD symptoms, age, cognitive control). Within the BPD group, childhood maltreatment moderated the association between symptom severity and VPT egocentric bias, such that greater childhood maltreatment and greater symptom severity were associated with increased bias. Overall, findings indicate selective, context-dependent alterations of SOD in BPD, characterized by heightened imitative interference and increased egocentric bias rather than a global deficit. Early adversity appears to shape variability in cognitive SOD in BPD.

articles_hidden.title: Safety, Compatibility and Reconnection: Understanding Restorative Nature Through the Lens of Chronic Low Back Pain
articles_hidden.authors: Alexander Smith; Kayleigh Wyles; Patricia Schofield; Sam William Hughes
articles_hidden.abstract: Chronic low back pain (cLBP) is a pervasive and debilitating condition that is often resistant to conventional pain management strategies. This has driven a growing interest in novel psychosocial approaches, such as the use of restorative nature-based environments as part of pain self-management strategies. However, many assumptions regarding restorative nature spaces are based on the perspective of healthy individuals. A population living with cLBP may conceptualise or identify restorative nature spaces differently, given such factors as risk of reinjury or physical limitations. Two focus groups were conducted with a cLBP group (n = 7, Mage = 55.57, 6 females) to explore what a restorative outdoor nature space means through the lens of chronic low back pain. Thematic Analysis generated four Themes (Safety, Confidence, and Control; Embodied Capability; Reclaiming Self Beyond Pain; and Engagement with Living Nature). The present study highlights the necessity of inclusion of lived experience and perspective when discussing how best to incorporate restorative nature spaces into pain self-management or green social prescribing frameworks for the chronic pain community. Future research can build upon the present research to codesign tailored nature-based interventions for people with a lived experience of chronic pain.

articles_hidden.title: Using Virtual Reality (VR) to Facilitate Context Reinstatement in Eyewitness Interviewing: Effects on Memory Performance and Retrieval Experience
articles_hidden.authors: Britt Heuker of Hoek; Noortje Sanders; Peter W. de Vries; Iris van Sintemaartensdijk; Lynn Weiher; Steven James Watson
articles_hidden.abstract: Using Virtual Reality to recreate environmental cues present during encoding to generate virtual context reinstatement (VCR) may be a promising tool to enhance eyewitness memory. However, VCR’s effectiveness relative to mental (MCR) and physical (PCR) context reinstatement remains unclear, as do mechanisms underlying its potential effects. The present study employed a between-participants experimental design to compare the effectiveness of VCR with PCR and MCR for supporting eyewitness recall while examining the role of cognitive load, stress, rapport, and neurodiversity in retrieval across reinstatement methods. Participants (N = 52) directly observed a mock crime and completed a delayed recall task (2-7 days) under one of three reinstatement conditions (MCR, PCR, VCR). Results provided preliminary evidence that VCR is as effective as traditional methods. Cognitive load was negatively associated with correct recall, suggesting retrieval demands play an important role in eyewitness recall irrespective of reinstatement modality. Qualitative findings further suggested that retrieval success depends on active engagement with reinstatement cues and the management of cognitive demands during recall, including attentional control and retrieval monitoring. Together, these findings provide preliminary support for VCR as a suitable alternative when PCR is not feasible and emphasizes the role of cognitive load in eyewitness memory retrieval.

articles_hidden.title: Intrinsic connectivity signatures of anxiety sensitivity from connectome based predictive modeling
articles_hidden.authors: Dahyun Won; Hakin Kim; Justin Minue Kim; Juyoen Hur
articles_hidden.abstract:
Anxiety sensitivity (AS) is a dispositional trait characterized by the fear of anxiety-related 
sensations based on beliefs that they may have harmful physical, cognitive, or social 
consequences. Despite its clinical significance as a transdiagnostic vulnerability factor, the 
intrinsic neural architecture underlying individual differences in AS remains poorly understood. 
We applied connectome-based predictive modeling (CPM) to resting-state fMRI data from a 
non-clinical sample (N = 86) to identify whole-brain intrinsic connectivity patterns predictive 
of individual differences in AS. In an exploratory follow-up analysis, we applied the trained 
model to an independent dataset to examine whether its predictive utility extended to panic 
symptom severity, a clinically related but distinct construct. The CPM model significantly 
predicted individual differences in AS (prediction 𝑅2  = .07, 𝑝𝑝𝑒𝑟𝑚  < .005) and was 
characterized primarily by reduced insula-temporal, insula-frontal, and temporo-parietal 
connectivity. However, the model did not significantly predict panic symptom severity in the 
independent sample. These findings suggest that individual differences in AS are reflected in 
distributed patterns of intrinsic functional connectivity involving the insula and broader 
cortical systems, providing a network-level characterization of the intrinsic neural architecture 
associated with AS.

articles_hidden.title: From Digital Workbooks to Digital Schoolbooks: Pre-Practice Instructional Support in Authentic Digital Mathematics Learning
articles_hidden.authors: Eileen Richter; Lukas Wesenberg; Felix Krieglstein; Nicklas Jakob Elia Vaupel; Peat Schmolke; Korbinian Moeller; Markus Spitzer
articles_hidden.abstract:
Digital learning platforms provide extensive support for learning mathematics but this support
typically happens during practice. However, less is known about whether instructional support
provided before practice by digital learning platforms is associated with better subsequent
performance in authentic large-scale digital learning settings. Here, we examined different
forms of instructional support embedded in a digital mathematics learning platform used in
schools across Germany. Initially designed primarily as a digital workbook for practicing
mathematical problems, the platform was recently extended toward a digital schoolbook by
adding blackboards that learners can access before practice to obtain additional instructional
support. In particular, Explore blackboards provide opportunities to inspect and connect
mathematical relationships, whereas Secure blackboards organize relevant definitions, rules,
examples, and relationships before practice. Using large-scale log data from 9,293 learners
across 74,801 problems and a within-subject design, we compared learners’ performance on
mathematical problems in a baseline condition (Exercise Only), in which they received no
additional instructional support, with their performance in three other conditions in which they
received instructional support before practice (i.e., Explore, Secure, and Explore & Secure).
We observed significantly lower error rates following all three forms of instructional support
relative to the Exercise Only condition. These findings extend previous work by showing that
instructional support provided by a digital learning platform before practice is associated with
better subsequent performance in an authentic, large-scale learning setting. More broadly, they
highlight the potential value of providing instructional support before practice on digital
mathematics learning platforms.

articles_hidden.title: School and Classroom Heterogeneity and Psychosocial Student Outcomes: Mapping an Emerging Interdisciplinary Research Field
articles_hidden.authors: Claudia Neuendorf; Svenja Hascher; Chenru Hou; Camilla Rjosk
articles_hidden.abstract: Schools and classrooms are developmental contexts that have major impacts on the lives of children and adolescents. Therefore, research in psychology and other disciplines has identified classroom composition as a crucial factor for the psychosocial development of students. Recent developments in multiple disciplines have increased the attention paid to classroom heterogeneity as a contextual factor. This systematic review is the first to integrate findings across a broad range of psychosocial outcomes, multiple heterogeneity dimensions, and diverse research disciplines. In addition to reviewing theoretical approaches from different fields and compiling evidence on the impact of school and classroom heterogeneity on psychosocial outcomes, we examined the current state of integration into a multidisciplinary emerging field and evaluated the maturity of this research field on the basis of all available evidence. We conclude that the field has already begun to integrate and that studies are building on theory and evidence from multiple disciplines of origin, whereas methodological variety between fields is still evident. Regarding the field’s overall maturity, we contend that the field is still immature and stuck in the phase of translating the concept(s) of heterogeneity into valid operationalizations that align with the various theoretical perspectives.

articles_hidden.title: Lived Experiences of Adulthood with Foetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder: A Qualitative  Analysis of Diagnosis, Support, Employment, and Mental Health
articles_hidden.authors: Hannah Quinn; Samuel Bennett
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Foetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder (FASD) encompasses lifelong neurodevelopmental difficulties that can affect cognitive, behavioural, and everyday functioning. Research and support have frequently focused on childhood and developmental outcomes, while comparatively less attention has been given to experiences of FASD during adulthood. Understanding the challenges and support needs of adults with FASD is therefore important for recognising the lifelong implications of the condition and informing appropriate support.
Methods: This qualitative study explored experiences of living with FASD during adulthood, with particular attention to diagnosis, support, employment, and mental health. Secondary qualitative data were collected from publicly available online sources, including social media posts and material published by FASD support organisations. Written and transcribed material relating to personal experiences of FASD was analysed using thematic analysis to identify recurring patterns and themes within participants' accounts.
Results: The analysis identified themes relating to FASD diagnosis that were consistent with issues reported in previous research. The findings also highlighted the perceived importance of appropriate and ongoing support in adulthood. Participants' accounts indicated that support could have implications across multiple areas of life, including employment and mental health. The findings further highlighted the value of incorporating the perspectives and experiences of people living with FASD when considering education, support, and approaches to FASD prevention.
Conclusions: The findings highlight the importance of recognising FASD as a lifelong condition and extending attention beyond childhood development to the experiences and support needs of adults. Greater consideration of the lived experiences of people with FASD may help inform approaches to adult support, education, and prevention. Further research involving adults with FASD is warranted to better understand their long-term experiences and identify effective forms of support across different areas of adult life.

articles_hidden.title: ‘The Weight of Early Stress and Trauma: An Analysis of How Adverse Childhood Experiences, PTSD, and CPTSD Influence Adult Obesity Rates’
articles_hidden.authors: Lynn Holleran; Samuel Bennett
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) have been associated with adverse health outcomes in adulthood, including obesity. Psychological responses to childhood adversity, including post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and complex post-traumatic stress disorder (CPTSD), may also be relevant to this relationship. However, the associations between childhood adversity, PTSD/CPTSD, and adult obesity remain incompletely understood. This study examined the relationships between ACEs, PTSD, CPTSD, and body mass index (BMI) in adults.
Methods: A cross-sectional correlational study was conducted using an anonymous online survey. Participants were recruited through social media and referrals. Ninety-five adults aged 18–73 years (M = 39.98, SD = 14.43; 69% female) completed measures of ACEs using the Adverse Childhood Experiences Questionnaire (ACEQ), PTSD and CPTSD using the International Trauma Questionnaire (ITQ), and demographic and self-reported height and weight measures from which BMI was derived. Correlational, regression, and between-group analyses were conducted to examine associations between ACE scores, PTSD/CPTSD severity, and BMI.
Results: ACE scores significantly predicted BMI (β = .69, p = .03), accounting for 4.9% of the variance. Participants with obesity reported significantly higher ACE scores than participants classified as healthy weight (p = .037). Positive but non-significant associations were observed between BMI and PTSD severity (r = .14) and CPTSD severity (r = .18). Participants meeting criteria for CPTSD reported significantly higher ACE scores than those who did not meet CPTSD criteria (p = .008). Female participants also reported significantly higher ACE scores than male participants (p = .027).

Conclusions: The findings provide evidence of an association between greater exposure to childhood adversity and adult BMI, consistent with previous research linking ACEs with obesity. Higher ACE exposure was also associated with meeting criteria for CPTSD, while associations between PTSD/CPTSD severity and BMI were comparatively weak and did not reach statistical significance. Given the cross-sectional design, self-reported measures, and relatively small sample, the findings should not be interpreted as evidence of causal relationships. Larger longitudinal studies are needed to clarify the mechanisms linking childhood adversity, trauma-related psychopathology, and obesity and to investigate implications for integrated approaches to trauma and obesity prevention and intervention.

articles.title: Systematic Evaluation of Nation-State Propaganda in LLM Outputs
articles.authors: Kevin T. Greene; Jacob N Shapiro
articles.abstract: The rapid growth and usability of AI is creating new risks to information quality, including the possibility that chatbot responses spread propaganda from state-backed influence campaigns. There is little systematic evidence regarding how frequently LLMs spread such narratives when responding to user queries. Previous attempts to assess these risks rely on small numbers of evaluation questions, use opaque query construction procedures, and fail to account for key sources of uncertainty in model responses. We address these gaps with an automated, reproducible pipeline that samples documented state-backed propaganda and news items, programmatically generates evaluation questions, and audits LLM-generated responses. We evaluate whether five prominent models: (1) reproduce arguments aligned with documented Kremlin propaganda narratives; (2) present the Kremlin perspective on events without providing corrective context; and (3) cite known propaganda outlets. We find substantially lower rates of propaganda-aligned responses and propaganda-source citation than prior small-sample work would suggest. These risks are particularly rare for questions resembling ordinary information searches about Ukraine. Our approach enables systematic comparisons across models and issue areas, supports ongoing monitoring, and could be extended to many other hotly-debated topics.

articles.title: Delisting and dispersal: author communities before and after removal from Scopus
articles.authors: Marek Deja
articles.abstract:
Purpose: Delisting removes a journal from an index but not its authors. This study asks whether cohorts disperse or share destinations and whether concentrated inflow is associated with receiving journals' subsequent delisting.

Design/methodology/approach: The analysis reconstructs interval-valued delisting dates from successive Scopus lists, assigns delisted event clocks to matched cohorts, and compares destination overlap with margin-preserving, opportunity-structured, and matched-observed benchmarks. A six-month-landmark discrete-time hazard model handles right censoring and competing exits.

Findings: Delisted-journal output averaged 66.7% below the post-event reference path. For 121 cohorts, median observed-to-expected overlap was 2.40 under the opportunity-structured benchmark. Across 55 matched sets, delisted cohorts overlapped 10.6 percentage points less than references (95% CI [-0.14, -0.07]), a gap that predated delisting and was smaller but present on venues new to the author. An exploratory hazard analysis showed a positive in-sample association between concentrated inflow and receiving journals' subsequent delisting, but extensive censoring and short follow-up preclude a stable magnitude claim.

Research limitations: Delisting is non-random; estimates are descriptive contrasts, benchmark deviations, and conditional in-sample associations.

Practical implications: Synthetic benchmarks establish residual cohort structure; matched observed cohorts test whether it is event-specific.

Originality/value: The study provides a two-stage design for event-specific concentration claims. Pairing a constrained randomisation with matched observed cohorts reversed the substantive conclusion.

articles.title: What the World Studies, Invents and Reports About Urban Heat
articles.authors: Narendra Kumar
articles.abstract: We assemble 20,422 scholarly papers on urban heat islands (1990–2025), read the 17,101 that carry an abstract sentence by sentence, and join them to 96,726 news articles (2021–2025), 4,123 patent families, 14,576 recorded heat incidents, registers of companies, funding rounds and government funding events, and the annual accounts of Indian companies. Eight results stand out. (1) The field grew about 9 times faster than the scholarly literature as a whole, and in 2015–2019 titles naming "extreme heat" overtook those naming "heat island". (2) Of 2,409 papers that attribute urban heat to a cause, 48% name urbanisation and land-use change; attribution to anthropogenic heat fell from 18.4% to 7.7%. (3) Research and news describe different problems: at equal text length, 28% of research openings raise mitigation against 1.6% of news leads, while 22% of news leads are forecasts or warnings against 1.4% of research. (4) They also describe different places: China accounts for 31% of the research and 2.3% of English-language coverage, and Delhi receives 7.4 times the coverage its research share would predict. (5) Invention has outrun science: patent families for cool and permeable pavements grew 12-fold in a decade against 2.4-fold for the research on them. (6) Across 194 studies the median reported cooling from urban trees is 2.0 °C (air temperature 2.0 °C, surface temperature 2.9 °C). (7) Between 2021–22 and 2024–25 news coverage moved from the hazard to the people exposed: workers, schools, the elderly and hospital patients each rose 1.4- to 2.4-fold as a share of heat articles while wildfire and drought fell by about half and climate change — raised in about one article in ten — fell by a quarter. (8) The market record is thin: 140 of 5.05 million companies state a heat or cooling purpose, and recorded capital is $2.7 billion of cooling-infrastructure finance against $48 million of venture funding; larger Indian cooling companies grew revenue 25% a year over three years against 16% for Indian companies generally. Every cause category extracted from the research was tested against an independent second reader; three failed, and no result reported here rests on them.

articles.title: Agreeing in Principle, Disagreeing on Policy: How Beliefs About the Gender Pay Gap Shape Fairness Concerns and Policy Preferences
articles.authors: Fabian Kalleitner; Jule Adriaans; Ole Brüggemann; Cristóbal Moya; Sandra Bohmann
articles.abstract: Willingness to reduce gender inequalities partly depends on whether people are aware of them and consider them unfair. Extending scholarship centered on inequality misperceptions, we focus on beliefs about the sources of the gender pay gap (GPG), experimentally varying people's ability to attribute pay disparities to women's choices. Preregistered survey experiments in the U.S. and Germany show that information about larger (vs. smaller) and within-job (vs. overall) GPGs independently increases awareness, raises perceived unfairness, and translates into general support for government action. Initially less-supportive groups (conservatives, men) showed some of the largest increases in general support. Yet, updated beliefs did not increase support for specific policies, such as pay transparency laws or gender quotas. These findings suggest that information campaigns can affect beliefs about GPG's size and sources, but even perceiving GPGs as unfair does not bridge the gap between abstract commitment to gender equality and concrete policy support.

articles.title: When Digital Exposure Meets Everyday Buying: Understanding Consumer Behaviour in FMCG
articles.authors: Rithik Bhattacharjee
articles.abstract: Consumers today may discover a product on social media, encounter it repeatedly through digital advertising, and still make the final purchase from a neighbourhood store. This study explores the relationship between digital exposure and everyday consumer behaviour in the fast-moving consumer goods (FMCG) sector. Using a consumer survey dataset containing 26 usable responses, the study examines purchase frequency, purchase channels, exposure to social-media promotions, reported influence of online advertising, customer satisfaction, and recommendation intention. The findings show that social-media exposure is relatively common, while reported influence of online advertising is more mixed. Traditional retail remains important, with kirana stores and supermarkets accounting for most reported purchase channels. Mean satisfaction was 3.92 out of 5 among respondents with valid satisfaction scores, while recommendation intention was predominantly positive. Exploratory statistical analysis did not identify a statistically significant association between online-ad influence and recommendation intention (χ² = 0.26, p = 0.61), nor a statistically significant relationship between satisfaction and recommendation intention (Spearman ρ ≈ 0.21, p ≈ 0.31). The findings suggest that digital visibility should not automatically be interpreted as behavioural influence. Consumer decisions appear to involve a broader combination of digital communication, product experience, purchasing convenience, availability, and customer service. Given the small and youth-concentrated sample, the study is exploratory and does not claim population-level generalizability. The paper highlights the need for larger and more diverse studies examining how digital engagement interacts with the wider FMCG consumer journey.

articles.title: Human Circuits in Cold War Taiwan: RCA, Labour Governance, and the Developmental State
articles.authors: Ethan Chiu
articles.abstract: Industrial development depends on institutions that organise technological learning and govern production. In Cold War Taiwan, these institutions also shaped who could challenge industrial harm. Drawing on field research, interviews, legal records, and institutional histories, this article argues that Taiwan’s developmental capacity was selective. A paired history of RCA Taiwan and the separate RCA-ITRI technology transfer project shows how investment promotion and labour governance privileged officially selected industrial objectives over workers’ independent authority. Public sponsorship equipped semiconductor learning with personnel, facilities, and foreign knowledge. Labour administration, managed representation, and corporate control of hazard information restricted workers’ demands for protection. Pay, housing, and production routines made exposure difficult to avoid, while repeated inspections failed to secure compliance. Missing records, withheld information, and corporate restructuring then obstructed compensation claims. Workers and their supporters challenged these barriers by assembling legal, scientific, and archival resources. Their struggle places labour protection within the history of developmental capacity, alongside the acquisition of technology.

articles.title: The City Multiple: Comparing Geographies of Digital Visibility across Google Maps, Instagram, Facebook, and TikTok
articles.authors: Reza Ardekani Shaker; Justus Uitermark
articles.abstract: Digital platforms have become key geospatial infrastructures through which cities are discovered, experienced, and evaluated. Whereas the extant literature has often focused on single platforms or assumed an undifferentiated platform urbanism, we know very little about how different platforms produce distinct geographies of urban visibility. To address this lacuna, we examine the spatially differentiated regimes of visibility that emerge when platforms mediate urban environments. In doing so, we distinguish between three dimensions of platforms’ geographies of digital visibility: (1) spatial inequality—how each platform distributes visibility across places; (2) spatial articulation—how platform visibilities map onto local urban geographies; and (3) spatial representation—the kinds of places and content that achieve visibility on each platform. Combining computational, geographic, and interpretive methods, we analyse how 6,682 eating and drinking establishments in Amsterdam are represented on TikTok, Instagram, Google Maps, and Facebook, and find strikingly weak correlations between their visibility on the four platforms. We find that each platform produces distinct structures of unequal visibility, with algorithmic-discovery platforms concentrating visibility more intensely than review-based systems. Neighbourhood-level analyses further show that platform-specific spatial articulations correspond to the gentrification and touristification of specific areas. Our findings contribute to the literatures on digital geography and platform urbanism by demonstrating that digital platforms generate multiple instantiations of the same city.

articles.title: Why Politicians Retweet: News Trustworthiness, Emotion, and Partisan Asymmetry in Elite News Sharing among US Congress Members
articles.authors: Apeksha Shetty; Esther Simmendinger; Jula Lühring; Annie Waldherr; David Garcia; Hannah Metzler
articles.abstract: On social media, politicians' retweets can determine which claims gain visibility in online and in wider political debate, yet the factors associated with these retweeting decisions remain poorly understood. Combining natural language processing measures of emotional tone and partisan cues with politician-level characteristics, we analyze the retweeting behavior of United States Members of Congress between 2021 and 2023 using multilevel logistic regression models. Using all news-related retweets during this period, paired with a negative sample of non-retweets, we examine how tweet content and legislators' ideological extremity predict the amplification of tweets linking to more and less trustworthy news domains. We find that partisan identity is a stronger predictor of retweeting than other factors. While politicians generally preferred retweeting content with links to trustworthy sources, this preference weakened when tweets contained party-related references. Anger and fear predicted higher retweeting likelihood when tweets referenced political opponents, while anger predicted lower retweeting likelihood when tweets referenced political allies. Furthermore, ideology conditioned how politicians responded to news trustworthiness: among Republicans, increasing ideological extremity was associated with weaker preference for trustworthy sources, with the most ideologically-extreme Republicans being especially likely to retweet tweets with links to less trustworthy domains. Together, these results suggest that politicians use retweets to reinforce partisan boundaries between 'us' and 'them'. This identity-centered pattern to retweeting explains how information from less trustworthy sources gains traction in polarized digital environments.

articles.title: When the Children’s Rights Normative Culture (CRNC) is Full of Holes: The Child’s Right to Mental Health in Post-Conflict Sool and Sanaag
articles.authors: Guleid Ahmed Jama; Marieke Janne Hopman
articles.abstract: This paper aims to understand the situation of children’s mental health rights in Sool and Sanaag. We apply the Children’s Rights Normative Culture (CRNC) model (Hopman et al. 2026) to a dataset of 85 research conversation conducted between May and November 2025 (40 children, 45 adults) in the two cities. A key finding from the research is that children’s mental health is not recognised as a distinct rights issue within the socio-legal orders applicable in the research area. Moreover, there is no clearly articulated or enforceable socio-legal obligation (from any socio-legal order) concerning the protection of children’s mental health. Nor do the socio-legal norms seem to establish specific remedial measures for children experiencing mental health difficulties. The language of rights is largely absent from people’s understanding of children’s mental health. Across clan, community, religious, and state normative orders, children are mainly seen through the family framework. The paper suggest that 1) children’s mental health should be seen as a children’s rights, 2) families, particularly mothers, and the community, should be engaged as key entry point for societal change, 3) space should be created for children where they can safely share their experiences and views at all levels, including the family, schools, community and post-conflict peacebuilding initiatives.

articles.title: Cultural Cognitive Scaffolding
articles.authors: Helena Miton
articles.abstract: In many domains, human life has undergone dramatic changes—globalized exchanges, complex technological systems, large societies—that would both require and result from rapid cognitive change. In this work, I introduce the Cultural Cognitive Scaffolding Hypothesis, which posits that (1) human cognition is uniquely culturally evolvable because our cognitive processes rely on environmental resources that are largely culturally evolvable, and, as a consequence, (2) it is these specific cultural innovations, called cultural cognitive scaffolds (CCS), that are responsible for much of the rapid, recent changes in human cognition. Importantly, to achieve this effect, these cultural innovations must balance cognitive impact and cultural success. The historical expansion of exchange networks offers an ideal case to illustrate how diverse cultural innovations helped manage the high uncertainty associated with exchanges across larger physical and cultural distances, and a window into how cultural success can be achieved for different cultural innovations. Finally, this framework has important implications for our understanding of the uniquely open-ended character of human culture.

articles.title: Examination of the News-Finds-Me Perception as an Expanded Bifactor Construct
articles.authors: Toby Hopp
articles.abstract:
Within the mass and political communication literatures, the news-find-me (NFM)
perception has been increasingly used to explain the democratically deleterious implications of a
reliance on incidental, socially mediated news contact. Despite these efforts, there does not
currently exist a consistent means of measuring the NFM construct. This study developed an
expanded NFM measure and evaluated it using a latent bifactor model specification. The results
suggested that a bifactor-(S·I 1) specification fit the data in a plausible manner, and, therein, that
there exist research scenarios where the use of such an approach may confer benefits to
researchers.

articles.title: Scrolling the Nation: Banal Digital Nationalism on Short-Form Video Feeds
articles.authors: Mihai Alexandru Bîclea
articles.abstract: This study inquired into the reproduction of banal digital nationalism on the algorithmically curated short-form video feeds. Rather than emphasizing overt nationalist content, I explored how situated, everyday user–platform interactions reproduce banal forms of nationalist ideology. Through digital diaries and post-hoc semi-structured interviews with Romanian users the analysis was attentive at the entanglement of social, affective and technological structures which habitually reinforce the physical and symbolic borders inherent in nationhood. Algorithmic “re-personalization” and “spacetimemattering” through memes, ads and nostalgic content were identified as forms of routine national (re-)production and normalization on the feed, users becoming oriented towards the nation and their being part of it beyond specific ideational contents. By focusing on an underexplored Eastern European context, the study contributes to research on digital nationalism while demonstrating the utility of new materialist sensibilities for investigating banal digital nationalism.

articles.title: Migration–Citizenship Trajectories and Institutional Incorporation: Long-Term Mental Health Consequences
articles.authors: Nan Zhang
articles.abstract: Migration does not necessarily produce equivalent changes in institutional membership. This study examines how geographical mobility and institutional citizenship unfold jointly across adulthood and whether differentiated pathways of institutional incorporation are associated with long-term mental health. We analysed longitudinal data from 8,297 adults aged 60–80 in the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS, 2011–2020). Sequence analysis reconstructed joint trajectories of rural–urban residence and institutional citizenship (hukou) between ages 15 and 60, which were linked to depressive symptoms (CES-D-10) using multilevel growth-curve models. Substantial inequalities emerged across migration–citizenship trajectories and persisted throughout later life. Rural–urban migrant workers retaining rural hukou, historically associated with more restricted access to urban social rights and protection, had depressive-symptom levels comparable to lifelong rural residents, whereas trajectories involving urban hukou were associated with more favourable outcomes. Longer migration duration was associated with modestly lower depressive symptoms among women, while the estimated association was essentially flat among men. The findings demonstrate that geographical mobility does not necessarily entail institutional incorporation and that the long-term consequences of migration depend on how geographical and institutional mobility are configured across adulthood.

articles.title: Data visualization: Spanish results in PISA across  waves by parental educational attainment
articles.authors: Manuel T. Valdés; Fabrizio Bernardi
articles.abstract: Using Spanish PISA microdata from 2003–2025, we analyze performance trends in mathematics and reading by parental educational attainment. Results show a steady decline in scores among students from highly educated families, starting as early as 2012 in mathematics and 2015 in reading.

articles.title: The Influencer I’ll Vote For: Mapping Politicians and Parties on TikTok
articles.authors: Marcos Echevarria-Eirea
articles.abstract: TikTok, and social media generally, continue to rise as important spheres of political communication and information. Mapping how political elites use these platforms thus remains consequential to our understanding of the political arena. However, due to its relative infancy, we have yet to thoroughly study these patterns on TikTok across countries. In response to this shortcoming, this paper introduces Mapping Politicians and Parties on TikTok (MPPTikTok), a dataset of TikTok accounts for national MPs and parties across 17 Western democracies, comprising over 2,190 usernames. Using these to collect ≈260,000 posts, I then describe the supply of content (presence and posting activity) and the engagement it receives across party families. Both radical party families are proportionally more present, post more, and receive more engagement than the Mainstream. The Radical Left leads most clearly in proportional presence and posting activity, while achieving engagement levels comparable to the Radical Right, with differences between them depending on the metric.

articles.title: Calibrating Synthetic Respondents: A Within-Persona Experiment on Public Reactions to Protest in Turkey
articles.authors: MEHMET FUAT KINA; Helin Yaren Ekmen
articles.abstract: Large language models are increasingly used to simulate survey respondents, yet the inference pipeline that turns a persona into a response is rarely calibrated for the population and outcome it is applied to. This study makes population- and outcome-specific calibration the research task itself. Using a nationally representative survey in Turkey as the benchmark, we construct persona-conditioned synthetic respondents for all 2,615 survey participants and search a structured space of persona content, sampling strategies, temperatures, model backbones, and prompt framings. Calibration is assessed against two held-out outcomes that carry the response structures on which social movement research typically rests, a rare binary measure of protest participation and a five-point attitude item, and the selected protocols differ between the two. We then run a within-persona synthetic experiment that places the same protest for Kurdish-language education in a political opportunity and a political threat context. The threat context lowers simulated movement legitimacy and willingness to attend, and the simulated contrasts differentiate by political orientation, ethnicity, and education in the directions theory anticipates. Calibration is a precondition for reading synthetic experiments, not a robustness check appended to them.

articles.title: Issues and Challenges of Poverty and International Labor Migration in Nepal
articles.authors: Shyam Kumar Karki
articles.abstract: This paper aims to discuss the opportunity and challenges of the foreign labor market for Nepalese workers and Nepal’s government policy. The study was carried out in the form of a qualitative research method, where secondary data were used. The collected data were analyzed using the content analysis method after a close reading of the sources. This paper discussed the current situation of government policy, manpower agencies, problems of migrant workers, and the way of using the remittance. This research found that the government policy is less effective, and manpower agencies are not following the government rules and regulations. Since the last two decades, remittances have been a significant contributor to the Nepalese economy. Many scholars argued that remittance helps to reduce the country’s poverty rates. However, Nepalese workers face numerous problems in the home country and destination countries. Migrant workers are being charged high service charges and misguided by the local agent and manpower agencies in the home country Nepal. They face problems in destination countries such as low remuneration, sexual abuse, and risky job environment. Most of the remittances are using daily expenses such as purchasing foods. This paper explores these vulnerabilities of migrant workers and suggests stakeholder interventions to make safer migration and sustainably use a remittance.

articles.title: Does exposure to information on ethnic minorities’ greater welfare dependency affect attitudes to welfare and welfare recipients? A pre-registered, population-based survey experiment
articles.authors: Thijs Lindner; Willem de Koster; Jeroen van der Waal
articles.abstract: The relationship between ethnic diversity and welfare attitudes has been the subject of much research. However, little is known about how exposure to information on the overrepresentation of ethnic minority individuals among welfare recipients affects attitudes to welfare recipients in general. We scrutinize a potential information exposure effect, and assess two contrasting scenarios, i.e., exposure to aforementioned information might strengthen either negative stereotypes of welfare recipients or the notion that welfare dependency is the result of structural conditions. Additionally, we hypothesize that the former (latter) response is more likely among those with more (less) ethnocentric attitudes. We tested this by conducting an original pre-registered survey experiment among members of a high-quality probability-based panel designed to represent the Dutch population (n = 1,527). The treatment group was exposed to information depicting the overrepresentation of Dutch citizens with a Moroccan migration background among welfare recipients in the Netherlands, while the control group was not. It was only among the more ethnocentric respondents that exposure to the treatment increased support for the notions that welfare recipients: 1) are lacking work ethic; and 2) are themselves to blame for their condition. There was 3) no treatment effect on support for welfare schemes in general. We discuss the implications of these findings for a variety of academic debates and make suggestions for further research.

articles.title: The Politics of Threat Construction: Securitisation as a Site of Contestation in Georgia’s Public Sphere
articles.authors: Mariam Bibilashvili; Zinaida Bechná; Kornely Kakachia
articles.abstract: Moving beyond studies on contemporary security challenges posed by information manipulation, economic coercion, and military pressure, this article problematises the securitisation of foreign interference narratives by political leaders through the case of Georgia (2023–2025). The analysis draws on 325 social media posts by high-level officials and ten in-depth interviews with civic actors resisting state narratives. It relies on securitisation theory to (1) examine how political elites frame domestic actors as instruments of the Western interference despite the country’s constitutionally anchored pro-European orientation and overwhelming public support for EU integration, and (2) explore how counter-securitisation unfolds among civic actors. The findings reveal a structured securitising narrative grounded in sovereigntist logic, invoking historical memory, identity threats, and conspiracy framings to delegitimise civic actors as rootless and foreign aligned. However, rather than generating stable audience acceptance this securitising move triggers counter-securitisation as civic actors contest the proposed threat hierarchy, reframe Russia and democratic backsliding as primary dangers, and additionally mobilise performative resistance through street protest. The analysis highlights the agency of civic actors who simultaneously occupy the positions of securitised subjects and a segment of the audience and complements post-structuralist understandings of the securitisation as a co-constitutive and iterative rather than a linear process.

articles.title: Regressive Restoration: A Process Model of Belief Rigidity Under Epistemic Destabilization
articles.authors: Mitchell Sanders
articles.abstract: Beliefs do more than represent the world; they can also regulate uncertainty, affect, identity, and significance. This article introduces regressive restoration as a temporal regulatory process in which epistemic destabilization increases reliance on coherence-restoring beliefs, the immediate stabilizing effects of those beliefs reinforce commitment, and that commitment subsequently reduces epistemic flexibility. Epistemic destabilization refers to conditions in which cues for determining what is credible, coherent, or socially shared become fragmented, overloaded, unreliable, or contested. The model proposes that available integrative resources– the momentary attentional, affective, and uncertainty-tolerance resources needed to remain engaged with conflicting information– moderate whether destabilization promotes adaptive accommodation or regressive restoration. The model distinguishes short-term stabilization from maladaptive rigidity. Coherence restoration is context-sensitive and may be functional, whereas rigidity is indicated when closure-oriented responses resist correction or persist across contexts in which reflective integration is possible. Regressive restoration is defined as a process rather than a trait or latent factor, and identity consolidation is treated as an important but nonessential amplifier. Five propositions specify the model’s distinctive predictions concerning regulatory function, temporal ordering, motivational amplification, correction resistance, and cross-context generalization. A focused empirical agenda is proposed to test whether immediate coherence, affective relief, or significance restoration predicts later belief rigidity beyond established informational and motivational mechanisms.

articles.title: Distributed Citizenship in Local-Oriented Online Communities: A Behavioral Repertoire of Civic Roles Across 50 North American City Groups
articles.authors: Yibin Fan
articles.abstract: Local-oriented online communities increasingly serve as informal spaces where residents exchange local knowledge, discuss public issues, and encounter local news. Yet existing research often treats these communities as digital third spaces, with less attention to how civic labor is distributed among participants. This study understands these communities as components of local information infrastructures, examining how civic roles are distributed by analyzing year-long data from 50 highly active North American city subreddits in 2024. Focusing on 43,263 sustained users, we combine media-domain matching, LLM-assisted topic classification, latent profile analysis, and qualitative case comparison. The analysis identifies six behavioral civic roles: National News Commentators, Platform-Native Political Discussants, Local Civic Respondents, Cross-Scale Media Brokers, Local News Brokers, and Peripheral Generalists. The findings show that local-oriented online communities function as local information infrastructures which depend on uneven but complementary forms of resident participation.

articles.title: Who Sees Politics in Sports? Norm Endorsement and Partisan Judgments from the 2026 World Cup
articles.authors: Morgan Wack; Daniel Vogler; Manuel Arrigo; Christian Pipal; Lucas Paulo da Silva
articles.abstract: Most Americans say politics should stay out of sports. Yet whether this norm is truly binding depends on whether people apply it when their own side violates the norm. To test this "apolitical sports" norm, we fielded a two-wave matched panel survey around the 2026 FIFA World Cup (N1=988; N2=699). During the tournament, U.S. President Donald Trump called FIFA to have an American player's red-card suspension lifted. We asked respondents to judge the incident directly and to judge a message on players' shirts, varied to support or protest a contentious U.S. policy. Overall, endorsing the norm predicted lower tolerance for political expression in sports, within each party separately, with a smaller own-side advantage. Following this widely reported violation, Democrats raised their endorsement while Republicans did not. What divided partisans most was what they counted as a violation, with Republicans reporting less political interference. In short, while both sides agreed with the norm, they disagreed about whether it had been broken. Our findings suggest that partisan accommodation can influence how citizens recall and conceive of potentially norm-violating events.

articles.title: Different spaces, different citizens? Explaining online and offline volunteering and citizenship behavior through the Civic Voluntarism Model
articles.authors: Arjen de Wit; Marlou Ramaekers; Stephanie Maas; Rene Bekkers
articles.abstract: Online ways of communication have radically changed the face of volunteerism, often described as ‘virtual volunteering’, ‘online volunteering’ or ‘digital volunteering’. In this paper we examine if those individuals engaged in online spaces, both in formal organizations and in self-organized communities, are different from those engaged in offline (in-person) volunteering. To understand how the four distinct types of voluntary participation (offline volunteers, online volunteers, offline self-organized citizens, online self-organized citizens) attract the same or different individuals, we anchor our analysis in the Civic Voluntarism Model (CVM). Using panel survey data from the Netherlands, we find that offline and online volunteers show higher engagement and especially networks, and this also holds for people who participate as citizens in their neighborhood. ‘Being asked’ to volunteer is the strongest correlate of volunteering, both offline and online, as well as offline citizenship. Recruitment networks are less important for online participation. Strikingly, online self-organized platforms are able to reach new groups of citizens that are not stratified by similar prerequisites for participation. These findings provide valuable insights for volunteer managers, activists, and policy makers who use online channels to recruit and retain volunteers.

articles.title: What Affective Polarization Is Made Of: Components, Targets, Cleavages and Emotions in Five Multiparty Democracies
articles.authors: Mabelle Kretchner; Bendegúz Plesz; Eran Halperin; Julia Elad-Strenger; Sivan hirsch hoefler; Adva Gruenwald; Zsolt Boda
articles.abstract: The more affective polarization (AP) is studied, the clearer it becomes that a single score conceals what it is made of. The score has two sides, ingroup attachment and outgroup hostility, and the two need not be balanced. AP runs toward different targets, it runs along a different divide in each system, and the affect itself is made of distinct emotions. Comparative work has taken up each of these layers, but in the studies we are aware of, never all together, so what any given score is made of is still not known: two democracies with similar AP levels may be facing quite different things. Drawing on preregistered survey data from five multiparty democracies (Germany, Hungary, Italy, Poland, Israel; N = 5,151), we map all four layers in one design: AP and its two sides toward parties, voters, and ideological blocs; where attachment and hostility sit across the parties of each system; and the associations of six discrete emotions with AP. In all countries, AP drew more on ingroup attachment than on outgroup hostility, and disappointment and anger rather than hatred were associated with AP toward parties and voters. What differed was where the affect settled: which parties concentrated it, and whether the ideological bloc carried it at all. Hatred appeared only at the bloc level and only in some systems, at the target whose scores were otherwise among the lowest. We discuss the importance of unfolding these layers together in comparative research, for a better understanding of AP and for addressing it.

articles.title: Evaluating the discrepancies in funding metadata across bibliographic and administrative databases: the case of South Korea’s public research funding
articles.authors: Soohong Eum
articles.abstract: Funding metadata underpins the identification of the relationship between research funding and outputs, yet its coverage and accuracy vary across databases. I examine discrepancies in funding metadata for South Korean government-funded research by comparing records from South Korea’s National Science & Technology Information Service (NTIS) with Web of Science and OpenAlex. Linking NTIS-reported publications across these three sources reveals substantial divergence: few project identifiers and publication-project pairs were captured across all three databases. These discrepancies stem from multiple compounding factors, including incomplete database indexing, optional or inconsistent funder acknowledgement policies, and variations in how project identifiers are described and extracted. Accounting for identifier variations and multi-phase project structures recovers additional matches but does not substantially close the overall gap. A logistic regression model further demonstrates that whether funding sources are acknowledged is linked to structural factors, such as stakeholder complexity regarding the co-authors and institutions involved in a publication. This indicates that acknowledgement omissions are driven not merely by technical limitations in metadata collection, but also by institutional constraints surrounding research funding. Furthermore, acknowledgement lag patterns, where the time gap between project execution and publication active years is virtually zero, point to systemic weaknesses in administrative reporting workflows. The paper concludes by recommending policy actions for funding agencies to ensure the interoperability and reliability of NTIS records. These findings underscore the need to evaluate funding metadata discrepancies not merely as a technical indexing challenge, but as an issue deeply embedded within the institutional structures of research systems.

articles.title: Between Finality and Accuracy: Vote Recount Institutions in European Democracies
articles.authors: Ivan Jarabinský; Patrik Mikóczi
articles.abstract: Vote recounts sit at the intersection of vote counting, dispute resolution, and post-electoral procedure, yet comparative knowledge of how democracies actually conduct them remains scarce. Drawing on a structured, focused comparison across ten European democracies that operate single-instance electoral judiciaries, we examine the institutional settings within which recounts take place. We frame the observed variation through what we term the finality-accuracy dilemma, the tension between treating certified results as settled and ensuring that declared results faithfully reflect voter preferences. Five dimensions structure our analysis, namely standing, threshold conditions, decision-making body, scope, and procedural deadlines. We identify five recurring configurations and find that decision-making body type aligns systematically with position on the finality-accuracy spectrum, with judicial bodies clustering on the finality side and parliamentary bodies adopting accuracy-leaning flexibility. No sampled system employs automatic margin-based triggers, and ordered recounts were partial rather than comprehensive in scope.

articles.title: Can volunteering substitute for paid work? Unemployment, volunteering, and life satisfaction across the life course
articles.authors: Arjen de Wit; Heng Qu; Rene Bekkers; Bianca Suanet
articles.abstract: Unemployment is consistently associated with decreased well-being, but other productive roles may partly compensate for the social and psychological resources lost through job loss. Using a mega-analysis on six longitudinal panel studies covering over 500,000 observations across 20 European countries, we examine how age and volunteer status moderate associations between unemployment and life satisfaction. First-difference models show that transitions into unemployment are associated with declines in life satisfaction, with stronger negative effects observed among younger and middle-aged adults than among older adults. Contrary to expectations, volunteering does not consistently buffer the negative association between unemployment and life satisfaction, although supplementary analyses indicate that the compensatory role of volunteering may vary across age groups and national contexts. These findings indicate that volunteering is not a universal substitute for paid work and that the capacity of alternative productive roles to maintain well-being following job loss depends on broader social and institutional conditions.

articles.title: Resilience in a Hybrid Security Culture: Georgia between Institutional Continuity and Political Realignment
articles.authors: Mariam Bibilashvili
articles.abstract: Challenging the common understanding in the relevant literature, this study reconceptualizes resilience to hybrid threats as a politically mediated process rather than purely a matter of institutional capacity-building. To examine how policy frameworks and political rhetoric interact to shape resilience, it traces Georgia’s security culture in the aftermath of the Russo-Georgian war. Through intertextual discourse analysis, the article cross-examines the institutional architecture of digital resilience, encompassing cybersecurity (systemic), media regulation (protective) and media literacy (empowerment) measures, with the government’s shifting rhetoric (2023–2025), while interview data provide contextual insights. The analysis reveals a hybrid security culture manifested in fragmented governance and discursive struggle over resilience. Although formal policy frameworks normatively align with the West and consistently identify Russia as the principal security threat, governmental rhetoric portrays the same Western actors as sources of foreign interference and prioritizes political autonomy over cooperation while still invoking commitments to the constitutionally enshrined Euro-Atlantic trajectory. This dichotomy between institutional design and political discourse results in strategic ambiguity. It suggests that in hybrid regimes formal frameworks may function symbolically to signal external alignment, while practice is determined by short-term political calculations and discretionary authority, leaving institutions and societies vulnerable to evolving forms of foreign interference.

articles.title: Genital Modifications and Moral Boundary-making: Medical Perspectives on FGM/C versus FGCS in Belgium and the Netherlands
articles.authors: Hannelore Van Bavel
articles.abstract: This chapter investigates how medical professionals who perform female genital cosmetic surgery (FGCS) in Belgium and the Netherlands perceive and negotiate the boundary between FGCS and female genital mutilation (FGM). It draws on in-depth qualitative interviews conducted with 11 medical professionals between March 2024 and August 2025, as part of a broader study of genital self-image, motivations for FGCS, and clinical responses. FGM is criminalised in both countries, whereas FGCS is not, even though some procedures classified as FGCS technically fall within the legal and policy definitions of FGM. In 2008, professional societies in the Netherlands attempted to clarify the distinction but ultimately failed to establish concrete criteria, relying instead on what they regarded as a self-evident difference. Healthcare professionals are therefore left to interpret and navigate this boundary in practice, drawing on their own professional knowledge, moral reasoning, and sociocultural understandings. This ambiguity raises important questions about how medical professionals distinguish between FGM and FGCS in their everyday practice. Do they regard the two as fundamentally different, or do they recognise areas of overlap, and on what grounds? What forms of reasoning, knowledge, and professional or cultural frameworks inform their distinctions? To what extent do their views reflect, reproduce, or resist broader social, cultural, and political discourses?

articles.title: Genital Modifications and Moral Boundary-making: Medical Perspectives on FGM/C versus FGCS in Belgium and the Netherlands
articles.authors: Hannelore Van Bavel
articles.abstract: This chapter investigates how medical professionals who perform female genital cosmetic surgery (FGCS) in Belgium and the Netherlands perceive and negotiate the boundary between FGCS and female genital mutilation (FGM).
